items.text: משנת הפתיחה: רשימת הכריתות
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: List of 36 kareitot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates the 36 transgressions punishable by karet, including sexual offenses, idolatry, desecration of sacred items, and violations of festivals. It concludes by noting that Passover and circumcision are positive commandments (not kareitot).
items.desc: המשנה פותחת במניין שלושים ושש כריתות בתורה, ומפרטת את העבירות החמורות הכוללות עריות, עבודה זרה, חילול שבת, טומאת מקדש, אכילת קודשים, ועוד.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating there are 36 kareitot in the Torah and lists the first group of sexual offenses punishable by karet.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת במניין שלושים ושש כריתות ומפרטת את רשימת העבירות החייבות כרת.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah continues listing additional kareitot: blasphemy, idolatry, Molech worship, sorcery, Shabbat desecration, eating sacred food while impure, entering the Temple impure, eating forbidden fats and blood, leftover and piggul offerings, and slaughtering or offering outside the Temple.

The Mishnah concludes the list with eating chametz on Passover, eating and working on Yom Kippur, compounding anointing oil or incense, and anointing with sacred oil, then notes that Passover and circumcision are positive commandments (not kareitot).

The Mishnah states that for these offenses one is liable to karet for intentional violation, a חטאת (sin-offering) for unintentional violation, and an אשם תלוי (suspensive guilt-offering) for cases of uncertain sin, except for one who defiles the Temple or its sancta, which follows a sliding-scale offering — the words of Rabbi Meir.

The Sages add that the blasphemer is also excluded from the fixed sin-offering, citing the verse 'תּוֹרָה אַחַת יִהְיֶה לָכֶם לָעֹשֶׂה בִּשְׁגָגָה' (one law shall be for you for one who acts unintentionally), implying that the blasphemer, who performs no physical action, is excluded.

items.text: המשך המשנה: דיני חיובים ופטורין
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's ruling on liability
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states that for these transgressions, one is liable to karet for intentional violation, a chatat for unintentional violation, and an asham talui for cases of uncertainty, except for one who defiles the Temple or its sancta, which follows a sliding-scale offering.
items.desc: המשנה ממשיכה ומפרטת את החיובים על זדון כרת, שגגת חטאת, ולא הודע אשם תלוי, למעט המטמא מקדש וקדשיו שהוא בעולה ויורד, כדברי רבי מאיר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir rules that for these thirty-six transgressions, one is liable to karet (excision) for intentional violation, a chatat (sin-offering) for unintentional violation, and an asham talui (suspensive guilt-offering) for cases of uncertainty, except for one who defiles the Temple or its sancta, which follows a sliding-scale offering.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בקביעת החיובים על עבירות אלו: על זדון כרת, על שגגת חטאת, ועל לא הודע אשם תלוי, למעט מטמא מקדש וקדשיו שהוא בעולה ויורד, דברי רבי מאיר.

items.text: דברי חכמים: חריגת המגדף
items.text_en: Sages' objection: Blasphemer excluded
items.desc_en: The Sages argue that the blasphemer is also excluded from the asham talui, because blasphemy involves no physical action, as derived from the verse 'One Torah shall be for you for one who acts unintentionally'—excluding one who does no act.
items.desc: חכמים חולקים על רבי מאיר ומוסיפים שהמגדף אינו בכלל עולה ויורד, משום שאינו עושה מעשה, כפי שנאמר בתורה.

sub.desc_en: The Sages object that the blasphemer is also excluded from the asham talui category, because blasphemy involves no physical action, as derived from the verse 'תּוֹרָה אַחַת יִהְיֶה לָכֶם לָעֹשֶׂה בִּשְׁגָגָה' (One Torah shall be for you for one who acts unintentionally).
sub.desc: חכמים חולקים על רבי מאיר ומוסיפים שגם המגדף פטור מקרבן חטאת על שגגתו, משום שאינו עושה מעשה.

items.text: שאלת המניינים במשנה הראשונה
items.text_en: Opening question: Why the count?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies a number for the thirty-six kareitot. Rabbi Yochanan answers that it teaches liability for each transgression if done in one lapse of awareness. The same reasoning applies to the thirty-nine melakhot.
items.desc: הגמרא פותחת בשאלה: לשם מה נמנו חטאות הפנימיות? רבי יוחנן עונה: כדי לחייב על כל אחת ואחת אם עשאן כולן בהעלם אחד. הגמרא מביאה דוגמה דומה ממשנת אבות מלאכות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies a number for the thirty-six kareitot.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מה הצורך במניין החטאות הפנימיות במשנה?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that the tally teaches liability for each transgression if done in one lapse of awareness.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מה הצורך במניין החטאות הפנימיות במשנה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that the same reasoning applies to the thirty-nine melakhot, where the tally also teaches liability for each labor if done in one lapse of awareness.

items.text: מניין ארבעה מחוסרי כפרה
items.text_en: Count of four mechusrei kaparah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies four mechusrei kaparah. It answers: to exclude Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who says there are five, including a convert until blood is sprinkled for him.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת על מניין ארבעה מחוסרי כפרה, ומסבירה שהוא בא להוציא מדעת רבי אליעזר בן יעקב הסובר שגר מחוסר כפרה עד שיזרק דם עליו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies the count of four mechusrei kaparah (those lacking atonement).
The Gemara answers that the count excludes the opinion of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב (Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov), who holds there are five, including a convert until blood is sprinkled for him.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהמניין בא להוציא מדעת רבי אליעזר בן יעקב הסובר שגר מחוסר כפרה עד שיזרק דם עליו, ולכן תנא ארבעה.

items.text: מניין ארבעה מביאין על הזדון כשוגג
items.text_en: Count of four who bring for intentional as unwitting
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies four who bring a korban for intentional sin as if unwitting. It answers: to exclude Rabbi Shimon, who says the oath of deposit is not subject to such a korban for intentional sin.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת על מניין ארבעה המביאים על הזדון כשוגג, ומסבירה שהוא בא להוציא מדעת רבי שמעון הסובר ששבועת הפקדון לא ניתנה זדונה לכפרה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies the number 'four' for those who bring a korban for intentional sin as if unwitting.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה שמונה ארבעה מביאים על הזדון כשוגג: למה צריך למנות מספרם?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the number excludes Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the oath of deposit (שבועת הפקדון) is not subject to a korban for intentional sin.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהמניין בא להוציא מדעת רבי שמעון הסובר ששבועת הפקדון לא ניתנה זדונה לכפרה, ולכן לא נמנית במשנה.

items.text: Count of five who bring one korban for many sins
items.text_en: Count of five who bring one korban for many sins
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies five who bring one korban for many sins. It answers: because the Mishnah wants to teach the case of a nazir who contracts many impurities. The Gemara explains that this case follows Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that nazirite purity takes effect from the seventh day, unlike Rabbi who holds it takes effect from the eighth day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies the number five for those who bring one korban for many sins.
The Gemara answers that the number is needed to introduce the case of a nazir who contracts many impurities, which follows Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's view.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah followed Rabbi's view, the nazir's impurity would be a single extended impurity, not multiple separate ones.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must follow Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that nazirite purity takes effect from the seventh day.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda regarding a nazir: Rabbi says the verse 'he shall consecrate his head on that day' refers to the day of bringing his korban, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says it refers to the day of his shaving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda is about.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi interprets the verse 'he shall consecrate his head on that day' as the day of bringing his korban, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says it is the day of his shaving.

items.text: מניין חמישה מביאין קרבן עולה ויורד
items.text_en: Count of five who bring a sliding-scale korban
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies five who bring a korban oleh veyored. It answers: because the Mishnah teaches that a nasi is similar to them, and the count excludes Rabbi Eliezer, who says a nasi brings a goat.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת על מניין חמישה המביאים קרבן עולה ויורד, ומסבירה שהוא בא להוציא מדעת רבי אליעזר הסובר שנשיא מביא שעיר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies the number five for those who bring a korban oleh veyored (sliding-scale offering).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע המשנה מפרטת מניין חמישה המביאים קרבן עולה ויורד, הרי די היה לומר 'חמישה מביאין'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the number is needed because the Mishnah's continuation teaches that a nasi (king) is similar to them, and the count excludes Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: המניין בא להוציא מדעת רבי אליעזר, הסובר שנשיא מביא שעיר, ולכן המשנה מדגישה שחמישה בלבד מביאים קרבן עולה ויורד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the count of five excludes Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that a nasi brings a goat (not a sliding-scale offering).
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: המניין בא להוציא מדעת רבי אליעזר, הסובר שנשיא מביא שעיר, ולכן המשנה מדגישה שחמישה בלבד מביאים קרבן עולה ויורד.

items.text: מניין ארבעה אבות נזיקין
items.text_en: Count of four avot nezikin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies four avot nezikin. It answers: to exclude Rabbi Oshaya, who says there are thirteen, and to exclude Rabbi Chiyya, who says there are twenty-four, and to exclude the categories of masor and mefagel.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת על מניין ארבעה אבות נזיקין, ומסבירה שהוא בא להוציא מדעות רבי אושעיא ורבי חייא הסוברים שיש יותר אבות. לבסוף, הגמרא מביאה את דעת רבי חייא להוציא מסור ומפגל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies the count of four avot nezikin.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מה הצורך במניין 'ארבעה אבות נזיקין' במשנה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the count excludes Rabbi Oshaya's thirteen, Rabbi Chiyya's twenty-four, and the categories of masor and mefagel.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: המניין בא להוציא מדעת רבי אושעיא הסובר שיש שלושה עשר אבות נזיקין.

items.text: לימוד החילוק מכרת האחות
items.text_en: Derivation of liability for each transgression
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's explanation: one might think that doing all transgressions in one lapse incurs only one liability. Rabbi Yochanan answers that the verse 'karet' regarding a sister comes to divide liability for each transgression.
items.desc: הגמרא חוזרת לטעם המניין במשנה הראשונה, ומקשה: מדוע לא נאמר שפטור לגמרי? רבי יוחנן עונה שכרת האחות באה לחלק. הגמרא מביאה את דברי רבי יוחנן שהפסוק 'כי כל אשר יעשה' מלמד על חיוב על כל אחת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement that if one performed all transgressions in one lapse of awareness, one is liable for each one.
sub.desc: מר מציג את עיקרון המשנה: העושה כל העריות בהעלם אחד חייב על כל אחת ואחת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: one might think that performing all transgressions in one lapse incurs only one liability, not separate ones.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע לא נאמר שהעושה את כולן בהעלם אחד פטור לגמרי, או לכל הפחות חייב רק אחת?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that the verse specifying 'karet' regarding a sister comes to divide liability for each transgression.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן עונה שכרת האחות באה לחלק, ללמד שחייב על כל עברה בפני עצמה.

items.text: קושיית רב ביבי ותשובתו
items.text_en: Rav Bivi's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Bivi bar Abaye objects: perhaps the verse about a sister teaches only liability for that specific sin, not for all. The Gemara responds with a principle: anything that was included in a general rule and then specified teaches about the entire general rule. Rav Bivi then applies this principle to limit the analogy to arayot that have no permit during the lifetime of the one who forbids them.
items.desc: רב ביבי מקשה: אולי כרת האחות מלמדת רק על עצמה ולא על הכלל? הגמרא מביאה את הכלל 'כל דבר שהיה בכלל ויצא מן הכלל ללמד' ומסבירה שההיקש מלמד על כל העריות. רב ביבי עונה שההיקש מוציא את אשת איש.

sub.desc_en: Rav Bivi bar Abaye objects that the verse specifying a sister might only impose liability for that one sin, not for all arayot (forbidden relations) committed in one lapse of awareness.
sub.desc: רב ביבי מקשה: אולי כרת האחות מלמדת רק על עצמה, ולא על שאר העריות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara counters that Rav Bivi should accept the principle that anything included in a general rule and then specified teaches about the entire general rule, citing the example of peace-offerings (שלמים) that exclude Temple-maintenance offerings.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רב ביבי מהברייתא האומרת שיוצא מן הכלל ללמד על הכלל.

sub.text_en: Rav Bivi's application of the principle
sub.desc_en: Rav Bivi applies the principle to limit the analogy: just as a sister has no permit during the lifetime of the one who forbids her, so too only arayot without such a permit are included, excluding a married woman who has a permit during her husband's lifetime.
sub.desc: רב ביבי עונה: גם כאן יש מיעוט, כמו ששם יצאו קדשי בדק הבית.

items.text: תשובת רבי יונה או רב הונא
items.text_en: Alternative derivation: all arayot are analogous to sister
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona (or Rav Huna bar Yehoshua) says the verse 'for whoever does any of these abominations' teaches that all arayot are compared to a sister: just as one is liable for each act with a sister, so too for each act with any ervah.
items.desc: רבי יונה (או רב הונא בר יהושע) עונה שהפסוק 'כי כל אשר יעשה' מקיש את כל העריות לאחות, ולכן כולן חייבות בפני עצמן.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yona / Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yona (or Rav Huna bar Yehoshua) derives from the verse 'כי כל אשר יעשה מכל התועבות' that all arayot are compared to a sister, so one is liable for each act with any ervah individually.
sub.desc: רבי יונה (או רב הונא בר יהושע) עונה שהפסוק 'כי כל אשר יעשה' מקיש את כל העריות לאחות, ולכן כולן חייבות בפני עצמן.

items.text: שיטת רבי יצחק ומקור החילוק
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's view and alternative source for division
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak holds that the karet for a sister comes to teach that it is punished by karet, not lashes. For division, he derives from the verse about a niddah. The Rabbis use the sister verse for division among different types of sisters. The Gemara concludes with a discussion of the end of the verse.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה את שיטת רבי יצחק הסובר שכרת האחות באה לדון אותה בכרת ולא במלקות, ומקור החילוק הוא מפסוק 'ואל אשה בנדת טומאתה'. הגמרא דנה במקור החילוק לאחות שהיא אחות אב ואם, ומביאה את הפסוק 'ערות אחותו גלה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Yitzchak's view that the karet for a sister was singled out to teach that it is punished by karet, not lashes.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציגה את שיטת רבי יצחק הסובר שחייבי כריתות היו בכלל, וכרת האחות באה לדון אותה בכרת ולא במלקות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Yitzchak derive the principle of division (liability for each transgression)?
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מניין לרבי יצחק מקור לחלק בין אחות לאחיות אחרות?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yitzchak derives division from the verse about a niddah (menstruating woman).
The Gemara asks: Should the Rabbis also derive division from the same verse about a niddah?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והלא גם רבנן יכולים ללמוד חילוק מאותו פסוק?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: Yes, indeed they do.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והלא גם רבנן יכולים ללמוד חילוק מאותו פסוק?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For what purpose does the karet for a sister come, according to the Rabbis?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והלא גם רבנן יכולים ללמוד חילוק מאותו פסוק?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: The Rabbis require it to divide liability for one's sister, one's father's sister, and one's mother's sister.
The Gemara objects: Why is division needed for these? They are separate names and separate bodies.

The Gemara resolves: Rather, the verse divides liability for one's sister who is also one's father's sister and one's mother's sister (i.e., a single act with a relative who falls under multiple categories).
The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Yitzchak derive this matter (division for a sister who is also a father's sister and mother's sister)?
The Gemara answers: He derives it from the latter clause of the verse: 'He has uncovered his sister's nakedness.'
The Gemara asks: What do the Rabbis do with the mention of 'his sister' in the latter clause of the verse?
The Gemara begins to answer: They require it... (the text is cut off).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: והלא גם רבנן יכולים ללמוד חילוק מאותו פסוק?

items.text: Introduction: The dispute about punishing from logical inference
items.text_en: Introduction: The dispute about punishing from logical inference
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle that one does not punish based on logical inference, citing the case of one's sister who is both a paternal and maternal sister. Rabbi Yitzchak holds that one does punish from logical inference, or alternatively, he derives the punishment from the warning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle that one does not punish based on logical inference, citing the case of one's sister who is both a paternal and maternal sister.
Rabbi Yitzchak holds that one does punish from logical inference, or alternatively, he derives the punishment from the warning.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's principle: Dividing sin-offerings for separate prohibitions
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's principle: Dividing sin-offerings for separate prohibitions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Hoshaya states that wherever there are two prohibitions and one karet, the sin-offering is divided between them, as with anointing and compounding the anointing oil. The Gemara questions why the Torah wrote karet for one's sister, and explains the differing views of Rabbi Yitzchak and the Rabbis regarding the derivation of liability for a sister who is both a paternal and maternal sister.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Hoshaya states the principle that wherever there are two prohibitions and one karet, the sin-offering is divided between them, giving the example of compounding and applying the anointing oil.
The Gemara asks: Since the prohibitions are separate, why does the Torah write a separate karet for one's sister?

The Gemara explains that according to the Rabbis the verse teaches that punishment is not derived from an a fortiori inference, while according to Rabbi Yitzchak it comes to impose liability for a sister who is both a paternal and maternal sister.

The Gemara resolves that the Rabbis derive the halakha from the first 'his sister', while Rabbi Yitzchak holds that the first 'his sister' is the verse's normal style and derives the division from the second 'his sister' to divide liability for a sister who is both a paternal and maternal sister.

items.text: Support from the Mishnah: Compounding oil and incense
items.text_en: Support from the Mishnah: Compounding oil and incense
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a Mishnah listing those who compound the oil, compound the incense, and anoint with the anointing oil. The Gemara infers from the order that there is a division of sin-offerings between compounding oil and anointing, as they are separate prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites the Mishnah listing those who compound the oil, compound the incense, and anoint with the anointing oil.
The Gemara asks why the tanna placed the case of compounding incense between the two cases of anointing oil.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that just as incense is an independent prohibition with its own karet, so too compounding oil and anointing are each independent prohibitions.
The Gemara objects that if the tanna wanted to group the blendings together, he could have taught incense first, then oil, then anointing.
The Gemara resolves that the separation of the oil cases teaches that there is a division of sin-offerings between them, and concludes that this is proven.

items.text: The case of one who engages in male intercourse: Rabbi Yishmael vs. Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: The case of one who engages in male intercourse: Rabbi Yishmael vs. Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's enumeration of thirty-three sin-offerings, specifically regarding the case of one who engages in male intercourse. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Tanna counts males and includes both the active and passive participant, following Rabbi Yishmael who holds one liable for two. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction with the later case of the blasphemer, concluding that the beginning follows Rabbi Yishmael and the end follows Rabbi Akiva, and notes that for bestiality, even Rabbi Yishmael holds only one liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Tanna counts males or females, showing that either way the count of thirty-three is off.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the Tanna counts males and includes both the active and passive participant, following Rabbi Yishmael who holds one liable for two.
The Gemara objects that since the later case of the blasphemer follows Rabbi Akiva, the beginning should also follow Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Yishmael, citing Rabbi Avahu's distinction that Rabbi Akiva derives only one liability from the verse.
The Gemara resolves that the beginning follows Rabbi Yishmael and the end follows Rabbi Akiva, and questions why the same is not done for bestiality.
Abaye answers that for bestiality, even Rabbi Yishmael holds only one liability, because the verse is written regarding males.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's explanation: Thirty-three sin-offerings and three karet-offenses
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's explanation: Thirty-three sin-offerings and three karet-offenses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav states that the Tanna taught thirty-three sin-offerings and three karet-offenses, concluding with the karet-offenses. The Gemara supports this by noting that the Mishnah includes Passover and circumcision, which are positive commandments, and argues that they are listed to complete the count of karet-offenses, not to bring a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav states that the Tanna taught thirty-three sin-offerings and three karet-offenses, concluding with the karet-offenses.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah includes Passover and circumcision, which are positive commandments, in a list of karet-offenses.

The Gemara objects that if the intent were to bring a sacrifice for these positive commandments, it is impossible because all Torah violations are likened to idolatry, which is a 'sit and do not act' prohibition.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah lists Passover and circumcision only to complete the count of karet-offenses, not to bring a sacrifice.

items.text: Shabbat violation: Unintentional Shabbat with intentional labor
items.text_en: Shabbat violation: Unintentional Shabbat with intentional labor
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists only one sin-offering for Shabbat, when there are thirty-nine categories of labor. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Tanna refers to unintentional Shabbat with intentional labor, which incurs only one sin-offering. The Gemara notes that the Tanna prefers this case because it is not exempt from a sin-offering, unlike intentional Shabbat with unintentional labor which would require multiple sin-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists only one sin-offering for Shabbat, when there are thirty-nine categories of labor.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Tanna refers to unintentional Shabbat with intentional labor, which incurs only one sin-offering.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's explanation, interpreting the verse 'הנה' (these) as 'אחת' (one) for the case of unintentional Shabbat with intentional labor.
The Gemara objects that the Tanna could have taught the case of intentional Shabbat with unintentional labor, which would require thirty-nine sin-offerings.
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna prefers the case of unintentional Shabbat with intentional labor because it is not exempt from a sin-offering, unlike the alternative.

items.text: Idolatry: Unintentional idolatry with intentional service
items.text_en: Idolatry: Unintentional idolatry with intentional service
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the parallel case of idolatry, where the Mishnah lists unintentional idolatry with intentional service. It questions what constitutes unintentional idolatry, rejecting cases of mistaken identity or coercion, and concludes it refers to worship out of love or fear. The Gemara notes the dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding liability in such cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the parallel case of idolatry, citing the Mishnah's listing of unintentional idolatry with intentional service.
The Gemara asks what constitutes unintentional idolatry, rejecting the case of mistaken identity where one bows to an idol thinking it is a synagogue.
The Gemara rejects the case of bowing to a statue, distinguishing between accepting it as a deity (liable to stoning) and not (nothing).
The Gemara concludes that unintentional idolatry refers to worship performed out of love or fear of a person, not belief in the idol.
The Gemara notes that this explanation works for Abaye who holds one is liable, but questions what can be said for Rava who holds one is exempt.

items.text: Two answers for the case of one who is unaware of the prohibition of a specific idolatrous practice
items.text_en: Two answers for the case of one who is unaware of the prohibition of a specific idolatrous practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two explanations for a case where one is liable for only one sin-offering despite performing multiple idolatrous acts. Rav Pappa suggests a child captured among gentiles who knows idolatry is forbidden but not which practices. An alternative answer applies even to an adult who mistakenly interprets a verse to permit prostration to gods of silver and gold but not other types.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of one who says 'it is permitted' (אומר מותר), explaining that Rava's inquiry from Rav Nachman only addressed liability for one vs. two acts, not full exemption.
Rav Pappa answers that the case involves a child captured among gentiles who knows idolatry is forbidden but does not know that these specific practices are forbidden.
An alternative answer applies even to an adult who mistakenly interprets the verse 'לא תעשון אתי' to permit prostration to other types of gods but not those of silver and gold.

items.text: Rav Acha's statement: the Tanna lists by category name, not specific prohibitions
items.text_en: Rav Acha's statement: the Tanna lists by category name, not specific prohibitions
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika in the name of Rav Bibi says the Tanna lists by the category name of Shabbat and idolatry, not every specific prohibition. This is proven from the fact that the Tanna does not list 'one who has relations with his daughter from his rape victim,' which is a kareit but not explicitly written. The Gemara refines this: the Tanna lists only what is explicitly written, but then questions why 'bat ishto' (stepdaughter) and her descendants are not listed despite being written, concluding that the Tanna lists by category name.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika in the name of Rav Bibi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika in the name of Rav Bibi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika in the name of Rav Bibi states that the Tanna lists by the category name of Shabbat and idolatry, not every specific prohibition.
The Gemara asks: From where is this inferred? From the fact that the Tanna does not list 'one who has relations with his daughter from his rape victim,' which is a kareit but not explicitly written.
The Sages answer: The Tanna lists only what is explicitly written; what is not written he does not list.
The Gemara objects: But there is the case of one's wife's daughter, and the daughter of her daughter, and the daughter of her son, which are written explicitly, yet the Tanna does not list them.
The Gemara resolves: Rather, the Tanna lists by the category name of 'a woman and her daughter,' and similarly, he lists by the category name of Shabbat and idolatry.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Bibi from the case of 'ma'aleh' (offering limbs outside)
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Bibi from the case of 'ma'aleh' (offering limbs outside)
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Bibi's principle by citing a case where the Tanna lists 'ma'aleh' (offering limbs) as a separate kareit, even though it is a subcategory of idolatry. The Gemara explains that the Tanna lists Shabbat and idolatry by their category names because they are written as such in the Torah, but 'ma'aleh' is not written as a category name, so it is listed separately.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika raises a contradiction against Rav Bibi bar Abaye: if the Tanna teaches only general categories, why is the case of 'ma'aleh' (offering limbs outside) listed as a separate kareit?

Rav Bibi bar Abaye objects: if the Tanna lists categories, the mishna listing 36 kareitot should have 37, including 'ma'aleh' twice; but the Tanna could simply say he teaches the category of 'ha'ala'ah' (offering up).

The Gemara rejects the comparison: Shabbat and idolatry are taught in their own places (tractates Shabbat and Sanhedrin), so the Tanna can list them by category; but 'ha'ala'ah' (offering up) is not taught in its own place, so it cannot be treated as a category.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question: two kareitot and one lav (prohibition)
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question: two kareitot and one lav (prohibition)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about a case of two kareitot with one lav, such as slaughtering and offering outside. Rabbi Zeira explains that for one who derives the prohibition from a gezeirah shavah (verbal analogy), the warning (lav) is derived from the punishment, and for one who uses a hekesh (analogy), the verse equates slaughter to offering, so both require a warning before punishment.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about a case of two kareitot (extirpations) with one lav (prohibition), inquiring whether the warning (התראה) is required.
Rabbi Zeira responds that the case of slaughtering and offering outside involves two prohibitions (lavin), not one.
For one who derives the rule from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), the verse teaches that punishment (עונש) is not applied unless there was a prior warning (התראה).
For one who uses a היקש (analogy), the verse equates slaughter to offering, so both require a warning before punishment.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's second question: two deaths and one lav (Ov and Yid'oni)
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's second question: two deaths and one lav (Ov and Yid'oni)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about two death penalties with one lav, specifically Ov (necromancer) and Yid'oni (fortune teller). Rabbi Zeira refers to a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Tanna lists only Ba'al Ov in the list of kareitot because both Ov and Yid'oni are included in one lav, and the Torah opened with Ba'al Ov.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about two death penalties with one lav, specifically Ov (necromancer) and Yid'oni (fortune teller).
Rabbi Zeira refers to the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding why Yid'oni is listed in Sanhedrin but not in the list of kareitot.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Tanna lists only Ba'al Ov in the list of kareitot because both Ov and Yid'oni are included in one lav, and the Torah opened with Ba'al Ov.

items.text: Reish Lakish's opinion and the dispute with Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's opinion and the dispute with Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says Yid'oni is not listed because it lacks an action (ma'aseh). The Gemara explains why Reish Lakish does not accept Rabbi Yochanan's reason (they differ in death penalties). Rabbi Yochanan counters that a difference in death penalty does not constitute a difference in the lav. Rabbi Yochanan does not accept Reish Lakish's reason because the Tanna is Rabbi Akiva, who does not require an action. Reish Lakish responds that Rabbi Akiva does not require a major action (ma'aseh rabbah) but requires a minor action (ma'aseh zuta), and Ba'al Ov has the action of tensing his arms.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that Yid'oni is not listed among the kareitot because it lacks an action (מעשה).
The Gemara asks why Reish Lakish does not accept Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning that both are in one negative commandment.
Rav Pappa answers that Reish Lakish holds they differ in their death penalties, so they are separate negative commandments.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that a difference in death penalty does not constitute a difference in the negative commandment itself.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan does not accept Reish Lakish's reasoning that Yid'oni lacks an action.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds the Tanna of the kareitot list is Rabbi Akiva, who does not require an action for liability.
Reish Lakish responds that Rabbi Akiva does not require a major action (מעשה רבה) but does require a minor action (מעשה זוטא).
Reish Lakish specifies that Ba'al Ov involves the action of tensing his arms, and the blasphemer involves the action of moving his lips.

items.text: Challenge to Reish Lakish from the Mishnah on idolatry and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Reish Lakish from the Mishnah on idolatry and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Reish Lakish's view that tensing arms is a minor action even for the Rabbis, citing a Mishnah that lists actions for idolatry but not prostration, which Reish Lakish himself attributes to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yochanan says even the Rabbis consider bowing an action. This implies Reish Lakish holds that for the Rabbis, bowing is not an action, so how can tensing arms be one? The Gemara resolves that Reish Lakish meant tensing arms is a minor action only according to Rabbi Akiva, not the Rabbis. The Gemara then questions why the Tanna lists only 'megadef' (blasphemer) as lacking an action, and explains that the Tanna needed to teach that even though blasphemy's kareit is mentioned in the context of a sacrifice, one might think it requires an action like Rabbi Akiva, so it teaches that it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that tensing arms is a minor action even for the Rabbis, and challenges this by citing a Mishnah on idolatry that lists actions without prostration, questioning why prostration is included if it lacks action.
Reish Lakish attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Akiva, who does not require action, while Rabbi Yochanan says even the Rabbis consider bowing an action.
The Gemara resolves that Reish Lakish meant tensing arms is a minor action only according to Rabbi Akiva, not the Rabbis.
The Gemara questions why the Tanna lists only 'megadef' (blasphemer) as lacking action, and answers that the Tanna teaches one of two cases.

The Gemara explains that the Tanna needed to teach 'megadef' specifically, because one might think that since its kareit is mentioned in the context of a sacrifice, it requires an action like Rabbi Akiva's view, so the Tanna teaches that it does not.

items.text: Ulla and Rava's interpretation of Ba'al Ov, and Abaye's question
items.text_en: Ulla and Rava's interpretation of Ba'al Ov, and Abaye's question
items.desc_en: Ulla says Ba'al Ov in the list refers to one who burns incense to a demon. Rava objects that this is just idolatry, and instead says it refers to one who burns incense to a demon for the purpose of charming it. Abaye objects that this is a 'chover chaver' (sorcerer), and Rava responds that the Torah says such a 'chover chaver' is stoned. The Gemara then cites a baraisa that defines 'chover chaver' broadly, and Abaye adds a practical halacha about charming scorpions. The segment ends mid-sentence with a continuation of the discussion about Rabbi Yochanan's view on bowing as an action.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that the Ba'al Ov listed among the kareitot refers to one who burns incense to a demon.
Rava objects that if so, this is simply an idolater, which is already covered.
Rava instead explains that Ba'al Ov refers to one who burns incense to a demon for the purpose of charming it.
Abaye objects that this is simply a חובר חבר (sorcerer), which is a different prohibition.
Rava responds that the Torah says such a חובר חבר is punished by stoning, distinguishing it from the ordinary sorcerer.
The Gemara asks: then what is the ordinary חובר חבר that is only a לאו (prohibition)?
Rava cites a baraita that defines חובר חבר broadly, including even one who charms snakes and scorpions.
Abaye adds a practical halacha: one who charms a wasp or scorpion is forbidden, but if they are chasing him, it is permitted.
The Gemara begins a digression relating the discussion to Rabbi Yochanan's view that bowing is considered an action, but the segment cuts off mid-sentence.

items.text: Gemara's discussion: Is speech considered an action?
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion: Is speech considered an action?
items.desc_en: Rava argues that for a blasphemer (מגדף), speech is considered an action because it involves the heart, but generally, moving the lips is an action. Rabbi Zeira objects from the case of conspiring witnesses (עדים זוממין), where the verse says 'על פי' yet no action is involved. Rava distinguishes because witnesses involve sight (ראייה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether moving the lips is considered an action for a blasphemer (מגדף), and Rava answers that it is, because blasphemy involves the heart, but generally moving the lips is an action.
Rabbi Zeira objects from the case of conspiring witnesses (עדים זוממין), where the verse says 'על פי' yet no action is involved.
Rava distinguishes witnesses because they involve sight (ראייה), not speech as action.

items.text: Baraita: Dispute on liability for eating different types of חלב
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute on liability for eating different types of חלב
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma (Rabbi Yishmael) holds that one is liable for each type of חלב (ox, sheep, goat) separately, while the Sages say only one liability.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse and presents the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael holds one is liable separately for each type of חלב (forbidden fat), while the Sages hold only one liability.

items.text: Gemara's initial suggestion: Dispute over general prohibitions (לאו שבכללות)
items.text_en: Gemara's initial suggestion: Dispute over general prohibitions (לאו שבכללות)
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute is whether one is lashed for a general prohibition (לאו שבכללות). Rabbi Yishmael holds one is lashed, while the Sages hold one is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and the Sages is whether one is lashed for a general prohibition (לאו שבכללות).

items.text: Rejection: Rabbi Yishmael's actual reasoning from verse redundancy
items.text_en: Rejection: Rabbi Yishmael's actual reasoning from verse redundancy
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion, stating that Rabbi Yishmael actually holds that one is not lashed for a general prohibition, but here the verse is redundant, teaching division. The Sages explain the verse excludes חלב of wild animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion that Rabbi Yishmael holds one is lashed for a general prohibition, explaining that here the verse is redundant, teaching division (לחלק).
The Sages explain that the verse listing specific animals excludes חלב (forbidden fat) of wild animals (חיה).

items.text: Further refinement: Rabbi Yishmael's alternative proof from verse structure
items.text_en: Further refinement: Rabbi Yishmael's alternative proof from verse structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Sages' explanation and offers another proof for Rabbi Yishmael: if the verse had written 'כל חלב שור', one might learn from Sinai to include wild animals, so the extra words teach division. The Sages counter that the extra words exclude wild animals and birds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the Sages' previous explanation as insufficient, stating that the Rabbis spoke well to Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.text: Gemara's alternative reasoning for Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Gemara's alternative reasoning for Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative proof for Rabbi Yishmael: if the verse had written only 'כל חלב שור', the extra words 'כשב ועז' would be superfluous, teaching that they come to divide liability.

The Sages object that if the verse had written only 'כל חלב שור', one might derive a verbal analogy from Sinai to include wild animals and birds, so the extra words 'שור וכשב ועז' are needed to exclude them.
The Gemara again rejects the Sages' objection as insufficient, stating that the Rabbis spoke well to Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.text: Gemara's further alternative reasoning for Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Gemara's further alternative reasoning for Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers another alternative proof for Rabbi Yishmael: if the verse had written only 'כל חלב כשב' or 'כל חלב עז', the extra words 'שור וכשב ועז' would be superfluous, teaching that they come to divide liability.

items.text: Sages' counter-argument: The verse excludes wild animals and birds
items.text_en: Sages' counter-argument: The verse excludes wild animals and birds
items.desc_en: The Sages argue that if the verse had written 'כל חלב כשב', one might think only sheep fat is forbidden, and ox and goat are permitted. They then discuss why all three are needed, using the principle of learning from multiple cases (צריכי) to prevent erroneous inferences from each animal's unique features.

sub.desc_en: The Sages argue that if the verse had written only 'כל חלב כשב' (all fat of a sheep), one might think only sheep fat is forbidden, and ox and goat are permitted, because a sheep has an increased obligation regarding its tail (אליה).
Rabbi Chananya's teaching is cited: why does the verse list the sacrificial portions (אימורים) for a firstborn ox, sheep, and goat separately, as written in Numbers 18:17.
The repetitions are necessary: if only ox were written, one might think sheep and goat are not derived from it, because an ox has increased wine libations (נסכים).
If only sheep were written, one might think ox and goat are not derived, because a sheep has an increased obligation regarding its tail (אליה).
If only goat were written, one might think ox and sheep are not derived, because a goat has increased applicability regarding idol worship (עבודה זרה).

Since one case cannot be derived from another, perhaps two cases could be written and the third derived; but deriving ox from sheep and goat is refuted because sheep and goat are suitable for the Paschal offering (פסח).
If sheep were omitted and derived from ox and goat, that is refuted because ox and goat have increased applicability regarding idol worship (עבודה זרה).

If goat were omitted and derived from ox and sheep, that is refuted because ox and sheep each have a unique aspect of increased applicability (צד ריבוי). Therefore, all three cases are necessary and cannot be derived from each other.

items.text: Final resolution: Dispute over learning a negative command from a negative command (לאו מלאו)
items.text_en: Final resolution: Dispute over learning a negative command from a negative command (לאו מלאו)
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the dispute is about whether one can learn a negative command (לאו) from another negative command (לאו) that is linked to a קרת (cut-off) penalty. Rabbi Yishmael holds that one can learn division from the קרת, while the Sages hold that one cannot learn a לאו from a קרת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous objections and restates Rabbi Yishmael's original position that the extra words 'שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז' come to divide liability for each type.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the extra words come to permit the fat of wild animals, not to divide liability.
The Gemara answers that the verse is written in the context of consecrated animals, and a matter is learned from its context, so wild animals are not included.
The Gemara questions whether the Sages disagree with the principle that a matter is learned from its context.
The Gemara answers that everyone agrees on that principle; the dispute is about something else.

The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yishmael holds that one can learn a negative command (לאו) from another negative command (לאו) that is linked to a קרת (cut-off) penalty, while the Sages hold that one cannot learn a לאו from a קרת.

items.text: Alternative explanation: The Sages' reasoning regarding the tail (אליה) of non-sacred animals
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: The Sages' reasoning regarding the tail (אליה) of non-sacred animals
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is given: the Sages hold that the extra words 'שור וכשב ועז' come to permit the tail (אליה) of non-sacred animals, which is otherwise forbidden. Rabbi Yishmael counters that if so, the verse should have written only 'שור וכשב', and 'עז' is extra, teaching division.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation for the Sages' position: the verse comes to permit the tail (אליה) of non-sacred animals, as Rav Mari told Rav Zevid that a common element among all three is required, and none exists.
The Gemara concludes that according to this view, the extra words come to permit the tail (אליה) of non-sacred animals.

Rabbi Yishmael argues that if the verse intended only to permit the tail, it should have listed only 'שור וכשב' (ox and sheep); the inclusion of 'עז' (goat) teaches division, imposing separate liability for each species.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina: Rabbi Yishmael concedes regarding a single sin-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina: Rabbi Yishmael concedes regarding a single sin-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that Rabbi Yishmael agrees that for the purpose of bringing a sin-offering, one brings only one, because the prohibitions are not analogous to those of forbidden relations (עריות).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that Rabbi Yishmael concedes that for a sin-offering one brings only one, because the prohibitions are not analogous to those of forbidden relations (עריות).

items.text: Baraita: Liability for multiple sins in one lapse of awareness
items.text_en: Baraita: Liability for multiple sins in one lapse of awareness
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one eats חלב and חלב in two separate lapses, he is liable for two; if he eats two types in one lapse, he is also liable for two.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verses 'ועשה אחת' and 'ועשה הנה' that one is liable separately for each sin, whether eating the same forbidden fat in two lapses or two different forbidden fats in one lapse.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Cases of multiple liabilities in one lapse
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Cases of multiple liabilities in one lapse
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda why two names in one lapse incur two liabilities, since lapses are needed to divide. Rav Chisda answers it is a case of eating חלב of נותר (remnant), which incurs both נותר and חלב. Rav Sheshet suggests it is a case of חלב of consecrated animals, following Rabbi Yehuda. The Westerners (מערבא) suggest it is a case of חלב of ox, sheep, and goat, following Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.text: Rami bar Chama's question to Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question to Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda why two names in one lapse incur two liabilities, since lapses are needed to divide.
Rav Chisda answers that it is a case of eating חלב of נותר (remnant), which incurs both נותר and חלב, but Rami bar Chama objects that it should also incur a liability for קודש (consecrated food).
Rav Sheshet suggests it is a case of חלב of consecrated animals, following Rabbi Yehuda who holds one is liable for three lashes.
The Westerners (מערבא) suggest it is a case of חלב of ox, sheep, and goat, following Rabbi Yishmael who holds one is liable for three lashes.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction with Reish Lakish's answer
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction with Reish Lakish's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility of explaining the Mishnah according to Rabbi Yishmael or Rabbi Yehuda, and instead presents Reish Lakish's answer in the name of Bar Tauteini: the case involves eating in two dishes, according to Rabbi Yehoshua who holds that dishes divide the liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility of explaining the Mishnah according to Rabbi Yishmael, citing Rabbi Chanina that Rabbi Yishmael would also require only one sin-offering.
The Gemara also rejects explaining the Mishnah according to Rabbi Yehuda, citing Rabbi Eliezer that Rabbi Yehuda would also require only one sin-offering.

sub.text: Reish Lakish in the name of Bar Tauteini
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Bar Tauteini
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish resolves the contradiction by stating the Mishnah deals with eating in two dishes, according to Rabbi Yehoshua who holds that dishes divide liability.

items.text: The Mishnah's ruling on eating forbidden fat
items.text_en: The Mishnah's ruling on eating forbidden fat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who eats chelev of neveilah receives two sets of lashes, and chelev of consecrated animals receives two lashes; Rabbi Yehuda says three for consecrated chelev.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: one who eats chelev of neveilah receives two sets of lashes, chelev of consecrated animals receives two lashes, and Rabbi Yehuda says three for consecrated chelev.

items.text: The Rabbis' reasoning for two lashes on consecrated chelev
items.text_en: The Rabbis' reasoning for two lashes on consecrated chelev
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi asks Rava: for Rabbi Yehuda, three verses provide three prohibitions, but what is the Rabbis' reasoning? The Gemara explains that the Rabbis consider the verse 'chukat olam' as referring to consecrated items and 'all chelev of ox' as referring to non-consecrated items, and both are necessary to teach that each category independently prohibits its fat.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi asks Rava: for Rabbi Yehuda, three verses provide three prohibitions, but what is the Rabbis' reasoning for only two lashes?

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis consider the verse 'chukat olam' as referring to consecrated items and 'all chelev of ox' as referring to non-consecrated items, and both are necessary.
The Gemara explains that if only the verse for consecrated items were written, one might think non-consecrated items are permitted, so the verse 'all chelev of ox' was needed.

sub.text: Gemara's further elaboration of the necessity
sub.text_en: Gemara's further elaboration of the necessity
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if only the verse for non-consecrated items were written, one might think consecrated items' fat is permitted since their meat is permitted, so both verses are necessary.

items.text: Dispute over learning a law from its context and from a negative commandment
items.text_en: Dispute over learning a law from its context and from a negative commandment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the verse 'chelev of ox' is written in the context of consecrated items, while the Rabbis disagree. The Gemara clarifies that all agree on the principle of 'davar halamed me'inyano' (a law learned from its context), but they dispute whether one can learn a negative commandment from another negative commandment and from a karet penalty.

sub.text: Gemara's statement of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's statement of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yehuda holds the verse 'chelev of ox' is written in the context of consecrated items.
The Gemara asks: Does this imply that the Rabbis reject the principle of 'davar halamed me'inyano' (a law learned from its context)?
The Gemara resolves that all agree on the principle of context, but they dispute whether one can learn a negative commandment from another negative commandment and from a karet penalty.

items.text: The hekesh between chelev and blood
items.text_en: The hekesh between chelev and blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the verse 'all chelev and all blood you shall not eat' which Rabbi Yehuda uses to teach that blood also receives two lashes, and the Rabbis use to teach that blood and its flesh combine for the measure of an olive's bulk. The Gemara explains the necessity of the hekesh for various details, including the exclusion of blood of creeping things and the inclusion of snake blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yehuda, for what purpose does the verse 'all chelev and all blood you shall not eat' come, since he already derives the prohibition from another verse?
The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yehuda requires the verse for a hekesh (juxtaposition), as taught in a baraita: just as for chelev one is flogged twice, so too for blood one is flogged twice.
The baraita records the position of the Chachamim (Sages) that blood has only one prohibition.
The Gemara objects: why is chelev special that it receives two lashes without a hekesh, since blood also has two prohibitions written?
The Gemara revises: rather, the hekesh teaches that just as for chelev one is flogged three times, so too for blood one is flogged three times.
The Gemara objects: what is special about chelev that it receives three lashes, since blood also has two prohibitions plus the prohibition of zarut (non-priest partaking)?

The Gemara resolves: the hekesh is necessary because one might think that since blood is excluded from tum'ah (ritual impurity), it should also be excluded from zarut, so the hekesh teaches otherwise.
The Gemara asks: according to the Rabbis, for what purpose does the hekesh come?
The Gemara answers: the Rabbis require the hekesh for the teaching that just as chelev is discrete from its flesh, so too blood is discrete from its flesh and does not combine.
The baraita continues: exclude the blood of sheratzim (creeping animals), since their blood is not discrete from their flesh, so they combine.
The Gemara objects: is this halakha derived from here? It is derived from the verse 'and this is impure for you' which teaches that the blood of a sheretz and its flesh combine.

The Gemara resolves: without the hekesh, one might think the combination applies only to tum'ah (ritual impurity) but not to achilah (consumption), so the hekesh teaches that it applies to consumption as well.

items.text: Ravina's ruling on snake blood
items.text_en: Ravina's ruling on snake blood
items.desc_en: Ravina states that the blood and flesh of a snake combine for the measure of an olive's bulk, based on the hekesh that any creature whose blood is not distinct from its flesh combines.

sub.desc_en: Ravina rules that the blood and flesh of a snake combine for the measure of an olive's bulk, and the Gemara questions what this adds beyond the existing hekesh.

The Gemara explains that without Ravina's statement, one might have thought only creeping animals (שרצים) combine because they are included in טומאה (ritual impurity), but the hekesh teaches that any creature whose blood is not distinct from its flesh combines.

items.text: Rava's explanations of the three karets and five negative commandments for blood
items.text_en: Rava's explanations of the three karets and five negative commandments for blood
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the three karets mentioned regarding blood refer to blood of non-consecrated animals, consecrated animals, and tamtzit (blood that oozes after the main flow). The Gemara questions this for the Rabbis and even for Rabbi Yehuda, and suggests instead that one refers to blood of kisui (covering). Rava also explains the five negative commandments for blood.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the three mentions of karet for blood refer to blood of non-sacred animals, blood of sacrificial animals, and blood of exudate (tamtzit).
The Gemara notes that Rava's explanation works well for Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that blood of exudate incurs karet.
The Gemara objects: for the Rabbis (who do not hold that tamtzit incurs karet), and even for Rabbi Yehuda who derives karet for tamtzit from 'all blood', what is the third karet for?
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'all blood' that karet applies to blood of non-sacred animals and blood of exudate, not just sacrificial blood.
The Gemara resolves: rather, the three karets refer to blood of non-sacred animals, blood of sacrificial animals, and blood of covering (kisui).
Rava further explains the five negative commandments for blood: non-sacred animals, sacrificial animals, covering, limbs, and exudate.

items.text: Rabbi Ila's ruling on eating ma'aser grain, wine, and oil outside Jerusalem
items.text_en: Rabbi Ila's ruling on eating ma'aser grain, wine, and oil outside Jerusalem
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila states that one who eats ma'aser grain, wine, and oil outside Jerusalem receives three sets of lashes. The Gemara questions how this is possible given the principle that one is not lashed for a general negative commandment, and explains that the verses are superfluous and come to divide the prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: רבי אילא (Rabbi Ila) rules that one who eats second tithe of grain, wine, and oil outside Jerusalem receives three sets of lashes.
The Gemara objects that one is not flogged for a general negative commandment, yet the prohibition of eating second tithe outside Jerusalem is general.
The Gemara answers that this case is different because the verses are superfluous, allowing separate prohibitions.

The Gemara explains that the verse 'וְאָכַלְתָּ לִפְנֵי ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ' (Deut 14:23) already implies the prohibition outside Jerusalem, so the additional verse 'לֹא תוּכַל לֶאֱכֹל בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ' (Deut 12:17) comes to divide the prohibitions for each type of produce.

The Gemara concludes that without the superfluous verse, one might think the prohibition is only a positive commandment (עשה) with no lashes; therefore the extra verse establishes separate negative prohibitions.

items.text: Gemara's question on the superfluous verse
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the superfluous verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah wrote 'lo suchal' as a negative commandment, and why it specified 'ma'aser degancha' separately, concluding that it teaches a separate prohibition for each type of grain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah wrote 'lo suchal' as a negative commandment, and why it specified 'ma'aser degancha' separately, concluding that it teaches a separate prohibition for each type of grain.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's ruling and the derivation of three lashes
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's ruling and the derivation of three lashes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that one who eats lechem, kali, and karmel is liable for three lashes. The Gemara defends this against the principle of 'lav shebichlalot' by showing that each term is superfluous and cannot be derived from the others, thus each is a separate prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak rules that one who eats bread, parched grain, and fresh stalks before the omer is flogged with three sets of lashes, and the Gemara notes that this is exceptional because the verses are superfluous.
The Gemara suggests that the verse could have written only 'bread' and derived the other two from it, but refutes this because bread has an increased obligation with regard to חלה (dough offering).

The Gemara suggests writing only 'parched grain' and deriving the others from it, but refutes this because parched grain is in its unadulterated form and has an increased obligation with regard to meal offerings, unlike bread and fresh stalks.

The Gemara suggests writing only 'fresh stalks' and deriving the others from it, but refutes this because fresh stalks have not changed from their original state, and then proposes deriving one from the other two.

The Gemara considers omitting 'bread' and deriving it from parched grain and fresh stalks, but refutes this because those two are in their unadulterated form; it then considers omitting 'fresh stalks' and deriving it from bread and parched grain, but refutes this because those two have an increased obligation with regard to meal offerings.

Rabbi Yitzchak resolves that the verse could omit 'parched grain' and derive it from bread and fresh stalks, with each serving as a counterexample to the other's unique feature, proving that all three are superfluous and each is a separate prohibition.

items.text: Clarification of the verse's structure
items.text_en: Clarification of the verse's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the placement of 'kali' in the middle of the verse indicates that both lechem and karmel are liable through kali, meaning each is a separate prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: perhaps only the superfluous mention of parched grain (קָלִי) incurs a separate liability, while eating bread and fresh stalks together incurs only one set of lashes.

The Gemara rejects the challenge by noting that the verse places קָלִי (parched grain) in the middle, indicating that both bread and fresh stalks are each liable through the mention of parched grain, thus each is a separate prohibition.

items.text: Exhortations on the importance of gezeirah shavah
items.text_en: Exhortations on the importance of gezeirah shavah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai, Rabbi Simai, Abaye, and Rav Ashi each emphasize that gezeirah shavah is a fundamental principle of Torah, citing examples of piggul, notar, the daughter of an anus, and stoning for sorcery, all derived through gezeirah shavah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai exhorts that a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) should never be lightly regarded, citing that the prohibition of piggul is a fundamental Torah principle derived only through a verbal analogy.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Zavda bar Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Zavda bar Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Zavda bar Levi's teaching that the punishment of karet for piggul is derived via a verbal analogy from the verse about notar.

Rabbi Simai similarly exhorts that a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) should never be lightly regarded, noting that the prohibition of notar is a fundamental Torah principle derived only through a verbal analogy.
The Gemara explains the verbal analogy for notar: the word 'קֹדֶשׁ' (sacred) in Leviticus 19:8 is compared to the same word in Exodus 29:34, identifying the subject as notar.
Abaye adds that the prohibition against intercourse with one's daughter from a raped woman is a fundamental Torah principle derived only through a verbal analogy.

sub.text: Rava citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.desc_en: Rava, citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi, explains that the prohibition is derived via a verbal analogy of 'הֵנָּה' (they) and the punishment of burning via a verbal analogy of 'זִמָּה' (lewdness).
Rav Ashi adds that the list of those liable to stoning is a fundamental Torah principle derived only through a verbal analogy.

A baraita supports Rav Ashi's statement by deriving stoning for certain forbidden relations from the verbal analogy of 'דְּמֵיהֶם בָּם' (their blood shall be upon them) used for necromancers and sorcerers.

items.text: Laws of compounding anointing oil
items.text_en: Laws of compounding anointing oil
items.desc_en: A baraisa states that one who compounds anointing oil for study or public use is exempt, but for anointing is liable. The Gemara derives this from a gezeirah shavah with incense, and discusses the difference between oil and incense regarding partial amounts.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one who compounds the anointing oil for study or for public use is exempt, but for anointing is liable; one who anoints with it is exempt unless it is the oil made by Moses.
The Gemara derives the exemption for compounding oil for public use from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on 'מתכנתו' with incense, where the verse 'לא תעשו לכם' permits making it for the community.
The Gemara objects that by the same analogy, incense compounded in halves should be exempt, contradicting Rava's ruling that it is liable.
Rava distinguishes: for oil, the verse prohibits only making it like the original, so half is permitted; for incense, the verse prohibits any making, since it is offered in halves daily.

items.text: Discussion on the weights of anointing oil ingredients
items.text_en: Discussion on the weights of anointing oil ingredients
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the weights of the ingredients, questioning why cinnamon is brought in two halves, and discusses the concept of 'hechrea' (balancing) in weighing, concluding that God knows the exact balance.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the weights of the anointing oil ingredients and their total sum.
The Gemara questions why the baraita states the total, and raises the possibility that calamus might weigh like cinnamon, making the total two thousand.
The Gemara rejects the possibility by noting that the verse's wording 'half so much' applies only to cinnamon, not to calamus.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether weighing is done with a surplus or precisely; Abaye cites the verse 'בד בבד' and Rav Yehuda's statement that God knows the surpluses, implying there is a surplus.
Rav Yehuda explains that cinnamon is brought in two halves because each weighing requires a surplus, and God knows the exact surpluses.
Ravina explains that 'בד בבד' means one must not weigh one ingredient against another, but each must be weighed independently.

items.text: Dispute on the preparation of anointing oil
items.text_en: Dispute on the preparation of anointing oil
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei argue about how Moshe prepared the anointing oil: Rabbi Yehuda says he boiled the roots, while Rabbi Yosei says he infused the oil with the scent of the roots by boiling them in water and then skimming the oil.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that the anointing oil was prepared by cooking the roots in the oil.
Rabbi Yosei objects that the oil is insufficient to cook the roots, as they would absorb it all.
Rabbi Yosei explains the alternative method: boil the roots in water, float the oil on top to absorb the fragrance, then skim it off.
Rabbi Yehuda begins his response to Rabbi Yosei, but the text cuts off at the end of the segment.

items.text: Opening Gemara: The miracles of the anointing oil
items.text_en: Opening Gemara: The miracles of the anointing oil
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by noting that many miracles occurred with the anointing oil from beginning to end, starting with only twelve log and yet being sufficient for anointing the Tabernacle, its vessels, Aaron and his sons, and future high priests and kings, and it remains for the future, as the verse says 'this' (numerically twelve log).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by questioning whether only one miracle was performed with the anointing oil, and then enumerates the many miracles from its initial twelve log measure to its enduring existence for the future.

The Gemara cites the verse 'this shall be a sacred anointing oil to Me throughout your generations' and notes that the word 'zeh' has the numerical value of twelve, proving the original twelve log remained intact.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda's list of miracles and laws of anointing
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda's list of miracles and laws of anointing
items.desc_en: A baraita taught by the Sages, with Rabbi Yehuda stating that many miracles occurred with the anointing oil. It then lists that even a high priest who is the son of a high priest requires anointing, but a king who is the son of a king is not anointed, except in cases of dispute like Solomon, Joash, and Jehoahaz.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yehuda's statement that many miracles occurred with the anointing oil from its initial preparation to its end, detailing the initial twelve log and the absorption by the cauldron, roots, and fire, and that it sufficed for anointing the Tabernacle, its vessels, Aaron, and his sons during the seven days of inauguration.

The baraita continues by stating that High Priests and kings were anointed with this oil, that even a High Priest who is the son of a High Priest requires anointing, but a king who is the son of a king is not anointed, and it explains the exceptions of Solomon, Joash, and Jehoahaz due to disputes.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation for anointing high priest's son and king's son
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for anointing high priest's son and king's son
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a high priest's son requires anointing, deriving it from the verse 'the anointed priest under him from his sons'. It then asks for the source that a king's son is not anointed, with Rav Acha bar Yaakov citing the verse 'he and his sons' as an inheritance. It then explains that Solomon was anointed due to Adoniyah's dispute, and Rav Pappa derives from the verse 'in the midst of Israel' that anointing is needed only when there is no peace.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a high priest's son requires anointing.
The Gemara derives the requirement from the verse 'the anointed priest under him from his sons', showing that only an anointed son becomes high priest.
The Gemara asks for the source that a king's son is not anointed.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov cites the verse 'he and his sons' to show that kingship is an inheritance, so no anointing is needed for a king's son.
The Gemara asks why Solomon was anointed and how we know that a dispute requires anointing, rather than the king simply granting the kingship.
Rav Pappa derives from the verse 'in the midst of Israel' that anointing is needed only when there is no peace, explaining Solomon's anointing due to Adoniyah's dispute.

items.text: Baraita: Kings of David's house are anointed, but not kings of Israel
items.text_en: Baraita: Kings of David's house are anointed, but not kings of Israel
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Jehu was anointed only due to the dispute with Joram, and then clarifies that the rule is: kings of the house of David are anointed, but kings of Israel are not. The source is the verse 'Arise, anoint him, for this is he' – this one requires anointing, not another. The Gemara questions why Jehu was anointed with the sacred oil, and answers that it was with pure balsam oil.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that Jehu was anointed only due to the dispute with Joram.
The Gemara questions why the baraita gives this reason, since Jehu was a first king and should require anointing anyway.
The Gemara explains that the baraita is incomplete and actually teaches that kings of David's house are anointed, but kings of Israel are not; Jehu was anointed only due to the dispute.
The Gemara cites the verse 'Arise, anoint him, for this is he' to prove that only kings of David's house require anointing.
The Gemara questions how Jehu could be anointed with the sacred anointing oil due to a dispute, implying misuse of consecrated property.
Rav Pappa answers that Jehu was anointed with pure balsam oil, not the anointing oil, just as was done for Jehoahaz.

items.text: Gemara: Discussion on Jehoahaz and the identity of Shallum
items.text_en: Gemara: Discussion on Jehoahaz and the identity of Shallum
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the claim that Jehoiakim was older than Jehoahaz, citing the verse listing Josiah's sons. Rabbi Yochanan identifies Jehoahaz as both Zedekiah and Shallum. The Gemara resolves that Jehoiakim is older but called 'firstborn' because he was first to reign. It then discusses the order of kings and explains why Shallum is called third and fourth. A baraita explains that Shallum was named for his complete deeds, and his original name was Mattaniah, changed to Zedekiah by Nebuchadnezzar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Jehoiakim was actually older than Jehoahaz, citing the verse listing Josiah's sons and Rabbi Yochanan's identification of Jehoahaz with Zedekiah and Shallum.

The Gemara resolves that Jehoiakim was indeed older, and the term 'firstborn' refers to being first to reign; it also addresses the objection about appointing a younger son over an older one by citing Jehoram's case.
The Gemara explains why Shallum is called both third and fourth: third in birth order, fourth in the order of kings, listing the sequence of reigns.
A baraita explains that Shallum was named for his complete deeds and that his original name was Mattaniah, changed to Zedekiah by Nebuchadnezzar.
The baraita explains that Nebuchadnezzar named him Zedekiah, meaning God will justify the judgment if he rebels, citing the verse about his rebellion.

items.text: Gemara: Was the anointing oil still extant?
items.text_en: Gemara: Was the anointing oil still extant?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the anointing oil still existed, citing a baraita that when the ark was hidden, the jar of manna, the flask of anointing oil, Aaron's staff, and the chest sent by the Philistines were also hidden. It was King Josiah who hid them. Rabbi Elazar derives this through verbal analogies of 'there', 'generations', and 'charge'. Rav Pappa concludes that later anointing was with pure balsam oil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the anointing oil still existed in the days of Jehoahaz, citing a baraita that when the Ark was sequestered, the jar of manna, the flask of anointing oil, Aaron's staff, and the Philistines' chest were also sequestered.
The baraita lists the items sequestered with the Ark and identifies Josiah as the one who hid them, citing the verse about placing the Ark in the Temple.
Rabbi Elazar derives the placement of the manna with the Ark through a verbal analogy of 'there' (שם) from the verses about the Ark and the manna.
Rabbi Elazar derives the placement of the anointing oil with the Ark through a verbal analogy of 'generations' (דורות) from the verses about the manna and the oil.
Rabbi Elazar derives the placement of Aaron's staff with the Ark through a verbal analogy of 'charge' (משמרת) from the verses about the manna and the staff.
Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty by explaining that later anointing was performed with pure balsam oil, not the original anointing oil.

items.text: Baraita: Method of anointing kings and priests
items.text_en: Baraita: Method of anointing kings and priests
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that kings are anointed in the shape of a crown, and priests in the shape of a Greek 'chi'. There is a dispute between two baraitot: one says first pour oil on the head then between the eyelids, the other reverses the order. The Gemara explains this as a dispute between Tannaim: one holds pouring is superior (citing the verse), the other holds smearing is superior (because it was used for service vessels). The Gemara reconciles the verse 'he poured... and then anointed'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that kings are anointed in the shape of a crown, and priests in the shape of a Greek 'chi', as explained by Rav Menashya.
One baraita states that first one pours oil on the head, then places oil between the eyelids; another baraita reverses the order.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the two orders to a dispute between Tannaim: one holds that anointing (between the eyelids) is preferable, the other that pouring (on the head) is preferable, each with its own reasoning.
The Gemara raises an objection from the verse that says 'he poured' and then 'he anointed', and resolves that the pouring was for the sake of the anointing, thus the anointing is the primary act.

items.text: Baraita: The oil on Aaron's beard and the bat kol
items.text_en: Baraita: The oil on Aaron's beard and the bat kol
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the oil flowing down Aaron's beard like two pearl drops. Rav Kahana taught that when he would speak, they would rise and sit at the roots of his beard. Moses worried about misuse of the oil, but a bat kol assured him that just as dew has no misuse, so the oil on Aaron's beard has none. Aaron then worried, and a bat kol assured him that neither he nor Moses misused it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing how the oil on Aaron's head descended to his beard, forming two drops like pearls.
Rav Kahana adds that when Aaron would speak, the drops would rise and sit at the roots of his beard, preventing them from falling.
Moses expresses concern that he might have misused the anointing oil, which caused the extra drops.
A bat kol reassures Moses that just as dew has no misuse, so the oil on Aaron's beard has no misuse.
Aaron worries that although Moses did not misuse the oil, he himself might have.
A bat kol assures Aaron that just as Moses did not misuse the oil, neither did he.

items.text: Baraita: Anointing kings at a spring and omens
items.text_en: Baraita: Anointing kings at a spring and omens
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that kings are anointed only at a spring, so that their kingdom may be drawn out, as with Solomon at Gihon. Rav Ami then gives omens: to know if the year will be long, light a lamp during the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur; to know if a business venture will succeed, raise a chicken; to know if one will return from a journey, stand in a dark house.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that kings are anointed only at a spring, citing the anointing of Solomon at Gihon.
Rav Ami gives an omen: to know if one will live out the year, light a lamp during the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur and see if its light continues.
The Gemara adds another omen: to know if a business venture will succeed, raise a chicken; if it becomes fat and beautiful, the venture will succeed.
The Gemara gives a third omen: to know if one will return from a journey, stand in a dark house and see if one can see.

items.text: Aggadic advice on omens and Torah study
items.text_en: Aggadic advice on omens and Torah study
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the significance of omens, citing Abaye's advice to eat certain foods at the start of the year as a good omen. Rav Mesharshiya instructs his sons on the proper order of study and to focus on their teacher's face, and to review teachings over water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the idea that seeing a reflection of a reflection can indicate someone's return, but the Sages dismiss this as unreliable and potentially harmful.
