Abaye advises eating specific foods at the start of the year as a good omen, since omens are considered significant.
Rav Mesharshiya instructs his sons on the proper order of study, to focus on their teacher's face, and to review teachings over water for continuity.
Rav Mesharshiya adds advice on dwelling in humble places and eating simple food over luxurious alternatives.

items.text: Interpretation of Hannah's prayer: horn vs. flask
items.text_en: Interpretation of Hannah's prayer: horn vs. flask
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'Rama karni' (He raised my horn) rather than 'Rama paki' (He raised my flask), noting that David and Solomon, anointed with a horn, had enduring kingdoms, while Saul and Jehu, anointed from a flask, did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Hannah said 'רָמָה קַרְנִי (my horn is exalted)' rather than 'רָמָה פַּכִּי (my flask is exalted),' because David and Solomon, anointed from a horn, had enduring kingdoms, while Saul and Jehu, anointed from a flask, did not.

items.text: Mishnah: One who compounds the incense
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who compounds the incense
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who compounds the incense to teach or give to the community is exempt from punishment, but if done to smell it, he is liable. One who merely smells it is exempt from punishment but liable for me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of one who compounds the incense: exempt if for teaching or community, liable if for smelling, and one who merely smells is exempt from punishment but liable for me'ilah.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is there me'ilah for smell?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is there me'ilah for smell?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication of me'ilah for smell, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's statement that sound, sight, and smell have no me'ilah. It answers that me'ilah applies only before the smoke column rises, as after the mitzvah is performed, there is no me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether me'ilah applies to smell, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's statement that sound, sight, and smell have no me'ilah.
The Gemara answers that me'ilah applies only before the smoke column rises, as after the mitzvah is performed, there is no me'ilah.

items.text: Challenge from Terumat HaDeshen and Eglah Arufah
items.text_en: Challenge from Terumat HaDeshen and Eglah Arufah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that after a mitzvah is performed there is no me'ilah, citing Terumat HaDeshen and Eglah Arufah which require burial. It resolves that these are two verses that come as one, and therefore do not teach a general rule. The discussion includes the views of Rabbi Dosa and the principle of two verses that come as one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that after a mitzvah is performed there is no me'ilah, citing Terumat HaDeshen which requires burial and yet one may still commit me'ilah with it.
The Gemara answers that Terumat HaDeshen and the priestly garments are two verses that come as one, and therefore do not teach a general rule.
The Gemara objects that this answer works for the Rabbis, but what can be said according to Rabbi Dosa who holds a different view regarding the garments.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Dosa argues that the priestly garments are fit for an ordinary priest, and the verse 'והניחם שם' teaches that they may not be used on another Yom Kippur.
The Gemara provides an alternative answer: Terumat HaDeshen and Eglah Arufah are two verses that come as one, and therefore do not teach a general rule.

The Gemara concludes that even for those who hold that two verses that come as one do teach a general rule, here they certainly do not teach, because each verse contains a מיעוט (limitation) excluding other items.

items.text: Baraita: Ingredients of the incense
items.text_en: Baraita: Ingredients of the incense
items.desc_en: A baraita details the ingredients and weights of the incense, including the requirement that if honey is added it is invalidated, and if any ingredient is missing the one who compounds it is liable for death. Rabbi Shimon explains the purpose of certain ingredients.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the ingredients and weights of the incense, including Rabbi Natan's addition of Jordan balsam.
The baraita states that adding honey invalidates the incense, and omitting any ingredient incurs the death penalty.
Rabbi Shimon explains that צרי (balsam) is a resin, and that urine would be better for steeping the clove but is not brought into the Temple.

items.text: Support and challenge regarding the incense's sanctity
items.text_en: Support and challenge regarding the incense's sanctity
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's statement that all actions with the incense must be in the sanctuary. It then challenges with a baraita about consecrated property that includes items fit for communal offerings, suggesting incense is given to artisans as payment. Rabbi Oshaya and Rav Yosef offer resolutions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's statement that all actions with the incense must be in the sanctuary, citing the verse 'קֹדֶשׁ הִיא קֹדֶשׁ תִּהְיֶה לָכֶם'.

The Gemara challenges with a baraita about consecrated property that includes items fit for communal offerings, suggesting incense is given to artisans as payment, implying it is not entirely sanctified.
Rabbi Oshaya resolves that the baraita refers to the leftover incense (מוֹתַר הַקְּטֹרֶת) which is given to artisans as payment after being redeemed, not the incense itself.

Rav Yosef objects that the baraita about leftover incense does not include the phrase 'חוֹזְרִין וְלוֹקְחִין אוֹתָהּ מִתְּרוּמָה חֲדָשָׁה' (they go back and buy it from the new terumah), unlike other cases of leftover offerings.
Rav Yosef resolves that the baraita refers to one of the incense ingredients (סַמְמָנֵי הַקְּטֹרֶת) that is fit for communal offerings, not the incense itself.

items.text: Baraita: Amount of incense and its surplus
items.text_en: Baraita: Amount of incense and its surplus
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the incense was made in 368 maneh, 365 corresponding to the solar year, with three extra maneh for the High Priest's handful on Yom Kippur. The surplus was given to artisans as payment, as detailed in another baraita.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the incense was made in 368 maneh, 365 for the solar year, and three extra for the High Priest's handful on Yom Kippur, with the remainder given to artisans as payment.
A supporting baraita details the procedure for the surplus incense: it is set aside for artisan wages, redeemed against their funds, given to them, and then repurchased from the new chamber funds.

items.text: Baraita on leftover incense and the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages
items.text_en: Baraita on leftover incense and the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that leftover incense was prepared in halves once every sixty or seventy years, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that an individual who prepared it in halves is liable. The Sages say it was prepared daily in its proper measure and then brought in.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that leftover incense was blended in halves once every sixty or seventy years, and therefore an individual who blended it in halves is liable, per Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that he did not hear the same ruling for thirds or quarters, while the Sages say the incense was prepared daily in its proper measure and then brought in.

items.text: Support for Rava's statement on anointing oil prepared in halves
items.text_en: Support for Rava's statement on anointing oil prepared in halves
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita supports Rava, who said that one who prepared the anointing oil in halves is liable, based on the verse 'and the incense which you shall make' implying any amount, since it was offered in two halves daily.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita supports Rava, who said that one who prepared the anointing oil in halves is liable, based on the verse 'and the incense which you shall make' implying any amount, since it was offered in two halves daily.

items.text: Baraita on grinding and storing the incense, and the extra three maneh for Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Baraita on grinding and storing the incense, and the extra three maneh for Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: A baraita describes that the incense was ground twice a year, stored differently in summer and winter, and when grinding one says 'grind well'. Three extra maneh were used by the High Priest on Yom Kippur, ground extremely fine, as derived from the verse 'dakka'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing the practice of regrinding the incense twice a year, with different storage methods for summer and winter, and the formula recited while grinding.
The baraita continues by detailing the use of the extra three maneh of incense for the High Priest's handful on Yom Kippur, which was ground extra fine, as derived from the verse 'dakka'.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yochanan on speech and spices
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yochanan on speech and spices
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the practice of saying 'grind well' supports Rabbi Yochanan, who said that just as speech is bad for wine, so speech is good for spices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the practice of saying 'grind well' supports Rabbi Yochanan, who said that just as speech is bad for wine, so speech is good for spices.

items.text: Derivation of the eleven incense ingredients from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of the eleven incense ingredients from the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that eleven spices were told to Moses at Sinai. Rav Huna derives this from the verse, counting 'samim' twice, nataf, shechelet, chelbenah, and levonah zakhah. The Gemara then engages in a detailed hermeneutical analysis using the principle of כלל ופרט וכלל, addressing potential objections and alternative interpretations, including a teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael and a statement by Reish Lakish.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that eleven spices were told to Moses at Sinai.
Rav Huna derives the eleven spices from the verse by counting 'samim' twice, nataf, shechelet, chelbenah, and levonah zakhah.
The Gemara objects that the verse could be interpreted as a כלל ופרט וכלל (generalization-detail-generalization), limiting the ingredients to those similar to the specified ones.
The Gemara explains that all three details are necessary: nataf teaches tree spices, shechelet teaches ground spices, and galbanum is needed for itself.
The Gemara rejects the need for galbanum as a detail, since it is included for its own sake, and the generalization can be derived from 'take for you'.
The Gemara questions why the second 'samim' should not be two like the first, and answers that the verse order indicates it doubles the total.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches the same hermeneutical principle of כלל ופרט וכלל, supporting the Gemara's approach.
The baraita rejects the possibility that the second generalization and detail are like the first, insisting on the first version.
The Gemara clarifies the baraita's difficulty: the second 'samim' could be two like the first, but the verse order refutes this.
The Gemara explains the second difficulty: one might derive from levonah zakhah that an item with a pleasant scent but no smoke is included, which is rejected.
The Gemara answers that if levonah zakhah were meant as a detail, it would be written in the middle, but it is not.
The Gemara objects that placing levonah in the middle would make twelve spices, so it suggests writing galbanum at the end instead.
Reish Lakish resolves the issue by deriving from the word 'ketoret' itself that only items that produce smoke and rise are included.

items.text: Lesson from chelbenah: inclusion of sinners in a fast
items.text_en: Lesson from chelbenah: inclusion of sinners in a fast
items.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna quoting Rabbi Shimon Chasida teaches that any fast without sinners from Israel is not a fast, as chelbenah, which has a bad smell, was included among the incense spices. Abaye derives this from a verse in Isaiah.

sub.text: Rav Chana bar Bizna quoting Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna quoting Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna, citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida, teaches that any fast without sinners from Israel is not a fast, using the inclusion of foul-smelling chelbenah among the incense spices as proof.
Abaye offers an alternative derivation from the verse 'וַאֲגֻדָּתוֹ עַל אֶרֶץ יְסָדָהּ' (and His bundle on the earth) to support the same principle.

items.text: Baraita on anointing with sacred oil: exemption for animals, vessels, gentiles, and the dead
items.text_en: Baraita on anointing with sacred oil: exemption for animals, vessels, gentiles, and the dead
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who anoints an animal, vessels, gentiles, or the dead with the sacred oil is exempt. The Gemara questions why gentiles are exempt since they are 'adam', and answers with a verse that only Israel are called 'adam'. Further objections from other verses are addressed, and an alternative explanation is given based on the principle of 'kol she-yeshno be-sach'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who anoints an animal, vessels, gentiles, or the dead with the sacred oil is exempt, and the Gemara begins to question why gentiles are exempt since they are 'adam'.
The Gemara answers that only Israel are called 'adam' based on the verse 'וְאַתֵּן צֹאנִי צֹאן מַרְעִיתִי אָדָם אַתֶּם' (Ezekiel 34:31), excluding gentiles.
The Gemara objects with the verse 'וְנֶפֶשׁ אָדָם שִׁשָּׁה עָשָׂר אָלֶף' (Numbers 31:40) which refers to gentiles as 'adam', and the answer is that this term serves to exclude animals.
The Gemara objects with the verse about Nineveh (Jonah 4:11) where gentiles are called 'adam', and the answer is that this term also serves to exclude animals.

The Gemara offers an alternative explanation based on the principle taught before Rabbi Elazar: anyone included in the prohibition of anointing is also included in the prohibition of being anointed, and gentiles are not included in the former.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on anointing kings and priests, and the measure for liability
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on anointing kings and priests, and the measure for liability
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that one who anoints kings or priests is liable according to Rabbi Meir but exempt according to Rabbi Yehuda. The measure for liability is disputed: Rabbi Meir says any amount, Rabbi Yehuda says a kezayit. Rav Yosef explains their dispute regarding the measure and regarding the status of kings and priests as 'zarim'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who anoints animals, vessels, gentiles, or corpses is exempt, but anointing kings or priests is disputed: Rabbi Meir deems liable, Rabbi Yehuda exempts; the measure for liability is any amount (Rabbi Meir) or a kezayit (Rabbi Yehuda), with a clarification that Rabbi Yehuda's exemption applies only to kings and priests.

Rav Yosef explains that Rabbi Meir derives the measure for placing (נתינה) from the measure for anointing (סיכה), which is any amount, based on the verses 'על בשר אדם לא ייסך' and 'ואשר יתן ממנו על זר'.
Rav Yosef explains that Rabbi Yehuda derives the measure for placing from general giving (נתינה דעלמא), which is a kezayit, but agrees that anointing kings and priests is valid with any amount.
Rav Yosef explains the dispute regarding kings and priests: Rabbi Meir considers them 'zarim' (strangers) now, while Rabbi Yehuda requires that the person be a stranger from beginning to end.
Rav Ika notes that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda follow their respective reasoning, as taught in a baraita.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Bat Kohen who ate terumah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Bat Kohen who ate terumah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a bat kohen who married a Yisrael and ate terumah, stating she repays the principal but not the fifth, and her death is by burning. Rabbi Meir adds that if she married a disqualified person, she repays both principal and fifth and is executed by strangulation, while the Sages say both cases are the same as the first.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic case: a bat kohen who married an Israelite and ate terumah repays the principal but not the fifth, and her death is by burning.
Rabbi Meir adds that if she married a disqualified person, she repays both principal and fifth and is executed by strangulation.
The Sages say that in both cases she repays only the principal and her death is by burning.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages is specifically about the anointing oil and the changes we have learned, but regarding any other anointing, all agree it is the size of an olive.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages is specifically about the anointing oil and the changes we have learned, but regarding any other anointing, all agree it is the size of an olive.

items.text: Discussion on anointing oil prohibition
items.text_en: Discussion on anointing oil prohibition
items.desc_en: A baraita taught before Rabbi Elazar states that whoever is included in the prohibition of anointing is included in the prohibition of 'bal yisach' (not to be anointed). Rabbi Elazar approves. Then Rav Chananya teaches before Rava that a High Priest who takes anointing oil from his head and puts it on his innards is liable. Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi why this differs from a kohen who anoints with terumah oil, and Rav Ashi answers that terumah becomes desacralized once used, but anointing oil retains its sanctity.

sub.desc_en: A baraita taught before Rabbi Elazar states that whoever is included in the prohibition of anointing is included in the prohibition of 'bal yisach' (not to be anointed).
Rabbi Elazar approves, noting that the verse 'לֹא יִיסָךְ' can be read as 'לֹא יַסִּיךְ' (he shall not anoint).
Rav Chananya teaches before Rava that a High Priest who takes anointing oil from his head and puts it on his innards is liable, citing the verse 'עַל בְּשַׂר אָדָם לֹא יִיסָךְ'.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi why this differs from a kohen who anoints with terumah oil, where the beneficiary may use it without concern.

Rav Ashi answers that terumah becomes desacralized once used (as per 'וּמֵתוּ בוֹ כִּי יְחַלְּלֻהוּ'), but anointing oil retains its sanctity because the Torah calls it 'שֶׁמֶן מִשְׁחָה' even after application.

items.text: Exclusion of one who defiled the Temple from a suspended guilt-offering
items.text_en: Exclusion of one who defiled the Temple from a suspended guilt-offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is liable for certain transgressions except for one who defiled the Temple and its sanctities, who does not bring a suspended guilt-offering. The Gemara asks why not also exclude one for whom Yom Kippur has passed. Resh Lakish answers that the Mishnah only excludes cases where the sin exists but the Torah exempts, but after Yom Kippur the sin is atoned. Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to a kicker who says Yom Kippur does not atone, and if he repents after Yom Kippur he must bring a suspended guilt-offering, while Resh Lakish holds Yom Kippur atones even for a kicker.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is liable for certain transgressions except for one who defiled the Temple and its sanctities, who does not bring a suspended guilt-offering.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not also exclude one for whom Yom Kippur has passed from bringing a suspended guilt-offering.
Resh Lakish answers that the Mishnah only excludes cases where the sin exists but the Torah exempts, but after Yom Kippur the sin is atoned and no longer exists.
Rabbi Yochanan says the Mishnah refers to a kicker who says Yom Kippur does not atone, and if he repents after Yom Kippur he must bring a suspended guilt-offering.
The Gemara notes that Resh Lakish holds Yom Kippur atones even for a kicker.

items.text: Dispute about one who says 'let my sin not be atoned'
items.text_en: Dispute about one who says 'let my sin not be atoned'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a dispute between Abaye and Rava about one who says 'let my sin not be atoned.' Abaye says it is not atoned, Rava says it is atoned. They agree that if one says 'let it not be offered,' it is not atoned, but they disagree when one says 'let it be offered but not atone.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Abaye and Rava about one who says 'let my sin not be atoned,' with Abaye saying it is not atoned and Rava saying it is atoned.
The Gemara clarifies that if one says 'let it not be offered,' all agree it is not atoned, citing the verse 'he shall offer it for his acceptance.'
Abaye argues that if one says 'let it be offered but not atone,' it does not atone because he explicitly said it should not atone.
Rava argues that since he said 'let it be offered,' atonement (כפרה) comes automatically (ממילא), regardless of his stipulation.

items.text: Rava's retraction and the baraita about Yom Kippur atonement
items.text_en: Rava's retraction and the baraita about Yom Kippur atonement
items.desc_en: Rava retracts based on a baraita that teaches Yom Kippur only atones for penitents, not for non-penitents. The Gemara clarifies that 'penitents' refers to those who say 'let it atone for my sin' and 'non-penitents' to those who say 'let it not atone for my sin,' and concludes that Rava's retraction is proven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rava retracted his earlier position, citing a baraita.
The baraita argues that Yom Kippur atones only for penitents, using a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from sin-offerings and concluding with the word 'אך' (only) to exclude non-penitents.
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'penitents' and 'non-penitents' in the baraita, rejecting the simple interpretation that they refer to inadvertent and intentional sinners.
Ulla cites Rabbi Yochanan's case of one who ate forbidden fat, set aside a sacrifice, then apostatized and returned, where the sacrifice is rejected.
The Gemara objects that even if the sacrifice is rejected, the person himself is still eligible for atonement.
The Gemara resolves that 'penitents' are those who say 'let it atone for my sin' and 'non-penitents' are those who say 'let it not atone for my sin,' concluding that Rava's retraction is proven.

items.text: Contradiction between baraitot on Yom Kippur atonement
items.text_en: Contradiction between baraitot on Yom Kippur atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two baraitot: one says Yom Kippur atones regardless of observance, another implies it only atones for penitents. Abaye resolves that one is Rabbi's view according to Rabbi Yehuda, the other is Rabbi's own view. Rava says both are Rabbi's own view, but Rabbi admits that for sins of Yom Kippur itself, it does not atone, and the Gemara discusses possible scenarios for karet on Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two baraitot: one says Yom Kippur atones regardless of observance, the other implies it only atones for penitents.

Abaye resolves that one baraita reflects Rabbi's view according to Rabbi Yehuda, and the other reflects Rabbi's own view, citing a baraita where Rabbi distinguishes between sins with and without repentance.
Rava says both baraitot are Rabbi's own view, but Rabbi admits that for sins of Yom Kippur itself, it does not atone, otherwise karet on Yom Kippur would be impossible to find.
The Gemara objects that karet could occur at night, but Rava's question about daytime karet remains.
The Gemara suggests scenarios where one dies suddenly during the day, leaving no time for atonement.

items.text: The blasphemer and the rule of karet
items.text_en: The blasphemer and the rule of karet
items.desc_en: The Mishnah adds that a blasphemer brings a sacrifice. The Gemara explains that the Sages heard Rabbi Akiva teach about a necromancer but not a wizard, and they asked why the blasphemer brings a sacrifice since there is no action. A baraita states that a blasphemer brings a sacrifice because karet is written regarding him, but the Gemara objects that this rule would apply to Passover and circumcision, which have karet but no sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah adds that the Sages include the blasphemer among those who bring a sacrifice, and the Gemara notes the question: what is the inclusion of the blasphemer, who has no action?
The Gemara explains that the Sages heard Rabbi Akiva teach about a necromancer but not a wizard, and they asked why the blasphemer brings a sacrifice since there is no action.
A baraita states that a blasphemer brings a sacrifice because karet is written regarding him, according to Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara objects that this rule would apply to Passover and circumcision, which have karet but no sacrifice.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's view on the mekallel
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's view on the mekallel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Akiva's reasoning that the mekallel brings a korban because the Torah wrote karet in the context of a korban, implying that one who is liable for karet must bring a korban. The Rabbis object that the mekallel has no action, so the Gemara asks what the karet written in the verse comes for. The Rabbis answer that it comes to give karet to the one who curses, learned from a gezeirah shavah with Pesach Sheni.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva's view is that the mekallel brings a korban because the Torah wrote karet in the context of a korban, implying that one liable for karet must bring a korban.
The Gemara quotes Rabbi Akiva's challenge to the Rabbis: since the mekallel has no action, what purpose does the karet written in the verse serve?
The Rabbis answer that the karet comes to impose karet on the one who curses, derived via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) with Pesach Sheni.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the meaning of 'megadef'
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the meaning of 'megadef'
items.desc_en: A baraisa presents two interpretations of the word 'megadef'. Isi ben Yehudah says it refers to one who blesses the Name, like a person who scrapes a bowl and diminishes it. Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah says it refers to an idolater, like one who scrapes a bowl without diminishing it. Another baraisa states that Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah holds the verse speaks of an idolater, while the Sages say it comes only to give karet to one who blesses the Name.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Isi ben Yehudah interprets the verse 'אֶת ה׳ הוּא מְגַדֵּף' as comparing the blasphemer to someone who says 'you scraped the bowl and diminished it,' holding that the mekallel is one who curses God.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah offers a different interpretation: the blasphemer is like one who says 'you scraped the bowl and did not diminish it,' holding that the mekallel is an idolater.
Another baraita is cited: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah says the verse speaks of an idolater, while the Sages say it comes only to impose karet on one who curses God.

items.text: Mishnah: Categories of women who bring korbanot
items.text_en: Mishnah: Categories of women who bring korbanot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three categories of women who miscarry: those who bring a korban that is eaten (e.g., miscarrying an animal form, sandal, afterbirth, or a formed fetus, and a maidservant), those who bring a korban that is not eaten (e.g., uncertain miscarriage or two women with opposite obligations), and those who do not bring a korban (e.g., miscarrying a sac of water, blood, or gninim, or fish, locusts, etc., or before 40 days, or a yotzei dofen). Rabbi Shimon obligates a korban for yotzei dofen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that some women bring a korban that is eaten, some bring a korban that is not eaten, and some do not bring at all.
Rabbi Meir lists women who bring a korban that is eaten: one who miscarries a form of beast, wild animal, or bird.
The Sages disagree, requiring that the miscarried form have a human shape.
The Mishnah lists additional cases where the woman brings a korban that is eaten: miscarrying a sandal, afterbirth, or formed fetus, and a maidservant who miscarries.
The Mishnah lists women who bring a korban that is not eaten: one who miscarries without knowing what, and two women who miscarry one liable and one exempt, with Rabbi Yosei's qualification.
The Mishnah lists women who do not bring a korban at all, with Rabbi Shimon obligating one who miscarries a fetus that emerged through the side (יוצא דופן).

items.text: Gemara: Source for the maidservant's obligation
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the maidservant's obligation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know a maidservant brings a korban. A baraisa derives from 'ishah' that a giyoret and a shifchah are included. The Gemara explains the need for the explicit teaching: one might have thought that a maidservant is exempt from the korban yoledet since it is a mitzvah specific to women, but the Mishnah teaches she is obligated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a maidservant (שפחה) is included in the obligation to bring a korban? It answers with a baraita that derives it from the word 'אִשָּׁה' (woman).

The Gemara asks why the Mishnah explicitly states 'וכן שפחה' (and similarly a maidservant), and explains that it was necessary because one might have thought a maidservant is exempt from the korban of a יולדת (woman who gave birth), since that obligation applies only to women, not men.

The Gemara explains the Mishnah's phrase 'וכן שפחה': one might have thought a maidservant is exempt from the korban yoledet because it is a women-specific mitzvah (מצוה), but the Mishnah explicitly teaches she is obligated.

items.text: Gemara: The procedure for two women with uncertain obligations and Rabbi Yosei's position
items.text_en: Gemara: The procedure for two women with uncertain obligations and Rabbi Yosei's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when two women miscarry and one is obligated and one is exempt, they bring one definite korban and one bird chatat as a safek, and stipulate. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei allows stipulation, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei says two women do not bring one chatat. Rava and Rabbi Yochanan resolve that Rabbi Yosei admits in the case of a mechusar kapparah, because there the korban is for permitting eating kodashim, not for atonement. A baraisa supports this: Rabbi Yosei says any chatat that comes for a sin is not brought by two.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what do the two women who miscarry (one liable, one exempt) do? It answers that they each bring a definite korban and a bird חטאת (sin-offering) as a ספק (doubtful case), and stipulate a condition.
The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Yosei actually allow a conditional stipulation (תנאה)? It cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei explicitly rejects such a stipulation.
Rava answers that Rabbi Yosei concedes in the case of one who lacks atonement (מחוסר כפרה), and Rabbi Yochanan agrees.
The Gemara explains the reason: in the other case, a man requires knowledge of his sin, but here the women bring a korban only to permit themselves to eat sacred food.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei says that any חטאת (sin-offering) that comes for a sin cannot be brought by two people together.

items.text: Gemara: The dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis regarding yotzei dofen
items.text_en: Gemara: The dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis regarding yotzei dofen
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning behind the dispute. Reish Lakish says Rabbi Shimon derives from 'v'im nikevah teiled' to include another type of birth, which is yotzei dofen. Rabbi Mani bar Pattish says the Rabbis derive from 'ishah ki tazria veyaldah' that she must give birth from the place where she conceives, excluding yotzei dofen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is Rabbi Shimon's reason for obligating a woman who miscarries a fetus that emerged through the side (יוצא דופן)? Resh Lakish answers that the verse 'וְאִם נְקֵבָה תֵּלֵד' includes another type of birth, namely יוצא דופן.
Rabbi Mani bar Pattish explains the Sages' reason: the verse 'אִשָּׁה כִּי תַזְרִיעַ וְיָלְדָה' requires that the birth be from the place where she conceives, excluding יוצא דופן.
The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Rabbis who exempt yotzei dofen from a korban.

Rabbi Mani bar Pattish explains that the Rabbis derive from the verse 'אִשָּׁה כִּי תַזְרִיעַ וְיָלְדָה' (a woman who conceives and gives birth) that she must give birth from the place where she conceives, excluding yotzei dofen.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on miscarrying on the night of the 81st day
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on miscarrying on the night of the 81st day
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Shammai exempts a woman who miscarries on the night of the 81st day from a korban, while Beit Hillel obligates. The Gemara presents the argument: Beit Hillel asks why the night differs from the day, since both are impure. Beit Shammai responds that the day is a time fit for a korban, but the night is not. Beit Hillel counters with the case of the 81st day falling on Shabbat, which is not fit for an individual korban but is fit for a communal korban. Beit Shammai retorts that the night is fit for neither. The Gemara adds that the blood of a woman who miscarries within the period of melo'ah is impure but she is exempt from a korban.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: a woman who miscarries on the night of the eighty-first day after giving birth to a female — Beit Shammai exempt her from the korban, and Beit Hillel obligate her.

Beit Hillel asks Beit Shammai: what is the difference between the night of the eighty-first day and the day itself? If they are equal regarding טומאה (ritual impurity), should they not be equal regarding the korban?
Beit Shammai answers: no, because on the day itself she emerged at a time fit for bringing a korban, but on the night she did not.
Beit Hillel objects: consider a woman who miscarries on the eighty-first day that falls on Shabbat, when she cannot bring a korban — yet she is still obligated to bring a korban later.
Beit Shammai answers: no, because Shabbat is fit for a communal korban (קרבן ציבור), but the night is fit for neither an individual nor a communal korban.
The Gemara concludes that the case of blood (of a woman who miscarries within the completion period) does not prove the point, as her blood is impure but she is exempt from the korban.

items.text: Opening Gemara: Beit Hillel's proof from the verse
items.text_en: Opening Gemara: Beit Hillel's proof from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Beit Hillel argues that the word 'לְבַת' (to a daughter) includes the night of the 81st day for a niddah, establishing that the night counts as part of the following day for sacrificial obligations.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Beit Hillel argues that the word 'לְבַת' (to a daughter) includes the night of the 81st day for a niddah, establishing that the night counts as part of the following day for sacrificial obligations.

items.text: Rabbi Hoshaya's question to Bar Kappara about a zav on the eighth night
items.text_en: Rabbi Hoshaya's question to Bar Kappara about a zav on the eighth night
items.desc_en: Rabbi Hoshaya, who studied under Bar Kappara and then Rabbi Chiyya, asks Bar Kappara whether Beit Hillel would exempt a zav who saw three emissions on the eighth night, since the verse only mentions a niddah, or if the same logic applies. Bar Kappara rebukes him and reiterates the verse's inclusion of the night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Hoshaya, who studied under Bar Kappara and then Rabbi Chiyya, and recounts that he asked Bar Kappara about a zav who saw three emissions on the eighth night.

Rabbi Hoshaya asks whether Beit Hillel's reasoning from the verse 'לְבַת' (to a daughter) applies only to a niddah who miscarries at night, exempting a zav who saw three emissions on the eighth night, or whether the same logic applies to a zav as well.

Bar Kappara rebukes Rabbi Hoshaya for leaving him, then answers by citing the verse 'לְבַת' (to a daughter) to include the night of the eighty-first day, implying the same inclusion for the eighth night.

items.text: Gemara's suggestion: a dispute between Tannaim
items.text_en: Gemara's suggestion: a dispute between Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the conflicting baraitot about a zav on the eighth night reflect a Tannaic dispute: one holds that the night is not lacking time (so he brings a sacrifice), the other that it is lacking time (so he does not).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the conflicting baraitot about a zav on the eighth night reflect a Tannaic dispute: one holds that the night is not lacking time (so he brings a sacrifice), the other that it is lacking time (so he does not).

items.text: Rav Huna bar Acha's resolution: both Tannaim agree the night is lacking time
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Acha's resolution: both Tannaim agree the night is lacking time
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Acha, citing Rabbi Elazar, explains that both Tannaim hold that the night is lacking time. The baraita that says he brings refers to a zav with two emissions (where the third on the eighth night completes the count), while the one that says he does not bring refers to a zav with three emissions (where all three are on the eighth night, so no sacrifice is brought). He further explains that a daytime emission on the seventh day does not count because it would be a sighting that interrupts the count.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Acha citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Acha citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Acha resolves the baraita dispute by asserting both Tannaim hold לילה מחוסר זמן (the night is lacking time), distinguishing between a zav with two emissions (who brings a sacrifice) and one with three (who does not), and explains that a daytime emission on the seventh day does not count because it interrupts the count.

items.text: Rava's objection and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.text_en: Rava's objection and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Huna bar Acha's explanation, asking why the baraita about not bringing was not taught in the context of the Mishnah's list of five who bring one sacrifice. The Gemara then cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: if a zav saw one emission at night and two during the day, he brings a sacrifice; if he saw two at night and one during the day, he does not bring.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Huna bar Acha's explanation, asking why the baraita about not bringing was not taught in the context of the Mishnah's list of five who bring one sacrifice.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: if a zav saw one emission at night and two during the day, he brings a sacrifice; if he saw two at night and one during the day, he does not bring.

items.text: Rav Yosef and Rav Sheishet's analysis of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Yosef and Rav Sheishet's analysis of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef supports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling by noting that the first emission at night is merely seminal fluid, and if he sees two more, they combine. Rav Sheishet objects, arguing that the first emission of a zav must be seen at a time of obligation; since the night is not a time of obligation, without Rabbi Yochanan's teaching we would not combine them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef supports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling by arguing that the first emission at night is merely seminal fluid, so if he sees two more, they combine.

Rav Sheishet objects, arguing that the first emission of a zav must be seen at a time of obligation; since the night is not a time of obligation, without Rabbi Yochanan's teaching we would not combine them.

items.text: Contradiction from Chizkiya and resolution: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is for the one who says the night is lacking time
items.text_en: Contradiction from Chizkiya and resolution: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is for the one who says the night is lacking time
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Chizkiya says one who becomes impure at night does not bring a sacrifice, while Rabbi Yochanan says even at night he brings. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's statement about two at night and one during the day is said according to the one who holds the night is lacking time. The Gemara then explains that Rabbi Yochanan's novel point is about one emission at night and two during the day, teaching that the night emission combines despite not being at a time of obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan actually holds that the night is lacking time (מחוסר זמן).
The Gemara objects that Chizkiya explicitly says one who becomes impure at night does not bring a sacrifice, implying night is lacking time.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan himself says even at night one brings a sacrifice, contradicting the notion that he holds night is lacking time.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's statement about two at night and one during the day not bringing a sacrifice is said according to the one who holds the night is lacking time.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yochanan needed to state this, as it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan needed to state the case of one emission at night and two during the day, teaching that the night emission combines despite not being at a time of obligation.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan's novel point is that one might think the night emission does not combine since it is not at a time of obligation, but he teaches that it does combine.

items.text: Mishnah: A woman with uncertain births and zivahs brings one offering
items.text_en: Mishnah: A woman with uncertain births and zivahs brings one offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a woman who has a doubt about five births and five zivahs brings one offering and may eat sacrifices; the remainder is not obligatory. If she has five definite zivahs and five definite births, she brings one offering but the remainder is obligatory. A story is told about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel who taught that a woman with definite births and zivahs brings one offering and the remainder is not obligatory, causing the price of bird offerings to drop.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: a woman with uncertain births and zivahs brings one offering and the remainder is not obligatory.
The Mishnah states the second case: with definite zivahs and births, she brings one offering but the remainder is obligatory.

sub.text: Story about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Story about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah recounts a story where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel taught that a woman with definite births and zivahs brings one offering without remainder, causing bird prices to drop.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita on a woman with definite and uncertain births/zivahs
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita on a woman with definite and uncertain births/zivahs
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: a woman with five definite births and five uncertain zivahs (or five definite births and five uncertain births) brings two bird offerings—one for the definite and one for the uncertain. The definite one is eaten and the remainder is obligatory; the uncertain one is not eaten and the remainder is not obligatory. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva dispute how she designates the offerings: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says she should specify 'on the last' for the definite, and for the uncertain, if there is a definite among them, she says 'on the definite'; Rabbi Akiva says she says 'on one of them' for both.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rule: a woman with five definite births and five uncertain zivahs (or births) brings two bird offerings—one for the definite and one for the uncertain—with different rules for eating and obligation.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri specifies how she designates the offerings: for the definite she says 'on the last', and for the uncertain, if there is a definite among them she says 'on the definite', otherwise 'on one of them'.
Rabbi Akiva holds that for both the definite and the uncertain offerings she says 'on one of them' and is exempt.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Rava, explains that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri compares the offerings to sin-offerings, where one must bring all until atonement is achieved, so here too she must specify each. Rabbi Akiva compares them to immersions, where one immersion purifies, so here too one designation suffices. Rav Papa objects: if Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri compares to sin-offerings, why does he allow the uncertain offering to be designated 'on one of them'? The Gemara cuts off mid-sentence.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak to Rav Pappa, citing Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak to Rav Pappa, citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Rava, explains that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri compares the offerings to sin-offerings (חטאות), where one must bring all until atonement, so here too she must specify each.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Rabbi Akiva compares the offerings to immersions (טבילות), where one immersion purifies, so here too one designation suffices.
Rav Pappa objects: if Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri compares to sin-offerings, why does he allow the uncertain offering to be designated 'on one of them' and be exempted? The Gemara cuts off mid-sentence.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's five conditional guilt-offerings
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's five conditional guilt-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement about five conditional guilt-offerings, citing a baraita that establishes a rule: wherever there is a distinction in sin-offerings, there is a distinction in guilt-offerings. It resolves the issue by explaining that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva concerns whether we suspect negligence regarding immersions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's list of five conditional guilt-offerings, asking whether bringing one exempts from the others, and cites a baraita that establishes a rule linking distinctions in sin-offerings to distinctions in guilt-offerings.
The Gemara resolves the issue by explaining that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva concerns whether we suspect negligence (פשיעה) regarding immersions.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: A brief statement marking the end of the previous chapter: 'We have returned to you, thirty-six.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'we return to you, thirty-six'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Four who require atonement and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's addition
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Four who require atonement and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's addition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists four categories of people who require atonement (מחוסרי כפרה): a zav, a zavah, a woman after childbirth, and a metzora. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds a convert (גר) and a nazirite (נזיר) to the list.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the four types of people lacking atonement (מחוסרי כפרה): a zav, a zavah, a woman after childbirth, and a leper.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds that a convert is lacking atonement until blood is sprinkled on him, and a nazirite is lacking for his wine, haircut, and impurity.
The Gemara begins its analysis, noting that the Mishnah distinguishes between a zav and a zavah because their impurity laws differ.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Why zav and zavah are counted separately
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Why zav and zavah are counted separately
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah counts zav and zavah as two separate categories: their impurity laws differ. A zav is not impure due to an accident (אונס) and is impure through emissions like days, while a zavah is impure due to an accident and not through emissions like days. The Gemara then questions why metzora and metzora'at are not also counted separately, but concludes that their essential impurity is the same (a k'gris), so they are not distinct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by explaining why the Mishnah counts zav and zavah as two separate categories: their impurity laws differ — a zav is not impure due to an accident (אונס) and a zavah is not impure through emissions like days.
A baraita is cited to support the distinction: the verse 'מבשרו' (from his flesh) excludes accidental emissions for a zav, and the Torah links the male to emissions and the female to days.

The Gemara questions why metzora and metzora'at are not also counted separately, given that their impurity laws differ — a metzora requires פריעה (uncovering) and פרימה (rending) and is forbidden in marital relations, while a metzora'at does not.

The Gemara resolves: zav and zavah have fundamentally different impurity (their essential impurity differs), but metzora and metzora'at share the same essential impurity — a k'gris (the size of a bean) — so they are not counted separately.

items.text: Gemara's discussion: Why the Tanna Kamma excludes a convert and a nazirite
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion: Why the Tanna Kamma excludes a convert and a nazirite
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna Kamma does not include a convert (גר) in the list of those requiring atonement, and answers that the Mishnah only lists those who are permitted to eat sacred foods, whereas a convert brings a sacrifice to become permitted to enter the congregation. Similarly, a nazirite is excluded because his sacrifice permits him to drink non-sacred wine. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's inclusion of a nazirite is for permitting himself, but the Gemara questions why he does not also include a defiled nazirite, and answers that his sacrifice is to begin his nazirite period in purity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna Kamma does not include a convert (גר) in the list of those requiring atonement, and answers that the Mishnah only lists those who are permitted to eat sacred foods, whereas a convert brings a sacrifice to become permitted to enter the congregation.
The Gemara asks why the Tanna Kamma does not include a nazirite, and answers that his sacrifice permits him to drink non-sacred wine.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov does not also include a defiled nazirite, and answers that his sacrifice is to begin his nazirite period in purity.

items.text: Baraita on the convert's sacrifice and Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Baraita on the convert's sacrifice and Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a convert is prohibited from eating sacred foods until he brings his bird-offering (קין). If he brought one bird in the morning, he may eat sacred foods in the evening. The baraita details that all bird-offerings in the Torah consist of one sin-offering and one burnt-offering, but here both are burnt-offerings. The Gemara then analyzes the verse 'כַּאֲשֶׁר תַּעֲשׂוּ כֵּן יַעֲשֶׂה' to derive that a convert brings a burnt-offering and peace-offering from cattle, but not a meal-offering. Rav Pappa explains that a bird is included, and the Gemara concludes with a derivation from the verse 'אִשֵּׁה רֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ' to include a bird burnt-offering.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that a convert is prohibited from eating sacred foods until he brings his bird-offering (קין), and notes that while all other bird-offerings consist of one sin-offering and one burnt-offering, here both birds are burnt-offerings.

The baraita continues by listing that if the convert brought his obligation from cattle, a burnt-offering and peace-offering, he fulfills his duty, but a meal-offering and peace-offering does not suffice, and the bird-offering was only prescribed to be lenient.

The Gemara asks why a meal-offering and peace-offering do not suffice, and derives from the verse 'כַּאֲשֶׁר תַּעֲשׂוּ כֵּן יַעֲשֶׂה' that just as the community brings a burnt-offering and peace-offering, so too the convert brings a burnt-offering and peace-offering.

The Gemara objects that if the verse 'כַּאֲשֶׁר תַּעֲשׂוּ' is applied strictly, then a single cattle offering should not suffice either, and Rav Pappa answers that the verse includes a bird, and all the more so a cattle burnt-offering.
The Gemara objects that if the verse includes a bird, it should also include a meal-offering, and the Gemara answers that the word 'כֵּן' (thus) in the verse excludes a meal-offering.
The Gemara resolves the derivation by citing a baraita that from the verse 'אִשֵּׁה רֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ לַה׳' a bird burnt-offering is included, as it is entirely for God.

items.text: Derivation that a ger brings only blood-offerings, not meal-offerings
items.text_en: Derivation that a ger brings only blood-offerings, not meal-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that from the verse 'as you do, so shall he do' we learn that the ger's offering must be of blood, like the community's offerings. It rejects the possibility that it must be a burnt-offering or peace-offering specifically, concluding that the ger is compared only to 'your offerings' in general.

sub.desc_en: The baraita asks whether the ger's offering could include a meal-offering (מנחה), and answers that the verse 'כן' excludes it.
Another baraita cites the verse 'ועשה אשה ריח ניחוח' and derives that the ger's offering must be of blood (מיני דמים), like the community's offerings.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the ger must bring specifically a burnt-offering (עולה) and peace-offering (שלמים), like the community.
The baraita resolves that the verse 'ככם כגר יהיה' teaches that the ger is compared only to 'your offerings' in general, not to a specific type.

items.text: Rabbi's derivation: ger requires circumcision, immersion, and blood presentation
items.text_en: Rabbi's derivation: ger requires circumcision, immersion, and blood presentation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives from 'kakhem' (like you) that just as the ancestors entered the covenant only through circumcision, immersion, and blood presentation, so too the ger must undergo these three rites.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives from 'kakhem' (like you) that just as the ancestors entered the covenant only through circumcision, immersion, and blood presentation, so too the ger must undergo these three rites.

items.text: Can a ger bring a single bird? Discussion of obligation vs. donation
items.text_en: Can a ger bring a single bird? Discussion of obligation vs. donation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a ger can bring a single bird, noting that no such offering exists in the Torah. A baraita is cited that from 'vehikriv oto' we learn that even a single bird is acceptable for a vow, but for an obligation we have not found such a case. The example of a yoledet (woman after childbirth) who brings a single bird for a chatat is rejected because she also brings a lamb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is impossible for a ger to bring a single bird, because no such offering is found in the entire Torah; the only bird-offering is a pair (קן), which is a leniency.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that from 'וְהִקְרִיבוֹ' we learn that even a single bird is acceptable for a vow, but concedes that for an obligation we have not found such a case.
The Gemara objects further by citing the case of a yoledet (woman after childbirth) who brings a single bird for a chatat, but answers that this is because she also brings a lamb alongside it.

items.text: Scriptural sources for the three rites of the ancestors
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for the three rites of the ancestors
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides scriptural proofs for each of the three rites mentioned by Rabbi: circumcision from Joshua 5, blood presentation from Exodus 24, and immersion derived from the fact that sprinkling blood requires immersion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi's statement that the ancestors entered the covenant only through circumcision, blood presentation, and immersion, and then provides scriptural support for circumcision from Joshua 5 or Ezekiel 16.

sub.text: Gemara's proof for blood presentation and immersion
sub.text_en: Gemara's proof for blood presentation and immersion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara proves blood presentation from Exodus 24 and derives immersion from the principle that there is no sprinkling without immersion.

items.text: Can we accept gerim today without a Temple?
items.text_en: Can we accept gerim today without a Temple?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether we can accept gerim nowadays when there is no Temple for the blood presentation. Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers with a verse that implies acceptance even without a Temple. A baraita then states that a ger nowadays must set aside a quarter for his bird-offering, but Rabbi Shimon reports that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai abolished this due to potential stumbling, and Rav Idi bar Gershom rules in accordance with Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since the Temple no longer exists, should we stop accepting gerim (converts) because they cannot bring the required blood offering?
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers by citing a verse (Numbers 15:14) that implies gerim are accepted even without a Temple, as the verse speaks of a ger in the midst of Israel.
A baraita states that a ger nowadays must set aside a quarter (of a dinar) for his bird-offering (kin), implying that gerim are still accepted.
Rabbi Shimon reports that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai already voted to abolish this requirement due to the potential stumbling (takala) of the ger mishandling the funds.
Rav Idi bar Gershom rules in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, that the requirement to set aside a quarter for the bird-offering is abolished.

items.text: Alternative version: dispute about ger toshav's Shabbat labor
items.text_en: Alternative version: dispute about ger toshav's Shabbat labor
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the baraita is presented, discussing the ger toshav (resident alien) and his permission to work on Shabbat. Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon dispute the degree of leniency compared to a Jew on Chol HaMoed or a weekday.

sub.desc_en: Introduces an alternative version of the baraita regarding the ger toshav (resident alien) and his permission to work on Shabbat, comparing it to a Jew on Chol HaMoed.
Rabbi Akiva rules that the ger toshav may work on Shabbat only as a Jew may on a festival day (Yom Tov).
Rabbi Yosei rules that the ger toshav may work on Shabbat for himself as a Jew may on a weekday.
Rabbi Shimon rules that both the ger toshav and resident slaves may work on Shabbat for themselves as a Jew may on a weekday.

items.text: Mishnah: Those who bring a single offering for multiple transgressions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those who bring a single offering for multiple transgressions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who bring an offering for intentional sin as if it were unintentional: one who has relations with a designated maidservant, a nazirite who became impure, false oath of testimony, and false oath of deposit. It then lists five who bring a single offering for multiple transgressions, including one who has relations with a maidservant multiple times and a nazirite who became impure multiple times.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing those who bring an offering for an intentional transgression as for an unwitting one: one who has relations with a designated maidservant, a nazirite who became impure, false oath of testimony, and false oath of deposit.

The Mishnah continues by stating that five individuals bring a single offering for multiple transgressions, listing one who has relations with a maidservant multiple times and a nazirite who became impure multiple times.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural derivations for each case in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural derivations for each case in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives each case: for the maidservant, from the verse 'be'eil ha'asham' that one offering covers multiple sins and that the unintentional is like intentional. For the nazirite, from the words 'peta' and 'pit'om' which include unintentional, intentional, and forced impurity, with a detailed analysis of why both words are needed. For false oath of testimony, because the word 've'ne'elam' is omitted. For false oath of deposit, by a verbal analogy of 'techeta' from the former. The Gemara then addresses a contradiction in the maidservant derivation, correcting it to say that the unintentional is like intentional.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that one who engages in intercourse with an espoused maidservant brings an offering for an intentional transgression as for an unwitting one?

The baraita derives from the verse 'וְכִפֶּר עָלָיו הַכֹּהֵן בְּאֵיל הָאָשָׁם' (and the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering) that one offering covers multiple sins and that the unintentional is like intentional.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that a nazirite who became impure brings an offering for an intentional transgression as for an unwitting one?
The baraita derives from the verse 'בְּפֶתַע פִּתְאוֹם' (unexpectedly, suddenly) that 'פֶּתַע' refers to unwitting and 'פִּתְאוֹם' to forced transgression.
Another baraita interprets 'פִּתְאוֹם' as intentional transgression, citing the verse 'וּפְתָאִים עָבְרוּ וְנֶעֱנָשׁוּ' (the thoughtless pass on and are punished).
The Gemara objects: Since 'פִּתְאוֹם' already implies unwitting, intentional, and forced, why write 'פֶּתַע' at all?
The Gemara explains: If only 'פִּתְאוֹם' were written, one might think the nazirite brings an offering only for unwitting transgression, not for forced or intentional.
The Gemara resolves: The Merciful One wrote 'פֶּתַע' (unwitting) to reveal that 'פִּתְאוֹם' includes forced and intentional, and even in those cases the nazirite is liable.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that one who falsely takes the oath of testimony brings an offering for an intentional transgression as for an unwitting one?
The baraita answers: In all other sliding-scale offerings the word 'וְנֶעְלַם' (it be hid) is stated, but here it is omitted, to render one liable for unwitting as for intentional.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that one who falsely takes the oath on a deposit brings an offering for an intentional transgression as for an unwitting one?
The Gemara answers: It is derived by a verbal analogy of 'תֶּחְטָא' (shall sin) from the oath of testimony.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that one who engages in several acts of intercourse with an espoused maidservant brings one offering for multiple transgressions?
The baraita derives from the verse 'וְכִפֶּר עָלָיו הַכֹּהֵן בְּאֵיל הָאָשָׁם' that one offering covers multiple sins, and the phrase 'וְנִסְלַח לוֹ' makes intentional like unwitting.
The Gemara objects: The verse is written regarding an intentional transgression, not an unwitting one.
The Gemara corrects: Rather, say that the phrase renders the unwitting like the intentional.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's inquiry: one who has relations with five maidservants in one lapse
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's inquiry: one who has relations with five maidservants in one lapse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina of Tirna asks Rabbi Yochanan whether one who has relations with five designated maidservants in a single lapse is liable for each or just one. Rabbi Yochanan answers that he is liable for each because the bodies are distinct, unlike multiple lapses with the same maidservant. The proof is from the verse 'isha' in the section on forbidden relations, which divides liability for each woman, and similarly for the maidservant.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina of Tirna asks Rabbi Yochanan whether one who has relations with five designated maidservants in a single lapse is liable for each or just one.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that he is liable for each and every one.
Rabbi Chanina asks what distinguishes this case from multiple lapses with a single maidservant, where only one offering is brought.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that with one maidservant the bodies are not distinct, but with five maidservants the bodies are distinct, requiring separate offerings.
Rabbi Chanina asks for the source that separate bodies matter in the case of a maidservant.

Rabbi Yochanan proves from the verse 'וְאִשָּׁה' (and a woman) in the section on forbidden relations, which divides liability for each woman, and similarly for the maidservant the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁכַּב אֶת אִשָּׁה' (who lies with a woman) teaches the same.

items.text: Continuation of Mishnah: multiple shifchot
items.text_en: Continuation of Mishnah: multiple shifchot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes that the phrase "וְהִיא שִׁפְחָה" teaches that each maidservant is a separate case, requiring a separate offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes that the phrase "וְהִיא שִׁפְחָה" teaches that each maidservant is a separate case, requiring a separate offering.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna for the nazirite who contracted multiple impurities
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna for the nazirite who contracted multiple impurities
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah about a nazirite who contracted multiple impurities. Rav Chisda identifies it as Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that nazirite purity takes effect from the seventh day. The Gemara explains why it cannot be Rabbi, and then cites a baraita to clarify Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda's position regarding the day of shaving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah about a nazirite who contracted multiple impurities.
Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that nazirite purity takes effect from the seventh day, so multiple impurities on the same day count as one.
The Gemara explains why the Mishnah cannot be Rabbi's view: if the impurity occurred on the seventh day it is one long impurity, and if on the eighth day each requires a separate offering.
The Gemara concludes that the Tanna must be Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi interprets the verse 'וְקִדַּשׁ אֶת רֹאשׁוֹ בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא' as referring to the day of bringing his offerings.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda holds that the verse refers to the day of his shaving, not the day of bringing offerings.

items.text: Mishnah: Multiple warnings for a sotah and multiple negaim for a metzora
items.text_en: Mishnah: Multiple warnings for a sotah and multiple negaim for a metzora
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man who warns his wife through multiple men, and a metzora who had multiple negaim, bring only one offering. However, if a metzora brought birds and then became a metzora again, the birds do not count until he brings his chatat; Rabbi Yehuda says until he brings his asham.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man who warns his wife through multiple men and a metzora who had multiple negaim bring only one offering.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that if a metzora brought birds and then became a metzora again, the birds do not count until he brings his asham.

items.text: Gemara: Source for multiple warnings and multiple negaim
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for multiple warnings and multiple negaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse "זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַקְּנָאוֹת" that one Torah applies to multiple warnings, and from "זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַמְּצוֹרָע" that one Torah applies to multiple negaim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the rule that multiple warnings are covered by one Torah, and answers from the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַקְּנָאוֹת' (this is the law of jealousies).
The Gemara asks the source for the rule that multiple negaim are covered by one Torah, and answers from the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַמְּצוֹרָע' (this is the law of the leper).

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah about the metzora who brought birds
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah about the metzora who brought birds
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that the metzora brings only one offering, and resolves it by explaining that the Mishnah is incomplete: it means that he brings only one offering, but the birds do not establish his status for poverty or wealth until he brings his chatat; Rabbi Yehuda says until he brings his asham.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a leper brought birds and then relapsed, the birds do not count until he brings his sin offering; Rabbi Yehuda says until he brings his guilt offering.
The Gemara objects: but you said earlier that he brings only one offering for several afflictions, so why would he need to bring another offering?
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is incomplete; it means he brings only one offering, but the birds do not establish his status for poverty or wealth until he brings his sin offering.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that the status is not established until he brings his guilt offering.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about which offering determines poverty/wealth for a metzora
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about which offering determines poverty/wealth for a metzora
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Shimon says the chatat determines, Rabbi Yehuda says the asham determines, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the birds determine. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says all three derive from the same verse "אֲשֶׁר לֹא תַשִּׂיג יָדוֹ בְּטׇהֳרָתוֹ", each interpreting it differently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: a metzora who brought his asham and then became wealthy — Rabbi Shimon says everything follows the chatat, Rabbi Yehuda says everything follows the asham.
A baraita adds that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says everything follows the birds.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says all three derive their positions from the same verse "אֲשֶׁר לֹא תַשִּׂיג יָדוֹ בְּטׇהֳרָתוֹ", each interpreting it differently: Rabbi Shimon holds it refers to the atoning item (chatat), Rabbi Yehuda to the qualifying item (asham), and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov to the item that causes purity (the birds).

items.text: Mishnah: Woman who had multiple births
items.text_en: Mishnah: Woman who had multiple births
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a woman who had multiple births within eighty days, and a woman who miscarried twins. Rabbi Yehuda says she brings an offering for the first and third but not for the second and fourth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman who had multiple births and miscarried within eighty days, and a woman who miscarried twins.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that she brings an offering for the first and third births but not for the second and fourth.

items.text: Gemara: Source for multiple births and explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for multiple births and explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from "זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַיּוֹלֶדֶת" that one offering covers multiple births, but not a birth and a zivah. It then explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, the first child causes the obligation and she counts from the first, while the Rabbis hold the second child causes it. The Gemara notes that the case of twins is necessary to teach that Rabbi Yehuda does not concede to the Rabbis there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one offering covers multiple births, and cites a Tanna before Rav Sheshet who derives from 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַיּוֹלֶדֶת' that one offering suffices for multiple births, but excludes a birth and a zivah.
The Gemara objects: if the baraita says she cannot bring one offering for a birth and a zivah, then if she ate blood and gave birth, would she also bring only one offering?

The Gemara resolves: rather, the baraita means that one offering covers multiple births within the same period (before or after the completion of days), but not across periods, as derived from 'זֹאת'.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, the first child causes the obligation and she counts from the first, while the Sages hold the second child causes it and she counts from the second.
The Gemara notes that the case of twins is necessary to teach that Rabbi Yehuda does not concede to the Sages there, as one might have thought he would.

items.text: Transition: A dilemma is raised
items.text_en: Transition: A dilemma is raised
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new unresolved question (אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ) that will be discussed in the following section.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new unresolved dilemma (אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ) that will be discussed in the following section.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehuda's view on impurity
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehuda's view on impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt: does Rabbi Yehuda consider a second offspring as non-existent for impurity and purity, so that the impurity of the second interrupts and then she counts the days of purity of the first? Or does he only hold that stringency (חומרא) but not leniency (קולא)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda applies his view that a second offspring is considered non-existent only to sacrifice, or also to impurity and purity, and whether he holds only stringency (חומרא) but not leniency (קולא).

items.text: Rav Huna's attempted proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Huna's attempted proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Huna from Sura cites a baraita: a woman who gave birth may have the Paschal lamb slaughtered and its blood sprinkled for her on day 40 for a male or day 80 for a female. Rav Chisda identifies this baraita as Rabbi Yehuda's view, who considers a second offspring as non-existent. The Gemara argues: if Rabbi Yehuda considered the second offspring as existent for impurity, how could she eat on day 40? She would still be impure from the second offspring. This proves that for both purity and impurity, Rabbi Yehuda considers the second offspring as non-existent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna from Sura cites a baraita that one may slaughter the Paschal lamb for a woman on day 40 for a male or day 80 for a female.
The Gemara objects that she is still impure, and Rav Chisda identifies the baraita as Rabbi Yehuda's view, who considers a second offspring as non-existent.

The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Yehuda considered the second offspring as existent for impurity, she could not eat on day 40, concluding that for both purity and impurity, Rabbi Yehuda considers the second offspring as non-existent.

items.text: Rejection: the baraita refers to a Paschal lamb brought in impurity
items.text_en: Rejection: the baraita refers to a Paschal lamb brought in impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: perhaps Rabbi Yehuda does consider the second offspring as existent for impurity, but the baraita deals with a Paschal lamb brought in a state of impurity (פסח הבא בטומאה), where even impure people may eat it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: perhaps Rabbi Yehuda does consider the second offspring as existent for impurity, but the baraita deals with a Paschal lamb brought in a state of impurity (פסח הבא בטומאה), where even impure people may eat it.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the Paschal lamb in impurity
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the Paschal lamb in impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: a Mishnah states that zavim, zavot, niddot, and yoldot may not eat from a Paschal lamb brought in impurity. The Gemara resolves: that Mishnah refers to those who have not immersed; the baraita deals with one who has immersed. Further discussion clarifies that a טבול יום of a zav is considered like a zav, but a מחוסר כיפורים of a zav is not considered like a zav, so she can eat on day 40 but not on day 80.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: how can the yoledet eat from the Paschal lamb brought in impurity, when a Mishnah explicitly forbids zavim, zavot, niddot, and yoldot from eating it?
The Gemara answers: that Mishnah refers to those who have not yet immersed; the baraita deals with one who has already immersed.
The Gemara objects: if she has already immersed, then on day 80 she should be fit to eat, but the baraita says she is not fit until day 80.

The Gemara answers: she is not fit on day 80 because the opinion holds that a טבול יום (one who has immersed but awaits sunset) of a zav is considered like a zav, and therefore she cannot eat until after sunset.
The Gemara objects: if a טבול יום of a zav is considered like a zav, then on day 40 she should also be unfit, but the baraita says she is fit on day 40.

The Gemara answers: on day 40 she is fit because the opinion holds that a מחוסר כיפורים (one who has not yet brought atonement offerings) of a zav is not considered like a zav, so she can eat on day 40 but not on day 80.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rava, who holds that a מחוסר כיפורים of a zav is like a zav, would resolve the baraita. Rav Ashi says Rava explains it as referring to day 40 from conception for a male and day 80 from conception for a female, and it follows Rabbi Yishmael who counts 41 and 81 days. The Gemara then questions that she would still be impure due to niddah, and resolves that it deals with a dry birth (לידה יבשתא), teaching that it is possible for the womb to open without blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rava, who holds that a מחוסר כיפורים (one lacking atonement) of a zav is like a zav, would resolve the baraita that permits slaughter on day 40 for a male.
Rav Ashi says Rava explains the baraita as referring to day 40 from conception for a male and day 80 from conception for a female, following Rabbi Yishmael who counts 41 and 81 days.
The Gemara objects that even so, she would still be impure due to niddah (menstrual impurity) from the birth.
