The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with a dry birth (לידה יבשתא), teaching that it is possible for the womb to open without blood.

items.text: Rabbi Shmaya's attempted proof from the verse 'sixty days'
items.text_en: Rabbi Shmaya's attempted proof from the verse 'sixty days'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmaya cites a baraita: the verse says 'sixty days' – one might think they can be either consecutive or scattered; the verse says 'day' – just as a day is consecutive, so all sixty must be consecutive. The Gemara asks: who is the author? If it is the Rabbis, they do not have scattered days. Therefore it must be Rabbi Yehuda, and since he gives her sixty consecutive days, this shows he holds a stringency (חומרא) and not a leniency (קולא).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmaya cites a baraita: the verse says 'שִׁשִּׁים' (sixty days), which could be consecutive or scattered, but the verse also says 'יוֹם' (day), teaching that just as a day is consecutive, all sixty must be consecutive.
The Gemara asks: who is the author of this baraita? If it is the Rabbis, they do not have scattered days (so the teaching would be redundant).
The Gemara concludes that the baraita must be Rabbi Yehuda's view, and since he gives her sixty consecutive days, this shows he holds a stringency (חומרא) and not a leniency (קולא).

items.text: Rejection: the baraita can be explained according to the Rabbis
items.text_en: Rejection: the baraita can be explained according to the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: the baraita can be about the Rabbis, dealing with a woman who gave birth to a male within the 80 days of a female. The Gemara explains that the case is twins: a female first and a male later, born on the 20th day of her purity. The baraita teaches that even then the sixty days must be consecutive, not scattered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by asserting that the baraita can be explained according to the Rabbis, dealing with a woman who gave birth to a male within the 80 days of a female.
The Gemara explains that the case is twins: a female first and a male later, born on the 20th day of her purity, so the days of the first are complete but the second's days are not.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita teaches that even in such a case the sixty days must be consecutive, not scattered, based on the analogy to 'day'.

items.text: Abaye's attempted proof from the verse 'thirty days'
items.text_en: Abaye's attempted proof from the verse 'thirty days'
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita: the verse says 'thirty days' – one might think they can be consecutive or scattered; the verse says 'day' – just as a day is consecutive, so all thirty must be consecutive. The Gemara asks who the author is, beginning a new line of inquiry.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces a baraita about 'thirty days' to argue that the days must be consecutive, and the Gemara begins to question its author.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous sugya: Rabbi Yehuda's position on scattered days
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous sugya: Rabbi Yehuda's position on scattered days
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a second proof that Rabbi Yehuda holds a stringency (scattered days count) but no leniency (they do not count for a second offspring). The proof is from a baraita about the six days of separation, which must be consecutive like the sixty days of the flood. The baraita cannot be the Rabbis' view, so it must be Rabbi Yehuda's, confirming the point.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a baraita about the six days of separation being consecutive like the sixty days of the flood, and argues that since the Rabbis do not hold scattered days count, the baraita must be Rabbi Yehuda's view, confirming that Rabbi Yehuda has a stringency but no leniency.

items.text: Mishnah: Those who bring a sliding-scale offering
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those who bring a sliding-scale offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the cases that require a korban oleh veyored: hearing a false oath, utterance of lips, impurity of the Temple and its holy things, a woman after childbirth, and a metzora.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the cases that require a korban oleh veyored (sliding-scale offering): hearing a false oath, utterance of lips, impurity of the Temple and its holy things, a woman after childbirth, and a metzora.

items.text: First baraita: Gradations of wealth in the sliding-scale offering
items.text_en: First baraita: Gradations of wealth in the sliding-scale offering
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that some bring a korban in wealth and poverty (yoledet), some only in poverty (metzora), and some in poverty and extreme poverty (hearing the voice, utterance, and impurity). A second baraita details the substitutions: yoledet brings one bird for one lamb, metzora brings two birds for two lambs, and the others bring two birds for one lamb, and in extreme poverty a tenth of an ephah for two birds.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita introduces three categories of the sliding-scale offering: some bring in wealth and poverty (yoledet), some only in poverty (metzora), and some in poverty and extreme poverty (hearing the voice, utterance, and impurity).

The second baraita details the substitutions: yoledet brings one bird for one lamb, metzora brings two birds for two lambs, and the others bring two birds for one lamb, and in extreme poverty a tenth of an ephah for two birds.

items.text: Derivation of the tenth of an ephah's value in prutot
items.text_en: Derivation of the tenth of an ephah's value in prutot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the tenth of an ephah is worth a prutah. It derives from the verse that a lamb costs a sela, and from the system of substitutions: the extreme poor bring one-sixteenth of the poor person's offering. Calculating the poor person's offering as a quarter (48 prutot), one-sixteenth is 3 prutot, but the baraita says a prutah. The Gemara resolves that the derivation is from the yoledet, where one bird is 1/32 of a lamb, and the extreme poor's offering is 1/32 of the poor's, which would be 1.5 prutot, but the Mishnah rounds to a prutah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the tenth of an ephah offering is worth a prutah.
A baraita establishes that a lamb costs a sela, as one who pledges a sela to the altar brings a lamb.
The Gemara proves that a lamb costs a sela from the verse about the ram of the guilt-offering and from the Mishnah that birds stood at a quarter (of a sela).
The Gemara derives that the extreme poor bring one-sixteenth of the poor person's offering, just as the poor bring one-sixteenth of the rich person's offering.
The Gemara calculates: the poor person's offering is a quarter (of a sela) = 48 prutot, so one-sixteenth is 3 prutot, contradicting the baraita that says a prutah.
The Gemara asks why the baraita says a prutah, when the calculation yields 3 prutot.
The Tanna derives from the yoledet, who brings one bird instead of a lamb, which is 1/32 of a lamb.
The Gemara objects: the extreme poor's offering is 1/16 of the poor's, derived from lamb and ram, which yields 1.5 prutot, not a full prutah.

items.text: Rava's resolution: The tenth of an ephah is 1/32 of the poor's offering, but no less than a prutah
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: The tenth of an ephah is 1/32 of the poor's offering, but no less than a prutah
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the entire derivation is from the yoledet: just as God had mercy on the poor to make their offering 1/32 of the wealthy's (the yoledet's lamb), so too He had mercy on the extremely poor to make their offering 1/32 of the poor's. This would be 1.5 prutot, but since it is improper to bring less than a prutah to the Temple, the Mishnah states it is a prutah.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves that the entire derivation is from the yoledet: the poor bring 1/32 of the rich, and the extreme poor bring 1/32 of the poor.
The Gemara objects that this calculation yields three-quarters of a prutah, not a full prutah.
The Gemara resolves that indeed it is three-quarters of a prutah, but it is rounded up to a prutah because it is not proper to bring less than a prutah to the Temple.

items.text: Mishnah: Differences between a shifchah and all other arayot
items.text_en: Mishnah: Differences between a shifchah and all other arayot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the distinctions between a designated maidservant and other forbidden relations: the punishment is an asham rather than a chatat, the offering is a male rather than a female, the man and woman are not equal in punishment or offering, and the law treats an unwitting act like a deliberate one, with liability for each act of intercourse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking what distinguishes a designated maidservant from all other forbidden relations, and answers that the punishment and offering differ: all others require a חטאת (sin-offering), while the maidservant requires an אשם (guilt-offering).
The Mishnah states that all other forbidden relations require a female offering, while the maidservant requires a male offering.
The Mishnah states that for all other forbidden relations, the man and woman are equal in lashes and offering, but for the maidservant, the man and woman are not equal in lashes or offering.

The Mishnah states that for all other forbidden relations, one who merely touches is treated like one who completes the act, and one is liable for each act of intercourse, but for the maidservant, the law is more stringent.
The Mishnah concludes that the maidservant is more stringent in certain respects, as indicated by the preceding distinctions.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Definition of shifchah charufah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Definition of shifchah charufah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a shifchah charufah as a half-slave half-free woman, citing the verse 'v'hofdeh lo nifdasah'. Rabbi Yehudah, Rabbi Yishmael, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov offer differing interpretations of the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the shifchah charufah (half-slave half-free woman) is treated with the same penalty for intentional and unintentional acts.
The Mishnah asks which woman qualifies as a shifchah charufah.
Rabbi Yehudah defines the shifchah as a woman who is half-slave and half-free, citing the verse 'וְהׇפְדֵּה לֹא נִפְדָּתָה'.
Rabbi Yishmael argues that the shifchah is a definite (full) Canaanite slave woman.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov states that all other forbidden relations are explicitly detailed, leaving only the half-slave half-free woman as the subject of the shifchah charufah law.

items.text: Gemara: Source that she is lashed and he is not
items.text_en: Gemara: Source that she is lashed and he is not
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the woman is lashed but the man is not. It cites a beraita deriving from 'bikoret tihyeh' that she is lashed, and 'tihyeh' excludes him. Rabbi Yitzchak and Rav Ashi explain that 'bikoret' refers to lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where it is derived that she is lashed and he is not.
The baraita derives from 'bikoret tihyeh' that she is lashed, and 'tihyeh' excludes him.
The Gemara asks how we know that 'bikoret' is a term for lashes.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that 'bikoret' means 'be examined' for lashes, citing the procedure of the court.
Rav Ashi explains that 'bikoret' refers to lashes that are measured to be divisible into thirds.

items.text: Gemara: When she is lashed, he brings a sacrifice
items.text_en: Gemara: When she is lashed, he brings a sacrifice
items.desc_en: A beraita states: when the woman is lashed, the man brings a sacrifice; when she is not lashed, he does not. Rava derives this from the verse order: 'bikoret tihyeh' precedes 'v'hevi et ashamo', implying that lashes are a prerequisite for the sacrifice. The Gemara rejects the possibility that she both receives lashes and brings a sacrifice, citing 'v'hevi et ashamo' – only he brings it.

sub.desc_en: A beraita states that when the woman is lashed, the man brings a sacrifice; when she is not lashed, he does not.
Rava derives from the verse order that lashes are a prerequisite for the sacrifice: if she is lashed, he brings the sacrifice; if not, he does not.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the verse excludes only the man from bringing a sacrifice, but the woman should both be lashed and bring a sacrifice.
The Gemara rejects the objection by citing the verse 'וְהֵבִיא אֶת אֲשָׁמוֹ לַה׳' (and he shall bring his guilt-offering to the Lord), implying only he brings it, not she.

items.text: Gemara: The shifchah must be a 'charufah' (designated)
items.text_en: Gemara: The shifchah must be a 'charufah' (designated)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that liability only applies to a shifchah who is 'charufah' (designated for a specific man), derived from the verse 'v'hi shifchah necherefet l'ish'. He explains 'necherefet' as meaning 'designated', citing verses. Rav Chisda adds that all those who married foreign women in Ezra's time had relations with shifchot charufot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that liability only applies to a shifchah who is 'charufah' (designated), deriving this from the verse and supporting it with other verses.
Rav Chisda adds that all those who married foreign women in Ezra's time had relations with shifchot charufot.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah's dispute on shifchah definition
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah's dispute on shifchah definition
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Tannaitic dispute about the definition of shifchah charufah. It explains the positions of Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, and Acheirim, deriving their views from the verses 'v'hofdeh lo nifdasah' and 'ki lo chufshah'. The Gemara clarifies the logic behind each opinion, including the derivation that she is betrothed to an eved ivri or eved kena'ani.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the verse 'והפדה' and the interpretive question of whether it refers to a fully redeemed shifchah.
The baraita resolves the contradiction: she is partially redeemed (חציה שפחה וחציה בת חורין) and betrothed to an eved ivri, according to Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yishmael states that the verse speaks of a Canaanite shifchah betrothed to an eved ivri, and the phrase 'והפדה לא נפדתה' is merely the Torah speaking in human language.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah says that all other forbidden relations are explicitly stated, and the only remaining case is a half-shifchah half-free woman betrothed to an eved ivri.
Acheirim derive from the verse 'כי לא חופשה' that the shifchah is a Canaanite shifchah betrothed to an eved kena'ani.
The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Yishmael, the verse 'והפדה לא נפדתה' is explained as human language, but from where does he derive that she is betrothed to an eved ivri?
The Gemara answers: from the verse 'כי לא חופשה', it implies that he (the eved ivri) is freed, indicating her betrothal to him.

sub.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's position seems identical to Rabbi Akiva's; it then explains that he is actually addressing Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah argues that generally he agrees with Rabbi Yishmael about human language, but here the extra verse 'כי לא חופשה' shows that the verse must be for a half-shifchah.
The Gemara asks: for Acheirim, the verse 'והפדה לא נפדתה' is explained as human language, but from where do they derive that she is betrothed to an eved kena'ani?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'כי לא חופשה' is applied to him (the eved kena'ani) since it is not needed for her status.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: General rules for arayot
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: General rules for arayot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states general rules for all forbidden relations: a minor is exempt, a sleeping person is exempt, and an unintentional act requires a chatat while intentional incurs karet. The Gemara questions apparent contradictions: here a minor is liable? Rav Yehudah explains the Mishnah means a minor is exempt and an adult is liable, but here (shifchah) even an adult is exempt. Similarly for sleep vs. awake.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states general rules for forbidden relations: a minor is exempt, a sleeping person is exempt, and an unintentional act requires a chatat while intentional incurs karet.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that here (regarding a shifchah charufah) a minor is liable, contradicting the general rule.
Rav Yehudah explains that the Mishnah means a minor is exempt and an adult is liable, but here even an adult is exempt, resolving the contradiction.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that here a sleeping person is liable, contradicting the general rule.
Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav explains that the Mishnah means a sleeping person is exempt and an awake person is liable, but here even an awake person is exempt, resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Gemara: Tanna's baraita and Rav Sheishet's objection
items.text_en: Gemara: Tanna's baraita and Rav Sheishet's objection
items.desc_en: A Tanna recites a baraita before Rav Sheishet equating various cases: completing the act is like beginning, intentional like unintentional, natural like unnatural, awake like asleep. Rav Sheishet objects: if it refers to shifchah charufah, completing is liable but beginning is not; intentional is liable but unintentional is not; natural is liable but unnatural is not (since 'shichvat zera' is written). If it refers to other arayot, the same problems arise.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recites a baraita before רב ששת (Rav Sheshet) listing four equivalences: completing the act is like beginning, intentional like unintentional, natural like unnatural, awake like asleep.
רב ששת (Rav Sheshet) objects: if the baraita refers to שפחה חרופה (an espoused maidservant), completing the act is liable but beginning is not, and intentional is liable but unintentional is not.
רב ששת (Rav Sheshet) continues: natural intercourse is liable but unnatural is not, since 'שכבת זרע' (lying carnally) is written, and the awake-asleep equivalence is also problematic.
רב ששת (Rav Sheshet) concludes: if the baraita refers to other עריות (forbidden relations), the same problems arise with the completing-beginning equivalence.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous Mishnah and transition
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous Mishnah and transition
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a textual difficulty by explaining that the Tanna taught the cases in reverse order, and then summarizes the distinctions between a designated slave-girl and other forbidden relations. The section ends with the formal conclusion of the chapter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tanna taught the cases in the order they appear, suggesting the opposite order was needed.

The Gemara answers that the Tanna taught the cases in reverse order, explaining that the designated slave-girl (שפחה חרופה) is exempt for incomplete relations because the verse requires 'שכבת זרע' (emission of seed).

The Gemara further explains that intentional but incomplete relations with the slave-girl are exempt like unintentional ones, and that an awake person having incomplete relations is exempt like a sleeping person, all because the verse requires 'שכבת זרע'.

The Gemara summarizes the distinctions: intentional and incomplete relations with the slave-girl are like unintentional relations with all forbidden relations, and an awake person's incomplete relations with the slave-girl are like a sleeping person's relations with all forbidden relations.
The chapter formally concludes with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

items.text: Mishnah: Testimony about eating forbidden fat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Testimony about eating forbidden fat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where witnesses say one ate forbidden fat, and the person either remains silent or denies it. It also discusses the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding two witnesses versus the person's denial, and the laws of multiple forbidden foods eaten in one lapse of awareness.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case where witnesses say one ate forbidden fat (חלב) and he brings a sin-offering.
The Mishnah presents the case of conflicting testimony (one witness says ate, one says did not eat) where the person brings a provisional guilt-offering (אשם תלוי).
The Mishnah states that if one witness says he ate and the person himself denies it, he is exempt.
The Mishnah introduces the dispute: if two witnesses say he ate and he denies it, Rabbi Meir holds him liable.
Rabbi Meir argues by kal vachomer (a fortiori): if two witnesses can bring him to a severe death penalty, should they not bring him to a light offering?
The Sages object: what if he could claim he was intentional (מזיד) and thus exempt from an offering?
The Mishnah states that if one ate forbidden fat (חלב) multiple times in one lapse of awareness, he is liable for only one offering.
The Mishnah states that if one ate multiple types of forbidden foods (חלב, blood, piggul, notar) in one lapse, he is liable for each one.
The Mishnah notes that this is a stringency of many types over one type.
The Mishnah concludes with the stringency of one type over many types: if one ate two half-olive portions of the same type in one lapse, he is liable; from two types, he is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's first analysis: Who is the Tanna of the Mishnah?
items.text_en: Gemara's first analysis: Who is the Tanna of the Mishnah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's first case: if two witnesses say he ate, and he is silent, he brings a sin-offering. But if one witness says so and he is silent, does he not bring? The Gemara suggests the Mishnah is Rabbi Meir's view, who holds that denial of two witnesses is not considered denial, but the Rabbis would exempt him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's first case: if two witnesses say he ate and he is silent, he brings a sin-offering; but if one witness says so and he is silent, does he not bring?
The Gemara objects from the middle clause: if one witness says he ate and he denies it, he is exempt, implying that if he is silent he would be liable, and all the more so with two witnesses.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's first case is where he denies them, and it follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that denial of two witnesses is not considered denial, but the Rabbis would exempt him.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches that this matter is a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis, and specifically when he denies them.

items.text: Alternative interpretation: 'They said to him' can mean one witness
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation: 'They said to him' can mean one witness
items.desc_en: Some say that the phrase 'they said to him' can refer to a single witness, as proven from a Mishnah in Yevamot. The Gemara then questions: if he denies the one witness, he is exempt (as per the middle clause), but if he is silent, he is liable. This is derived from the middle clause.

sub.desc_en: Some say that the phrase 'אמרו לו' (they said to him) can refer even to a single witness, citing a Mishnah in Yevamot where a woman is told by one witness that her husband died.
The Gemara proves from the continuation of that Mishnah that the term 'אמרו' (they said) is used even for a single witness, establishing a precedent for the current sugya.
The Gemara asks: if the person denies the single witness, how can he bring a חטאת (sin-offering)? The middle clause explicitly exempts him when he denies a single witness.
The Gemara answers: the case is where he is silent, and from the middle clause we infer that silence before a single witness makes him liable, while denial exempts him.

items.text: Final resolution: The Mishnah speaks of silence, and the source from the Torah
items.text_en: Final resolution: The Mishnah speaks of silence, and the source from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's first case is when he is silent, and the middle clause is when he denies. The Torah source for liability when silent is derived from the verse 'or his sin is made known to him' – even if others inform him, provided he does not deny them. The Gemara questions whether this is needed for two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's first clause always refers to a case where he does not deny them, and the Mishnah is structured as a general statement followed by an exception: when he is silent he brings a חטאת (sin-offering), but when he denies he is exempt.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'אוֹ הוֹדַע אֵלָיו חַטָּאתוֹ' (or his sin is made known to him) that even if others inform him he is liable, provided he does not deny them, as the verse implies 'from any source'.
The Gemara questions the baraita: if it deals with two witnesses, why would a verse be needed to teach that silence before two witnesses makes one liable, since that is obvious?

items.text: Gemara's inference from the mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah's phrasing that when witnesses do not contradict him, he is believed, implying the Sages' reasoning is based on credibility.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah's phrasing that when witnesses do not contradict him, he is believed, implying the Sages' reasoning is based on credibility.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir argues a kal vachomer: if two witnesses can bring the death penalty, they should certainly bring a lesser sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir introduces a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) regarding witnesses and sacrifice.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry into the Sages' reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry into the Sages' reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Sages' position is because a person is more credible than a hundred witnesses, or because of a migo: if he could claim he was intentional (and exempt), he is believed when he says he did not eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether the Sages' reasoning is that a person is more credible than a hundred witnesses, or because of a מיגו (a claim that if he could have lied to exempt himself, he is believed when he says he did not eat).

items.text: Practical difference between the two reasons
items.text_en: Practical difference between the two reasons
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical difference: if the reason is inherent credibility, it applies to both new and old impurity; if it is migo, the Sages exempt only for old impurity (where he could claim he immersed), but for new impurity he is liable because even claiming immersion would not help.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference emerges from the two possible reasons for the Rabbis' ruling.

The Gemara explains that if the reason is inherent credibility, the exemption applies to both new and old impurity; if it is מיגו (the claim that he could have said he immersed), the exemption applies only to old impurity, not new impurity.

The Gemara elaborates: for old impurity, the person could have claimed immersion, so the claim 'I was not impure' is credible; for new impurity, even claiming immersion would not help because witnesses saw him become impure now.

items.text: Attempt to resolve from a baraita
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir argues his kal vachomer and the Sages say 'a person is more credible than a hundred witnesses,' implying that is their reason.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the dispute by citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir argues a kal vachomer and the Sages respond that a person is more credible than a hundred witnesses, implying that is their reason.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's resolution: migo is the basis
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's resolution: migo is the basis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami says the Sages' reason is indeed migo, and the baraita means: because he could say 'I did not remain in my impurity' (i.e., I immersed), therefore he is more credible. The Gemara clarifies that this applies even to impurity, as he could claim he immersed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami resolves that the Sages' reason is always the principle of מיגו (since he could claim he immersed), and the baraita's phrase 'a person is more credible than a hundred people' is actually the conclusion of that reasoning.
The Gemara objects: if the logic is the same מיגו, then the case of fat (חלב) would be identical to impurity, yet the baraita distinguishes them.
The Gemara answers: in the fat case, the defendant could only claim he acted intentionally (מזיד), but in impurity, he can claim he immersed (טבלתי), so the מיגו applies differently.

items.text: Another baraita and the dispute about impurity
items.text_en: Another baraita and the dispute about impurity
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who confesses is liable, but if a single witness says he is impure and he denies it, he is exempt. Rabbi Meir argues his kal vachomer, and Rabbi Yehuda says a person is more credible. The Sages agree with Rabbi Yehuda for fats and entering the Temple, but not for impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: one who confesses is liable, but if a single witness says he is impure and he denies it, he is exempt.
The baraita asks: could it be that even two witnesses who contradict him also exempt him?
Rabbi Meir argues via קל וחומר (a fortiori reasoning): if two witnesses can bring a person to capital punishment, they should certainly bring him to a lesser sacrifice.
Rabbi Yehuda states that a person is more credible about himself than a hundred witnesses.
The Sages agree with Rabbi Yehuda regarding fats and entering the Temple, but not regarding impurity.

items.text: Gemara's question about the context
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the context
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to ask what case we are dealing with, introducing a new inquiry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case we are dealing with, introducing a new inquiry.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the old impurity case
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the old impurity case
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the case of old impurity is where witnesses say he ate sacred food while impure, and he denies being impure, but cannot claim he immersed because that would contradict his initial denial.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the case of old impurity cannot be resolved like the cases of forbidden fats and entering the Temple, where the defendant could claim he acted intentionally.
Ravina explains that the case involves witnesses who say he ate sacred food while impure, and he denies being impure, so he cannot later claim he immersed without contradicting his initial denial.

items.text: Rav Nachman and Rav Yosef on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Yosef on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules like Rabbi Yehuda, but Rav Yosef limits that ruling to a case where the person admits to himself, not when witnesses confront him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Yosef qualifies that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling applies only when the person admits בינו לבין עצמו (between himself and himself), not when witnesses confront him.

items.text: Three cases where Rabbi Meir concedes to the Sages
items.text_en: Three cases where Rabbi Meir concedes to the Sages
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish, Rav Sheshet, and Abaye each present a case where Rabbi Meir agrees with the Sages that the defendant is exempt because he could claim a reinterpretation of events.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish gives the first case where Rabbi Meir concedes: if witnesses say he engaged with a designated maidservant, he can claim he did not complete the act.
Rav Sheshet adds a second case: a nazirite who was told he became impure can claim he had his vow annulled.
Abaye adds a third case: if witnesses say he knew testimony, he can claim he did not intend to give testimony.

items.text: Debate on eating two olive-bulks of fat in one lapse
items.text_en: Debate on eating two olive-bulks of fat in one lapse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira questions why one is only liable for one sin-offering for eating two olive-bulks of fat in one lapse, and Abaye explains that separate lapses would require separate offerings, but here it is one lapse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one ate two olive-bulks of forbidden fat (חֵלֶב) in one lapse of awareness (הֶעְלֵם), he is liable only one sin-offering.
Rabbi Zeira strongly objects: why is he liable only one sin-offering — didn't he eat two olive-bulks of forbidden fat?
Abaye answers that separate lapses (הֶעְלֵמוֹת מְחוּלָּקוֹת) would require separate offerings, but here it is one lapse (הֶעְלֵם אֶחָד).

There is an alternative version: the objection is reversed — why would two lapses obligate two offerings, when the substance (forbidden fat) is one? Abaye again answers that separate lapses (הֶעְלֵמוֹת מְחוּלָּקִין) are the criterion.

items.text: Reish Lakish on eating from two dishes in one type
items.text_en: Reish Lakish on eating from two dishes in one type
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish explains that the Mishnah's case of one type but two dishes is according to Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds that separate dishes create separate obligations, and the Gemara debates whether this applies leniently or stringently.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who eats forbidden fat, blood, piggul, and notar in one lapse of awareness is liable for each.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling that one is liable for eating two half olive-bulks from one type is not obvious.

sub.text: Reish Lakish in the name of Bar Tutini
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Bar Tutini
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish explains that the case involves eating from two dishes, according to Rabbi Yehoshua who holds that separate dishes create separate obligations.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches liability, showing Rabbi Yehoshua applies his principle only as a stringency, not a leniency.
An alternative version applies the same explanation to the latter clause of the Mishnah, where two types yield exemption.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches exemption, showing Rabbi Yehoshua does not apply his principle as a leniency.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah calls it two types when it is actually one type eaten from two dishes.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah calls it two types because it was eaten from two dishes, and this shows Rabbi Yehoshua applies his principle both leniently and stringently.
The Gemara objects that if the latter clause involves one type and two dishes, the former clause must be one type and one dish, which is obvious.

items.text: Ravina's explanation with Rabban Gamliel's view
items.text_en: Ravina's explanation with Rabban Gamliel's view
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the Mishnah's case involves intermediate knowledge, and according to Rabban Gamliel, who holds there is no liability for half-measures, the person is liable for two sin-offerings.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that the Mishnah's case involves intermediate knowledge, and according to Rabban Gamliel, who holds there is no awareness for a half-measure, the person is liable.

The Gemara cites a baraita about one who writes two letters in two lapses of awareness, where Rabban Gamliel deems him liable and the Sages exempt, supporting the principle of no awareness for a half-measure.
The Gemara clarifies the dispute: Rabban Gamliel holds there is no awareness for a half-measure, while the Sages hold there is awareness for a half-measure.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the duration of eating
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the duration of eating
items.desc_en: The Mishnah debates how long one must eat to be liable, with Rabbi Meir comparing it to eating roasted grains and the Sages requiring the time of eating a half-loaf. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir is lenient or stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the question of how long one must eat to be liable, and presents Rabbi Meir's opinion comparing it to eating roasted grains.
The Sages state that one is liable only if the eating spans the time of eating a half-loaf from start to finish.
The Mishnah adds cases of eating impure foods and drinking a quarter-log of wine before entering the Temple, with Rabbi Elazar's leniency if one pauses or adds water.
The Gemara raises a question: does Rabbi Meir's opinion in the Mishnah intend to be stringent or lenient?
The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Meir is stringent, meaning even a very long eating time counts, while the Sages limit liability to the time of a half-loaf.
The Gemara alternatively suggests that Rabbi Meir is lenient, exempting if there is any interruption, while the Sages require continuous eating within the half-loaf time.
The Gemara resolves the question by citing the Sages' statement that the time is from start to finish within a half-loaf, implying Rabbi Meir's position is the lenient one.

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Meir is stringent
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Meir is stringent
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Meir were lenient, the Mishnah would have used the phrase 'if he delayed' (אם שהה) instead of 'until he delays' (עד שישהה). Therefore, Rabbi Meir must be stringent, requiring the entire eating to be within the time of eating a half-loaf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Meir is stringent, the Mishnah's phrase 'עד שישהא' (until he delays) makes sense, requiring his delay to be within the time of eating a half-loaf.
The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Meir were lenient, the Mishnah would have used 'אם שהה' (if he delayed), and concludes that Rabbi Meir is indeed stringent.

items.text: Ravnai's statement about different foods
items.text_en: Ravnai's statement about different foods
items.desc_en: Ravnai said in the name of Shmuel that for forbidden fats and neveilah, the time limit is from beginning to end within the time of eating a half-loaf. For impure foods, insects, and liquids, even if the eating spans the entire day, it must be within the time of eating a half-loaf. Rav Pappa explains that this means even if the eating takes all day, each olive-sized portion must be consumed within the time of eating a half-loaf.

sub.text: Ravnai in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Ravnai in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Ravnai states in the name of Shmuel that for forbidden fats and neveilah, the time limit is from beginning to end within the time of eating a half-loaf, while for impure foods, insects, and liquids, even if the eating spans the entire day, it must be within the time of eating a half-loaf.
Rav Pappa explains that Ravnai's statement means that even if the eating takes all day, each olive-sized portion must be consumed within the time of eating a half-loaf.

items.text: Objection from a baraita on combining foods
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita on combining foods
items.desc_en: A baraita states that all foods combine to disqualify the body with half a loaf. The Gemara asks if this means eating half a loaf within the time of eating a half-loaf. It answers that it means eating olive-sized portions one after another within the time of eating a half-loaf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that all foods combine to disqualify the body with half a loaf, implying a single eating event.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita means that one ate the entire half-loaf within the time of eating a half-loaf.
The Gemara answers that it means one ate olive-sized portions one after another within the time of eating a half-loaf.

items.text: Baraita detailing the law of combining foods and liquids
items.text_en: Baraita detailing the law of combining foods and liquids
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that all foods combine to disqualify the body with half a loaf within the time of eating a half-loaf. If one ate and then ate again, if the time from the start of the first eating to the end of the last eating is within the time of eating a half-loaf, they combine; otherwise not. It also discusses the permissibility for a pregnant woman to eat less than the minimum due to danger, and for a woman impure from corpse contact to nurse her son, who remains pure.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the rule that all foods combine to disqualify the body with half a loaf within the time of eating a half-loaf, and explains the combining rule for sequential eating.
The baraita states that one is not permitted to eat less than the minimum to go down and immerse, but a pregnant woman is permitted to eat less than the minimum due to danger.
The baraita adds that all liquids combine to disqualify the body with a quarter-log within the time of eating a half-loaf, with a similar sequential drinking rule.
The baraita concludes by permitting a woman impure from corpse contact to nurse her son, and the son remains pure.

items.text: Refutation of Ravnai
items.text_en: Refutation of Ravnai
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the baraita, which requires the entire eating to be within the time of eating a half-loaf, refutes Ravnai's statement. This is a conclusive refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the baraita, which requires the entire eating to be within the time of eating a half-loaf, refutes Ravnai's statement, declaring it a conclusive refutation.

items.text: Explanation of the law regarding eating less than the minimum
items.text_en: Explanation of the law regarding eating less than the minimum
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita means by 'they did not permit one to eat less than the minimum to go down and immerse.' Rav Yehuda explains: if one ate less than the minimum, they are not permitted to go down and immerse, because if they did and then completed the measure, it would combine, and they might mistakenly think the first immersion was effective, when only the last one counts.

items.text: Clarification of the law for a pregnant woman
items.text_en: Clarification of the law for a pregnant woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita permits a pregnant woman to eat less than the minimum only due to danger; if danger is the reason, she should be allowed to eat even a large amount. Rav Pappa explains that the baraita means they permitted her to eat less than the minimum, even a large amount, due to danger.

sub.desc_en: Gemara asks: the baraita says they permitted a pregnant woman to eat less than the minimum due to danger. Due to danger, even a lot she may eat! Rav Papa says: it means they permitted her less than the minimum, even a lot, due to danger.
Rav Pappa explains that the baraita means they permitted her to eat less than the minimum, even a large amount, due to danger.

items.text: Discussion of why the nursing son remains pure
items.text_en: Discussion of why the nursing son remains pure
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the son of a woman impure from corpse contact remains pure, since the milk should become impure. It first suggests that the milk was not made susceptible to impurity, but objects that a dirty drop on the nipple would make it susceptible. Rav Nachman bar Rav Abba says she expressed the milk in one squeeze, leaving no dirty drop. Rava objects, noting that the baby's mouth is full of milk, and that the place of milk is a spring. The Gemara then cites a baraita that woman's milk is impure even against her will, implying it is always susceptible. Rava concludes that the son is pure due to multiple doubts: perhaps he did not nurse the minimum measure, and even if he did, perhaps it was within the time of eating a half-loaf or beyond it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the son of a woman impure from corpse contact remains pure, since the milk should become impure.
The Gemara objects that even if the milk was not made susceptible, a dirty drop on the nipple would make it susceptible.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Abba's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Abba's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Abba answers that she expressed the milk in one squeeze, leaving no dirty drop on the nipple.
Rava objects with two points: the baby's mouth is full of milk, and the place of milk is a spring.
The Gemara cites a baraita that woman's milk is impure even against her will, implying it is always susceptible.
The Gemara infers that 'against her will' means she does not want it, yet the baraita says it is impure.
Rava concludes that the son is pure due to multiple doubts: perhaps he did not nurse the minimum measure, and even if he did, perhaps it was within the time of eating a half-loaf or beyond it.

items.text: Challenge to Rava's view that the place of milk is a spring
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava's view that the place of milk is a spring
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's statement that the place of milk is a spring and does not need intentional wetting. It cites a Mishnah where a woman's milk drips into an oven and the oven becomes impure, requiring an explanation of how the milk became susceptible. Rabbi Yochanan said it was due to a dirty drop on the nipple. The Gemara then questions whether Rava disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan, and cites a baraita listing nine liquids that are impure, implying that milk is not automatically susceptible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's view that the place of milk is a spring, implying it does not need intentional wetting (הכשר) to become susceptible to impurity.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a woman's milk drips into an oven and the oven becomes impure, and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation that the milk was made susceptible by a dirty drop on the nipple.
The Gemara objects that if one claims Rava disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan, a baraita listing nine liquids that are impure implies milk is not automatically susceptible, contradicting Rava.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: breast milk should be a severe impurity
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: breast milk should be a severe impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why breast milk is only impure as a liquid (requiring a quarter-log) and not a severe impurity like her saliva or flux, which are impure in any amount. It argues that if the source of milk is a fountain, it should be like her other bodily fluids.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges why breast milk is only impure as a liquid (quarter-log) and not a severe impurity like her saliva or flux, arguing that if the source is a fountain, it should be like her other bodily fluids.

items.text: Rava's statement and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's statement and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a Mishnah where Rava says breast milk is impure whether the baby wants it or not, implying it is a fountain. The Gemara resolves that 'not wanted' means the baby's mind is drawn to milk, but if the baby explicitly says he does not want it, the milk is pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a Mishnah where Rava says breast milk is impure whether the baby wants it or not, implying it is a fountain.
The Gemara resolves that 'not wanted' means the baby's mind is drawn to milk, but if the baby explicitly says he does not want it, the milk is pure.

items.text: Explanation of the Mishnah's requirement of waiting
items.text_en: Explanation of the Mishnah's requirement of waiting
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions 'and waited' regarding eating impure foods and drinking wine before entering the Temple. Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah means one ate impure foods, drank impure liquids, drank a quarter-log of wine, and waited the time it takes to eat a half-loaf, then entered the Temple—he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions 'and waited' regarding eating impure foods and drinking wine before entering the Temple.

Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah means one ate impure foods, drank impure liquids, drank a quarter-log of wine, and waited the time it takes to eat a half-loaf, then entered the Temple—he is liable.

items.text: Tannaitic debate on the prohibition of wine for priests
items.text_en: Tannaitic debate on the prohibition of wine for priests
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the verse 'Wine and strong drink do not drink' and derives that only an intoxicating amount is forbidden, specifically a quarter-log of forty-day-old wine. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar offer different interpretations: Rabbi Yehuda says wine is punishable by death, other intoxicants by a warning; Rabbi Elazar says if one dilutes the wine or pauses, he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'Wine and strong drink do not drink' and raises the possibility that it might forbid even a minimal amount or even from the vat.
The baraita derives from the word 'שכר' (strong drink) that only an intoxicating amount is forbidden, specifically a quarter-log of forty-day-old wine.
The baraita explains that the word 'יין' (wine) teaches that priests are warned even about a minimal amount and even from the vat.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that 'יין' alone would limit the prohibition to wine, but 'שכר' includes other intoxicants; wine is punishable by death, other drinks by a warning.
Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse to mean 'do not drink it in its intoxicating manner,' so if one pauses or dilutes it with any water, he is exempt.

items.text: Explanation of the dispute between the Tannaim
items.text_en: Explanation of the dispute between the Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the basis of the dispute: the first Tanna learns a gezerah shavah from 'shechar' to 'shechar' of a nazirite; Rabbi Yehuda does not learn this gezerah shavah; Rabbi Elazar holds that 'shechar' means anything intoxicating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the basis of the dispute between the Tannaim regarding the prohibition of wine for a priest serving in the Temple.
The Gemara explains that the first Tanna learns a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'שכר' to 'שכר' of a nazirite, thereby including all intoxicating drinks.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda does not learn this גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), so he limits the death penalty to wine alone.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar holds that 'שכר' means anything intoxicating, so he exempts a priest who diluted the wine or interrupted his drinking.

items.text: Practical ruling and incident with Rav Acha
items.text_en: Practical ruling and incident with Rav Acha
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who eats dried figs and drinks honey or milk and enters the Temple is liable, and this follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Yehuda bar Achotai rules like Rabbi Elazar, and Rav praises him. An incident with Rav Acha of Hutzaal, who was under a vow, comes before Rav Ashi, who delays judgment due to intoxication, and they discuss the difference between a quarter-log and more.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that one who eats dried figs and drinks honey or milk and enters the Temple is liable, and this follows Rabbi Yehuda's position.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Achotai and Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Achotai and Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Achotai rules the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Elazar, and Rav praises Rabbi Elazar as 'the best of the sages'.

sub.text: Rav Acha's inquiry to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha's inquiry to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha of Hutzaal, who was under a vow, comes before Rav Ashi, who delays judgment due to intoxication from the festival.
Rav Acha objects that Rav himself ruled like Rabbi Elazar, who permits diluted wine, yet Rav Ashi is acting strictly.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a quarter-log of wine and more than a quarter-log.

items.text: Derivation of the priest's teaching duties and ruling on drunk priests
items.text_en: Derivation of the priest's teaching duties and ruling on drunk priests
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds verses to include various categories of teaching, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda excludes Talmud from the prohibition of teaching while drunk. The Gemara asks if a baraita about a drunk priest ruling on a clean frog follows Rabbi Yosei, and answers it could even be the Rabbis, as it is a trivial matter. Rav rules like Rabbi Yosei, and explains that Rav himself taught while drunk because he was accustomed to teaching.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the verse 'וּלְהַבְדִּיל...' to include various categories of teaching: valuations, purity laws, rulings, midrashim, halacha, and Talmud.
The baraita records a dispute: the first Tanna excludes Mishnah from the prohibition of teaching while drunk, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda excludes Talmud.
The Gemara asks whether a baraita allowing a drunk priest to rule on a clean frog follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's view.
The Gemara answers that even the Rabbis could agree, because the matter is trivial and well-known.
Rav rules like Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, and the Gemara explains that Rav himself taught while drunk because he was accustomed to teaching and could not avoid it.

items.text: Mishnah: Four sin-offerings and one guilt-offering for one eating
items.text_en: Mishnah: Four sin-offerings and one guilt-offering for one eating
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who eats a single meal can be liable for four sin-offerings and one guilt-offering: a person who is impure eats forbidden fat that is leftover from sacrifices on Yom Kippur. Rabbi Meir adds that if it was Shabbat and he carried it out, he is also liable, but the Sages disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who eats a single meal can be liable for four sin-offerings and one guilt-offering: a person who is impure eats forbidden fat that is leftover from sacrifices on Yom Kippur.
Rabbi Meir adds that if it was Shabbat and he carried it out, he is also liable.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Meir, saying that carrying out is not included in the same category.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Meir accept איסור כולל and איסור מוסיף?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Meir accept איסור כולל and איסור מוסיף?
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Meir does not accept איסור חל על איסור (a prohibition taking effect on another prohibition), but he does accept איסור כולל and איסור מוסיף. It then illustrates this with a case of a person who is tahor (pure) and eats forbidden fat (חלב), then becomes tamei (impure), and then consecrates the fat, and then it becomes notar, and then Yom Kippur occurs, each step adding a new prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Meir does not accept איסור חל על איסור (a prohibition taking effect on another prohibition) but does accept איסור כולל (an inclusive prohibition) and איסור מוסיף (an added prohibition), and illustrates this with a multi-step case involving forbidden fat, impurity, consecration, notar, and Yom Kippur.

items.text: Challenge: Why not teach five sin-offerings for piggul?
items.text_en: Challenge: Why not teach five sin-offerings for piggul?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not list a case of eating a kezayit of piggul (a sacrificial offering that became invalid due to improper intent) as incurring five sin-offerings. It answers that the Mishnah deals with one animal, and piggul and notar cannot coexist in one animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not teach five sin-offerings and explain it as a case of eating an olive's bulk of piggul (a disqualified sacrifice), and answers that the Mishnah deals with one animal, and piggul and notar cannot coexist in one animal.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with one animal, and piggul and notar (leftover sacrificial meat) cannot coexist in a single animal.

items.text: Objection and resolution: piggul and notar in one limb
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: piggul and notar in one limb
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that piggul and notar can coexist in one animal if a limb of piggul is offered on the altar, causing its piggul status to lapse and become notar. It then answers that the Mishnah deals with one limb, and piggul and notar cannot coexist in one limb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one can find piggul and notar in one animal by bringing a piggul limb onto the altar, causing its piggul status to lapse and become notar, but the Mishnah deals with one limb, and piggul and notar cannot coexist in one limb.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with one limb, and piggul and notar cannot coexist in one limb.

items.text: Further objection: piggul and notar in half a limb
items.text_en: Further objection: piggul and notar in half a limb
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that piggul and notar can coexist in half a limb if part of the limb is placed on the altar and part is outside, citing Ulla's principle. The Gemara responds that the Mishnah deals with a case where the majority of the limb is on the altar or outside, not half and half.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that piggul and notar can coexist in half a limb if part is on the altar and part outside, citing Ulla's principle that a piggul offering placed on the altar loses its piggul status and becomes notar.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with a case where the majority of the limb is either on the altar or outside, not half and half, so piggul and notar cannot coexist in the same limb.

items.text: Resolution: one kezayit, and the case of Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Resolution: one kezayit, and the case of Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah deals with one kezayit, not two. It then questions this because the Mishnah includes Yom Kippur, which involves a kotevet (fat tail) that contains two kezaytim. Rabbi Zeira and Rav Papa offer solutions: eating the kulya (kidney) with its fat, or filling the kotevet with dates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah deals with one kezayit (olive-sized portion), not two, and thus the question of Rami bar Chama about following the majority in limbs is resolved.
The Gemara objects: the Mishnah includes Yom Kippur, and the kotevet (fat tail) of Yom Kippur contains two kezaytim, contradicting the resolution.
Rabbi Zeira answers that the case is where one ate a kulya (kidney) with its fat, which is only one kezayit.
Rav Papa answers that the case is where one filled the kotevet with dates, making it a single kezayit of fat.

items.text: Alternative version: Rav Adda bar Ahava's teaching
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rav Adda bar Ahava's teaching
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava teaches the Mishnah as 'five sin-offerings' and resolves it simply as eating a kezayit of piggul, without the earlier distinctions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Acha teaches the Mishnah as 'five sin-offerings' and resolves it simply as eating an olive's bulk of piggul, without the earlier distinctions.

items.text: Challenge: Why not teach six sin-offerings for blood?
items.text_en: Challenge: Why not teach six sin-offerings for blood?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not list a case of eating a kezayit of blood as incurring six sin-offerings. It answers that the Mishnah deals with one act of eating, and the sages determined that the throat cannot hold more than two kezaytim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not teach six sin-offerings and explain it as eating an olive's bulk of blood, and answers that the Mishnah deals with one eating, and the mouth cannot hold more than two olive's bulks.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with one act of eating, and the sages determined that the throat cannot hold more than two kezaytim.

items.text: Discussion of Rafram's statement on Shabbat and Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Discussion of Rafram's statement on Shabbat and Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses Rafram's statement that there is no eiruv and hotza'ah (carrying) on Yom Kippur, based on the Mishnah's phrasing. It questions this from a baraita about the scapegoat, and concludes that Rafram's statement is a mistake (ברותא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions Shabbat specifically, implying that without Shabbat there would be no liability for carrying.
Rafram answers that the Mishnah implies there is no eiruv and hotza'ah (carrying) on Yom Kippur, only on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that perhaps there is eiruv and hotza'ah on Yom Kippur, and the Mishnah means one is liable for both Shabbat and Yom Kippur.
The Gemara cites a baraita about the scapegoat, which permits a non-priest to send it even on Shabbat, to provide context for Rafram's statement.
Rafram applies his statement to the baraita, concluding that eiruv and hotza'ah apply only on Shabbat, not on Yom Kippur.
The Gemara objects that the scapegoat is a special case because its dispatch is integral to the Yom Kippur service, so it does not prove a general rule.
The Gemara concludes that Rafram's statement is a mistake (ברותא), meaning it is not accepted as halacha.

items.text: Mishnah: One act of intercourse incurs six sin-offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: One act of intercourse incurs six sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who has intercourse with his daughter incurs six sin-offerings: for his daughter, his sister, his brother's wife, his father's brother's wife, a married woman, and a niddah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one can be liable for six sin-offerings for one act of intercourse, listing the forbidden relationships: daughter, sister, brother's wife, father's brother's wife, married woman, and menstruant.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Meir and איסור מוסיף
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Meir and איסור מוסיף
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir, who rejects איסור חל על איסור, can hold a person liable for multiple prohibitions. It answers that he accepts איסור מוסיף, and illustrates with a case where a man's daughter becomes his sister-in-law, adding prohibitions for others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir, who rejects איסור חל על איסור (a prohibition taking effect on an existing prohibition), can hold a person liable for multiple prohibitions, and answers that he accepts איסור מוסיף (an added prohibition), illustrating with a case where a man's daughter becomes his sister-in-law, adding prohibitions for others.

items.text: Mishnah: One who has relations with his granddaughter
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who has relations with his granddaughter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the prohibitions incurred by one who has relations with his granddaughter, including בת בתו, כלתו, אשת אחיו, etc. Rabbi Yosei adds that if an elder married her, he is also liable for אשת אב.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the prohibitions incurred by one who has relations with his granddaughter, and adds Rabbi Yosei's opinion that if an elder married her, he is also liable for אשת אב (his father's wife).

items.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yosei's case
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yosei's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yosei can permit אשת אב, and Rabbi Yochanan explains it refers to a yevamah who fell to him for levirate marriage. Rabbi Yaakov clarifies that 'passed' means he violated the prohibition of כלת בנו, a secondary prohibition, as taught in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yosei can permit אשת אב (a father's wife) to the man, since she is forbidden to him.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the case is where the woman fell to him for יבום (levirate marriage), so she is permitted to him initially.
The Gemara asks: if she is permitted, why does the mishnah say 'עָבַר' (he passed/violated)?
Rabbi Yaakov explains that 'עָבַר' means he violated the prohibition of כלת בנו (his son's daughter-in-law), which is a secondary (שנייה) prohibition, not the primary one of אשת אב.

A baraita is cited to support Rabbi Yaakov's distinction: 'כַּלָּתוֹ' (his daughter-in-law) is a primary ערווה (forbidden relative), but 'כַּלַּת בְּנוֹ' (his son's daughter-in-law) is only a secondary prohibition, and this pattern extends to all subsequent generations.

items.text: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yosei accept איסור חל על איסור?
items.text_en: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yosei accept איסור חל על איסור?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yosei does not accept איסור חל על איסור, citing a Mishnah where he judges by the first prohibition. A baraita illustrates: if a mother-in-law becomes an אשת איש, he judges her for חמותו, not the later prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei accepts איסור חל על איסור (a prohibition taking effect on an existing prohibition), citing a Mishnah and baraita where he rules that a person is judged by the first prohibition that applied.
A baraita illustrates Rabbi Yosei's principle: if a mother-in-law becomes an אשת איש (married woman), he judges her for the original prohibition of חמותו (mother-in-law), not the later one.
The baraita adds the reverse case: if an אשת איש (married woman) becomes a mother-in-law, Rabbi Yosei judges her for the original prohibition of אשת איש (married woman).

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Yosei accepts איסור מוסיף
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Yosei accepts איסור מוסיף
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu and Rabbi Yochanan state that Rabbi Yosei concedes to איסור מוסיף. The Gemara explains the additional prohibition: if the elder has a son, the prohibition extends to the son, adding a new layer of prohibition for the elder himself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu states that Rabbi Yosei concedes to the principle of איסור מוסיף (an added prohibition).
Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan likewise affirms that Rabbi Yosei concedes to איסור מוסיף.
The Gemara asks what specific added prohibition exists in this case.
The Gemara explains: if the elder has a son, the prohibition extends to the son, thereby adding a new layer of prohibition for the elder himself.

items.text: Mishnah: One who has relations with his mother-in-law
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who has relations with his mother-in-law
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibitions for one who has relations with his mother-in-law, including חמותו, כלתו, etc. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri adds prohibitions for אם חמותו and אם חמיו, but the Sages say all three are the same prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the prohibitions for one who has relations with his mother-in-law, and records Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's opinion that he is liable for three specific prohibitions, to which the Sages respond that all three are the same category.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri adds that one is also liable for relations with אם חמותו and אם חמיו.
The Sages reject Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's addition, asserting that all three are the same prohibition.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Somchos agree
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Somchos agree
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Hoshaya states that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Somchos said the same thing. The Gemara notes the case of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and asks about Somchos, citing a Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Hoshaya states that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Sumchos said the same thing, and begins to cite the relevant Mishnah about Sumchos.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position is already known, and asks what Somchos' comparable statement is.
The Gemara introduces a Mishnah to identify Somchos' position.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Sumchus and the Sages
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Sumchus and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who slaughters an animal and its granddaughter, and then slaughters its daughter, receives forty lashes. Sumchus says in the name of Rabbi Meir that he receives eighty.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: one who slaughters an animal and its granddaughter, then its daughter, receives forty lashes; Sumchus in Rabbi Meir's name says eighty.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah: Rava and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah: Rava and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rava suggests that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's ruling applies only where the names are distinct, but not for 'it and its son' where the name is the same. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak counters that Sumchus's ruling applies only where the bodies are distinct, but here the bodies are not distinct, so perhaps he agrees with Rabbi Avahu's teaching that the verse makes them all one zimah.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions whether Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's ruling applies only where the names are distinct, but not for 'it and its son' where the name is the same.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak counters that Sumchus's ruling applies only where the bodies are distinct, but here the bodies are not distinct, so perhaps he agrees with Rabbi Avahu's teaching that the verse makes them all one zimah.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's question about one who has relations with his sister, paternal sister, and maternal sister
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's question about one who has relations with his sister, paternal sister, and maternal sister
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva asks Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua whether one who has relations with his sister, his paternal sister, and his maternal sister is liable once for all or for each one. They respond that they have not heard, but they have heard that one who has relations with five women who are niddot in one lapse of awareness is liable for each, and they reason a fortiori.

sub.desc_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva asks Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua whether one who has relations with his sister, his paternal sister, and his maternal sister is liable once for all or for each one. They respond that they have not heard, but they have heard that one who has relations with five women who are niddot in one lapse of awareness is liable for each, and they reason a fortiori.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah: The case is a woman who is both paternal and maternal sister
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah: The case is a woman who is both paternal and maternal sister
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the case is as stated, why is there a question? The names are distinct and the bodies are distinct! Rather, the case is one who has relations with his paternal sister who is also his maternal sister. The Sages respond that they have not heard, but they have heard about five niddot in one lapse, and they reason a fortiori.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the case is as stated in the Mishnah, why is there a question? The names are distinct and the bodies are distinct!

The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah: the case is one who has relations with his paternal sister who is also his maternal sister, raising the question of whether the distinct names or the single body governs.
The Sages respond that they have not heard about this case, but they have heard about one who has relations with five niddot in one lapse, where he is liable for each one.
The Sages reason a fortiori: if one is liable for each of five niddot under a single name, then for three distinct names he should certainly be liable for each.

items.text: Refutation of the a fortiori argument and a scriptural proof
items.text_en: Refutation of the a fortiori argument and a scriptural proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: The case of five niddot is different because the bodies are distinct. Rather, the verse 'the nakedness of his sister he has uncovered' teaches liability for a sister who is also a paternal and maternal sister.

sub.desc_en: Objection: What about five niddot — because their bodies are distinct!
The Gemara resolves the issue by citing the verse 'עֶרְוַת אֲחוֹתוֹ גִלָּה' (the nakedness of his sister he has uncovered) to teach liability for a sister who is also a paternal and maternal sister.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's scenario for the case
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's scenario for the case
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah explains that the case involves a wicked son of a wicked man: one who had relations with his mother and fathered two daughters, then had relations with one daughter and fathered a son, and that son had relations with his maternal sister who is also his sister and paternal sister.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah explains the scenario of a wicked son of a wicked man who had relations with his mother and daughters, resulting in a son who has relations with his maternal sister who is also his sister and paternal sister.

items.text: Baraita: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages about repeated acts
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages about repeated acts
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: If one had relations with her, and again, and again, Rabbi Eliezer says he is liable for each, while the Sages say only one. They agree that for five niddot in one lapse he is liable for each because the bodies are distinct. Rava questions the reasoning 'because he caused them' and suggests instead 'because the bodies are distinct'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer holds one is liable for each repeated act of intercourse with the same woman, while the Sages hold only one liability.
The baraita adds that the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer regarding five distinct niddot (menstruating women) in one lapse, because he caused their states.
Rava objects to the reasoning 'because he caused them', citing a baraita where he is liable only once despite causing multiple transgressions.
Rava resolves by replacing the reason with 'because the bodies are distinct', which justifies liability for each distinct woman.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning for repeated acts of cutting
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning for repeated acts of cutting
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about Rabbi Eliezer's view on one who cuts and cuts again: is it because he performed two acts, or because he cannot combine them? Rabba and Rav Yosef debate. Abaye objects from a baraita about Shabbat, and Mar bar Rabbanan explains that the case involves a branch over a fig tree cut at once, where Rabbi Eliezer is liable due to distinct names and bodies, but cutting two figs at once is exempt, while cutting one fig and then another is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about Rabbi Eliezer's view on one who cuts and cuts again: what is his reasoning?
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is because he performed two acts, and here too he performed two acts.
The Gemara proposes alternatively that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is because he cannot combine the acts, and asks which is correct.
Rabba holds that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is because he performed two acts, and here too he performed two acts.
Rav Yosef holds that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is because he cannot combine the acts, but if he could combine them, he would be liable only once.
Abaye objects to Rabba from a baraita about Shabbat: if Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is because he performed two acts, why is one who performs two primary categories of labor at once exempt?

Mar bar Rabbanan explains that the baraita deals with a branch over a fig tree cut at once, where Rabbi Eliezer is liable due to distinct names and bodies, but cutting two figs at once is exempt, while cutting one fig and then another is liable.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's question about a dangling limb
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's question about a dangling limb
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records another question of Rabbi Akiva: What is the law regarding a dangling limb on an animal? They said they have not heard, but they have heard that a dangling limb on a person is pure, and so they were...

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva asks about the law of a dangling limb on an animal.
The Sages respond that they have not heard a ruling on this, but they have heard that a dangling limb on a person is pure, and so they were...

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Bloodletting for boils on Passover eve
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Bloodletting for boils on Passover eve
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes a procedure for one with boils to undergo bloodletting on Passover eve, allowing both the patient and the doctor to offer the Paschal lamb. It concludes with a kal vachomer argument.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the ruling that those with boils may undergo bloodletting in Jerusalem on Passover eve, and both the patient and doctor may offer the Paschal lamb, concluding with a kal vachomer argument.

items.text: Gemara: The law of squeezing a boil and the principle of 'at the time of separation'
items.text_en: Gemara: The law of squeezing a boil and the principle of 'at the time of separation'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about squeezing a boil and the status of liquids. Shmuel states that the boil itself becomes susceptible to impurity. The Gemara raises a contradiction from the Mishnah about bloodletting, and resolves it with Rav Yosef's principle of 'splashing with full force'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about one who wipes a leek or squeezes hair/clothing, stating that liquid inside does not render susceptible but liquid that comes out does.
Shmuel states that the leek itself becomes susceptible to impurity because at the moment the water separates from it, it renders the leek susceptible.
The Gemara raises an objection from the Mishnah about bloodletting: if separation renders susceptible, then a dangling limb should render the person impure at the moment of separation.

The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rav Yosef's principle that the case involves liquids removed with great force, so the limb is pulled off in one motion and does not touch the person after detachment.
The Gemara identifies the context of Rav Yosef's statement: a baraita about a zav and a corpse-impure person walking in rain, where liquids flowing down are pure until they fully emerge.
Rav Yosef explains that once liquids fully emerge they render susceptible, but the baraita deals with liquids removed with great force, so they do not become impure upon separation.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's question about one who slaughters five sacrifices outside
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's question about one who slaughters five sacrifices outside
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Shimon regarding one who eats notar from five sacrifices in one lapse of awareness. Rabbi Yehoshua brings a kal vachomer from me'ilah, and Rabbi Akiva refutes it by distinguishing me'ilah from notar.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva asks the Sages about one who slaughters five offerings outside during one lapse of awareness, and they respond that they have not heard a ruling.
Rabbi Yehoshua reports a tradition about one who eats from one offering in five pots being liable for each pot due to me'ilah, and proposes a kal vachomer to the case of slaughtering five offerings.
Rabbi Shimon corrects the question: Rabbi Akiva actually asked about one who eats notar from five offerings, and the Sages again said they had not heard.
