Rabbi Yehoshua again cites his tradition about me'ilah and applies a kal vachomer to the case of notar from five offerings.
Rabbi Akiva challenges Rabbi Yehoshua: if it is a received halakha, they will accept it, but if it is based on a kal vachomer, there is a refutation; Rabbi Yehoshua invites him to respond.
Rabbi Akiva refutes the kal vachomer by distinguishing me'ilah, which has unique stringencies (treating the feeder like the eater and joining multiple acts), from notar, which lacks these.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying Rabbi Shimon's objection and the correct version of the question
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying Rabbi Shimon's objection and the correct version of the question
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's objection: the kal vachomer from me'ilah to slaughter is flawed because the one who eats benefits. It then presents the corrected version of the question regarding eating notar from five sacrifices, with Rabbi Yehoshua's kal vachomer from one sacrifice in five dishes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what bothered Rabbi Shimon about Rabbi Yehoshua's original kal vachomer, and explains that the objection is that the kal vachomer from me'ilah to slaughter is flawed because the one who eats benefits (נהנה), unlike the slaughterer.

The Gemara presents the corrected version of the question: regarding eating notar from five sacrifices, Rabbi Yehoshua's kal vachomer from one sacrifice in five dishes applies directly, without the flaw of benefit.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon's restatement and Rabbi Akiva's response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's restatement and Rabbi Akiva's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon restates the corrected question and Rabbi Yehoshua's kal vachomer, and Rabbi Akiva responds that if it is a tradition (הלכה) they will accept it, but if it is a logical argument there is a refutation.

items.text: Gemara: Did Rabbi Yehoshua accept Rabbi Akiva's refutation? A baraita resolves the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Did Rabbi Yehoshua accept Rabbi Akiva's refutation? A baraita resolves the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehoshua accepted Rabbi Akiva's refutation. A baraita is brought that rules: for one who eats five pieces of notar from one sacrifice in five dishes in one lapse, he brings one sin-offering; from five sacrifices in one lapse, he is liable. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda disagrees, stating a general principle: as they differ in sin-offerings, so they differ in ashamot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehoshua accepted Rabbi Akiva's refutation.
A baraita is brought to resolve the question, detailing the liability for eating five pieces of notar from one sacrifice in various scenarios.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda disagrees, stating a general principle that as they differ in sin-offerings, so they differ in ashamot.
The baraita concludes with a ruling that eating pieces from one sacrifice before blood sprinkling incurs liability for each piece due to מעילה (misappropriation).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's author and Rabbi Akiva's principle
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's author and Rabbi Akiva's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's omission of asham taluy for uncertainties, suggesting it follows Rabbi Yehoshua who rejected Rabbi Akiva's view. It then proposes that the Mishnah might be a dispute between Tanna'im, or that the Tanna accepts Rabbi Akiva on he'lem but disputes me'ilot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah does not include the case of bringing an asham taluy (conditional guilt offering) for uncertainties, and suggests that if it followed Rabbi Akiva, it should have included it.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah must follow Rabbi Yehoshua, who accepted Rabbi Akiva's principle regarding he'lem (unwitting acts) but not regarding me'ilot (sacrilege).
The Gemara objects that from the Mishnah's ruling that one is liable for each of five sacrifices even in one he'lem, it appears that Rabbi Yehoshua did not accept Rabbi Akiva's principle.
The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah reflects a dispute among Tanna'im, with some accepting Rabbi Akiva's principle and others rejecting it.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the Mishnah could follow Rabbi Akiva, with the Tanna accepting his view on he'lem but disputing him on me'ilot.

items.text: Amoraic definitions of five me'ilot
items.text_en: Amoraic definitions of five me'ilot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how five me'ilot are possible, and various Amoraim offer scenarios: Shmuel cites the five items that combine for olah, Chizkiyah says eating from five limbs, Resh Lakish says even one limb like the shoulder, Rabbi Yitzchak says five types of pottage, and Rabbi Yochanan says five tastes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the scenario of five me'ilot (misappropriations) is possible.
Shmuel answers that it refers to the five items that combine for an olah offering: meat, milk, wine, flour, and oil.
Chizkiyah answers that it is when one eats from five different limbs of the same animal.
Resh Lakish answers that even one limb, such as the shoulder, can yield five me'ilot.
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha answers that it is when one eats from five types of pottage.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that it is when one eats five distinct tastes.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's question to Rabbi Eliezer about multiple labors on multiple Shabbatot
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's question to Rabbi Eliezer about multiple labors on multiple Shabbatot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva asks Rabbi Eliezer whether one who performs many labors on many Shabbatot in one lapse is liable once or for each. Rabbi Eliezer argues via kal vachomer from niddah, but Rabbi Akiva refutes each proof, and Rabbi Eliezer's final analogy to bestiality is rejected as comparable to Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva asks Rabbi Eliezer whether one who performs many labors on many Shabbatot in one lapse is liable once or for each.
Rabbi Eliezer answers that he is liable for each, deriving this via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from niddah.
Rabbi Akiva objects that niddah has two prohibitions (one for each party), unlike Shabbat which has only one.
Rabbi Eliezer counters with the case of one who has relations with minor girls, which has only one prohibition yet incurs liability for each act.
Rabbi Akiva objects that minor girls will eventually become subject to the prohibition, whereas Shabbat has no future applicability.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer's third response and Rabbi Akiva's rejection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's third response and Rabbi Akiva's rejection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer proposes bestiality as a parallel, but Rabbi Akiva rejects it, stating that bestiality is comparable to Shabbat (and thus the analogy fails).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Akiva's question: what exactly was asked?
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Akiva's question: what exactly was asked?
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Akiva asked two questions: whether Shabbatot are considered separate entities, and whether sub-categories of labor are like primary categories. Rava explains the two possibilities: either the question was about Shabbatot with intent and labor error, or about labor intent and Shabbat error. The daf ends with Rabba's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what exactly Rabbi Akiva was asking Rabbi Eliezer: whether Shabbatot are considered separate entities or whether sub-categories of labor are like primary categories, and notes that if it were only one issue, the question could have been phrased differently.
Rava states that Rabbi Akiva asked two questions: whether Shabbatot are considered separate entities and whether sub-categories of labor are like primary categories.

The Gemara analyzes the two possible scenarios for the question about Shabbatot: either the case of Shabbat error with intent regarding labor was clear and the doubt was about labor error with Shabbat intent, or vice versa.
The daf ends with Rabba beginning a statement, which is cut off at the page break.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and unresolved answers
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and unresolved answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the question about whether Sabbaths are considered separate entities (gufin) was asked regarding the case of intentional Sabbath violation with unwitting labor, and the answer that they are like separate entities was not accepted. Similarly, the question about subcategories of labor (toladot) being like primary categories was answered affirmatively but not accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the question about whether Sabbaths are separate entities (גופין) was asked regarding the case of intentional Sabbath violation with unwitting labor, not the reverse.
The Gemara reports that the master answered that Sabbaths are like separate entities and that subcategories are like primary categories, but neither answer was accepted.

items.text: Rabbah's proof from the mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbah's proof from the mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbah cites a mishnah about the general principle of Shabbat: one who forgets the essence of Shabbat is liable for only one offering, while one who knows the essence is liable for each Shabbat, and one who knows it is Shabbat is liable for each primary category of labor. He notes that the mishnah does not say 'liable for each primary category of each Shabbat,' implying that Sabbaths are not separate entities.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah introduces his proof by citing the mishnah's general rule about Shabbat: one who forgets the essence of Shabbat is liable for only one offering.
The mishnah continues: one who knows the essence of Shabbat is liable for each Shabbat, and one who knows it is Shabbat is liable for each primary category of labor.
Rabbah notes that the mishnah does not say 'liable for each primary category of each Shabbat,' implying that Sabbaths are not separate entities for liability.

items.text: Identifying the mishnah as Rabbi Akiva's
items.text_en: Identifying the mishnah as Rabbi Akiva's
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the mishnah: it cannot be Rabbi Eliezer's, because the latter part says one who performs multiple subcategories of labor is liable only once, but Rabbi Eliezer holds one is liable for each subcategory. Therefore it must be Rabbi Akiva's, and from this we learn that the question about intentional Sabbath with unwitting labor was whether Sabbaths are separate entities, and the answer that they are was not accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose mishnah this is, suggesting it cannot be Rabbi Eliezer's because the latter part contradicts his view that one is liable for each subcategory of labor.

The Gemara concludes that the mishnah must be Rabbi Akiva's, and from this it learns that the question about intentional Sabbath with unwitting labor was whether Sabbaths are separate entities, and the answer that they are was not accepted.

items.text: Abaye's alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that Rabbi Akiva actually holds that Sabbaths are not separate entities, and the question was about whether the days in between serve as knowledge to separate (for unwitting Sabbath with intentional labor). The answer that they do separate was accepted, but the answer about subcategories was not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes an alternative interpretation: Rabbi Akiva was certain that Sabbaths are not separate entities, and the question was about whether the intervening days serve as knowledge to separate for unwitting Sabbath with intentional labor.
The Gemara reports that Abaye's teacher answered that the intervening days do separate, and Abaye accepted that, but the answer about subcategories was not accepted.

items.text: Rav Chisda's interpretation
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda holds that even Rabbi Akiva agrees that Sabbaths are separate entities, and the question was about whether the days in between serve as knowledge to separate. The answer that they do separate was accepted, but the answer about subcategories was not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asserts that even Rabbi Akiva agrees that Sabbaths are separate entities (כגופין דמיין), and the question was only about whether the intervening days serve as knowledge to separate (ידיעה לחלק).
Rav Chisda reports that the answer was that the intervening days do serve as knowledge to separate, and this answer was accepted.
Rav Chisda reports that the answer that subcategories (ולדות) are like primary categories was not accepted.

items.text: Rav Chisda's proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites a baraita about writing two letters in one lapse vs. two lapses, where Rabban Gamliel and the Sages disagree. Another baraita states that writing one letter each on two different Sabbaths, Rabban Gamliel exempts. Rav Chisda explains that this fits his view that Sabbaths are separate entities, and the exemption applies to the case of intentional Sabbath with unwitting labor.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda opens by citing a baraita about writing two letters in one lapse versus two lapses, where Rabban Gamliel and the Sages disagree.
A second baraita states that writing one letter each on two different Sabbaths, Rabban Gamliel holds liable and the Sages exempt.
The gemara notes that the initial assumption is that Rabban Gamliel follows Rabbi Akiva's view.

Rav Chisda explains that according to his view, the exemption in the baraita applies to the case of intentional Sabbath with unwitting labor, because Sabbaths are considered separate entities (כגופין דמיין).

items.text: Introduction of the baraita on liability
items.text_en: Introduction of the baraita on liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that holds one liable when there is unwitting Shabbat violation and intentional labor, because Shabbatot are considered separate entities and there is no awareness for a half-measure.

items.text: Rava's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava, who holds that Rabbi Akiva considers Shabbatot as one unit, questions how the baraita can be reconciled. He explains that Rabban Gamliel follows Rabbi Eliezer, who views Shabbatot as separate entities.

items.text: Analysis of the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the implications of Rabban Gamliel's concession, concluding that Rabban Gamliel follows the first tanna and Rabbi Eliezer follows Rabbi Yosei regarding the case of half a fig.

items.text: The kal vachomer argument and the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rava
items.text_en: The kal vachomer argument and the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a kal vachomer argument from niddah. It contrasts Rav Chisda's and Rava's interpretations of the question, and resolves the textual variant between 'niddah' and 'niddot'.

items.text: Explanation of 'days in between' for niddah
items.text_en: Explanation of 'days in between' for niddah
items.desc_en: Rava explains that in the context of niddah, 'days in between' refers to immersions between acts of intercourse, which serve as partial awareness to divide liability.

items.text: The case of minor girls and the kal vachomer debate
items.text_en: The case of minor girls and the kal vachomer debate
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Akiva asks about intercourse with a niddah multiple times, and a kal vachomer is debated, with the case of minor girls and animals brought as proofs.

items.text: Conclusion and introduction of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion and introduction of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the discussion and transitions to the Mishnah, which deals with cases of uncertainty regarding eating forbidden fat.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where one is uncertain which prohibited item they consumed or which act they performed, and rules that they bring a single asham talui. It also compares the number of asham talui offerings to the number of hatat offerings in cases of multiple uncertainties.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of uncertainty (forbidden fat vs. permitted fat, wife vs. sister, Shabbat vs. weekday) and rules that one brings a single provisional guilt offering.
The Mishnah compares the number of provisional guilt offerings to sin offerings: for a single lapse of awareness, one brings one offering.
The Mishnah rules that if knowledge intervened between acts, one brings a provisional guilt offering for each uncertain act.
The Mishnah extends the rule to multiple distinct prohibited items (fat, blood, piggul, notar), requiring a provisional guilt offering for each.

items.text: Amoraic dispute: one piece vs. two pieces
items.text_en: Amoraic dispute: one piece vs. two pieces
items.desc_en: Rav Asi and Chiyya bar Rav dispute whether the Mishnah's first case involves one piece (uncertain if it is forbidden fat or permitted fat) or two pieces (one forbidden, one permitted). Their disagreement is based on whether the biblical word is read as "mitzvah" (singular) or "mitzvot" (plural), reflecting different hermeneutical principles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Asi and Chiyya bar Rav disagree: Rav Asi says the Mishnah's case is one uncertain piece, while Chiyya bar Rav says it is two pieces.
The Gemara asks: On what basis do they disagree?
The Gemara explains that Rav Asi holds the written tradition (מסורת) is authoritative, so the singular form 'מצות' (mitzvat) is written, implying one piece.
The Gemara explains that Chiyya bar Rav holds the vocalized reading (מקרא) is authoritative, so the plural 'מצות' (mitzvot) is read, implying two pieces.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: Rav Huna (or Chiyya bar Rav) objects to Rav Asi: if the latter part of the Mishnah implies two pieces, then the first part must also be two pieces. Rav responds that the Mishnah can be explained differently: the first part is one piece, the latter part two pieces. Chiyya bar Rav then explains that the Mishnah's first clause is a general rule, and the second clause clarifies it.

sub.text: Rav Huna (or Chiyya bar Rav) to Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rav Huna (or Chiyya bar Rav) to Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna (or Chiyya bar Rav) objects to Rav Asi: if the latter part of the Mishnah implies two pieces, then the first part must also be two pieces.
Rav responds that the Mishnah can be explained differently: the first part is one piece, the latter part two pieces, and the latter part is stated even though it is obvious.
Chiyya bar Rav explains that the Mishnah's first clause is a general rule, and the second clause clarifies it with the example of two pieces.

items.text: Rav's ruling: two pieces liable, one piece exempt
items.text_en: Rav's ruling: two pieces liable, one piece exempt
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav: if one had two pieces (one forbidden fat, one permitted fat) and ate one, he is liable for an asham talui; but if he had one piece that is uncertain, he is exempt. Rava explains Rav's reasoning: the verse says "one of all the mitzvot" (singular), implying liability only when there is uncertainty between two distinct commandments.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Rav's ruling: with two pieces (one forbidden fat, one permitted fat) and eating one, one is liable for an asham talui; with one uncertain piece, one is exempt.

Rava explains Rav's reasoning: the verse says 'וְעָשָׂה אַחַת מִכׇּל מִצְוֹת ה (and does one of all the commandments of the Lord)' — implying liability only when there is uncertainty between two distinct commandments, as the word is written 'מִצְוַת' (singular) but read 'מִצְווֹת' (plural).

items.text: Abaye's objections from Rabbi Eliezer's rulings
items.text_en: Abaye's objections from Rabbi Eliezer's rulings
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav's position by citing Rabbi Eliezer's rulings: a koy (a doubtful animal) requires an asham talui, and a case of uncertain paternity also requires one. The Gemara identifies these as following Rabbi Eliezer's view, which holds that one is liable even without two distinct prohibitions, consistent with the reading "mitzvah" (singular).

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rav's position by citing Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that one is liable to bring a provisional guilt offering for eating the fat of a koy (a doubtful animal), which involves only a single uncertain item.

Rava answers that Rabbi Eliezer holds the written tradition (אֵם לַמָּסוֹרֶת) is authoritative, reading the singular 'מִצְוַת', so he obligates a provisional guilt offering even for a single uncertain item.
The Gemara raises another objection from a baraita about a case of uncertain paternity, where the parties must bring a provisional guilt offering, again involving only a single uncertain item.
The Gemara identifies that this baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer's opinion, thus it does not contradict Rav's position.

The Gemara raises a third objection from a mishna about a case of uncertain blood found on a cloth, where the couple is liable for a provisional guilt offering, again involving a single uncertain item.
The Gemara again identifies that this mishna follows Rabbi Eliezer's opinion, thereby resolving the objection.

items.text: Rav's ruling restated and alternative explanation by Rabbi Zeira
items.text_en: Rav's ruling restated and alternative explanation by Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya quotes Rav again: two pieces liable, one piece exempt. Rabbi Zeira explains Rav's reasoning differently: two pieces can be clarified (by inquiry), but one piece cannot. The Gemara notes the practical difference between Rava's and Rabbi Zeira's explanations: a case of a half-olive's bulk of forbidden fat.

sub.desc_en: רבי חייא (Rabbi Chiyya) quotes רב (Rav) restating the ruling: with two pieces, one forbidden and one permitted, one is חייב (liable) for an אשם תלוי (provisional guilt offering); with a single piece of uncertain status, one is פטור (exempt).
רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) explains רב's (Rav's) reasoning: with two pieces, it is possible to clarify the prohibition (by examining the remaining piece), but with one piece, clarification is impossible.
הגמרא (The Gemara) asks what practical difference exists between the explanation of רבא (Rava) and that of רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira), and answers: a case involving an olive-bulk and a half-olive-bulk.

הגמרא (The Gemara) resolves the difference: according to רבא (Rava), the plural 'מצוות' (commandments) is absent, so one is פטור (exempt); according to רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira), it is possible to clarify the prohibition, so one is חייב (liable).

items.text: Final objection and resolution
items.text_en: Final objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects to Rabbi Zeira from Rabbi Eliezer's ruling about a koy, which requires an asham talui even though its status cannot be clarified. Rabbi Zeira responds that Rabbi Eliezer holds that clarification is not required.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects to Rabbi Zeira by citing Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that one is liable to bring an asham talui for the fat of a koy, a case where clarification is impossible.
Rabbi Zeira responds that Rabbi Eliezer holds that clarification of the prohibition is not required, thus the objection is resolved.

items.text: Initial objections from baraitot
items.text_en: Initial objections from baraitot
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited that impose asham talui in cases of doubt, suggesting they follow Rabbi Eliezer who does not require establishment of the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a doubtful levirate birth that imposes an אשם תלוי (provisional guilt offering), challenging the view that establishment of the prohibition is required.
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer), who does not require the prohibition to be established for an אשם תלוי.
The Gemara raises another objection from a mishna about finding blood after intercourse, which imposes an אשם תלוי (provisional guilt offering) in a case of doubt.
The Gemara again answers that the mishna follows רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer), who does not require the prohibition to be established.

items.text: Rav's distinction between two pieces and one piece
items.text_en: Rav's distinction between two pieces and one piece
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Rav's ruling: if one had two pieces (one forbidden fat, one permitted) and ate one, he is liable for asham talui; if only one piece of uncertain status, he is exempt. Rav explains the rationale: with two pieces, the prohibition is established (ikvu'a issura); with one piece, it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Rav's ruling distinguishing two pieces (liable) from one uncertain piece (exempt).
Rav Nachman explains Rav's rationale: with two pieces the prohibition is established (איקְּבַע אִיסּוּרָא), with one piece it is not.

items.text: Distinction between ikvu'a issura and i efshar levareir
items.text_en: Distinction between ikvu'a issura and i efshar levareir
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the concept of 'ikvu'a issura' and the concept of 'i efshar levareir issureih' (impossibility to clarify the prohibition). Rava and Rabbi Zeira offer different cases to illustrate the difference, and Rav Nachman's view is also presented.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the concept of 'ikvu'a issura' (the prohibition is fixed) and 'i efshar levareir issureih' (impossibility to clarify the prohibition).
Rava illustrates the difference with a case where a gentile ate the first piece and an Israelite ate the second, so at the time the Israelite ate there is no 'mitzvot' (commandment) involved.
Rabbi Zeira explains that according to his view, the case involves impossibility to clarify the prohibition (i efshar levareir issureih).
Rav Nachman explains that according to his view, the case involves a fixed prohibition (ikvu'a issura).

items.text: Rava's objections from Rabbi Eliezer's rulings
items.text_en: Rava's objections from Rabbi Eliezer's rulings
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman by citing Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that one is liable for asham talui for the fat of a koy (a doubtful animal), and again cites the baraitot about a doubtful firstborn and about finding a blood stain, which impose asham talui without requiring ikvu'a issura.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman by citing Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that one is liable for asham talui for the fat of a koy, showing Rabbi Eliezer does not require ikvu'a issura.
Rava cites a baraita about a doubtful firstborn that imposes asham talui, identifying it as Rabbi Eliezer's position.
Rava cites a baraita about finding a blood stain that imposes asham talui without requiring ikvu'a issura.

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution: the baraitot follow Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution: the baraitot follow Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman is silent initially but later explains he could have answered that the baraitot follow Rabbi Meir, who also does not require ikvu'a issura, as seen in a beraita about slaughtering an asham talui outside the Temple. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Eliezer's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Nachman was silent, but after leaving he explained that he could have answered that the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, who does not require ikvu'a issura (establishment of the prohibition).

A baraita is cited: one who slaughters an asham talui (suspensive guilt-offering) outside the Temple — Rabbi Meir holds him liable, while the Sages exempt him, showing Rabbi Meir does not require ikvu'a issura.
The Gemara asks why Rav Nachman did not simply say the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, and answers that the baraita teaches that Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Eliezer's view.

items.text: Rabbah bar Avuha's ruling and Rav Ashi's qualification
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Avuha's ruling and Rav Ashi's qualification
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Avuha cites Rav that the case of a single uncertain piece is disputed between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages. The Gemara questions why Rabbi Eliezer would require eating the piece, since he allows donating an asham talui daily. Rav Ashi explains that Rabbi Eliezer follows Bava ben Buta's view that one must wait until entering a state of doubt.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Avuha cites Rav that eating a single piece of uncertain fat brings the case into the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Eliezer's liability depends on eating the piece, since he allows donating an asham talui daily even without eating.
The Gemara cites a baraita that Rabbi Eliezer permits donating an asham talui voluntarily every day, implying no need for a prior act of eating.
Rav Ashi explains that Rabbi Eliezer follows Bava ben Buta's view that one must wait until entering a state of doubt before bringing the asham talui.

items.text: Tosefta on two pieces and various scenarios
items.text_en: Tosefta on two pieces and various scenarios
items.desc_en: A baraita details cases of two pieces (one forbidden fat, one permitted) eaten by different people or with different intentions, with rulings on liability. The Gemara questions who authored the baraita, suggesting it is neither Rabbi nor the Rabbis, and Rav Ashi provides an explanation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents cases of two pieces (one forbidden fat, one permitted) eaten by different people, with the Tanna Kamma ruling liability or exemption based on order, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (Rabbi) always ruling liability.
The baraita continues with cases of intentional vs. unintentional eating, detailing liability patterns and Rabbi's dissenting opinion.
The baraita concludes with the case of both pieces eaten unintentionally, ruling both liable, with a rationale that exempting the second would establish the first as a definite חטאת (sin-offering).

The Gemara questions who authored the baraita, arguing that if it is Rabbi, the ruling is straightforward, but if it is the Rabbis, the second person's liability would imply bringing חולין (non-sacred animals) to the Temple courtyard, which is problematic.
Rav Ashi provides an explanation (the content of which is implied by the context but not fully quoted here) to resolve the difficulty.

items.text: Opening identification of the Mishnah's author
items.text_en: Opening identification of the Mishnah's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that one may donate a provisional guilt-offering daily. Therefore, the court tells the person to bring a provisional guilt-offering and stipulate: if the first ate fat, it is atonement; if not, it is a donation.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on multiple provisional guilt-offerings
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on multiple provisional guilt-offerings
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says that just as one brings a sin-offering for each certain transgression, so one brings a provisional guilt-offering for each uncertain transgression. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Shimon argue that one brings only one provisional guilt-offering, citing the verse 'upon his error which he erred' to limit liability.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira and Rava debate the principle of uncertain awareness
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira and Rava debate the principle of uncertain awareness
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states that the baraita teaches that uncertain awareness divides liability for sin-offerings. Rava disagrees, arguing that uncertain awareness does not divide liability; rather, the baraita means that just as certain awareness leads to a sin-offering for each act, so uncertain awareness leads to a provisional guilt-offering for each act.

items.text: Abaye challenges Rava with a logical argument
items.text_en: Abaye challenges Rava with a logical argument
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava: if uncertain awareness does not divide liability for sin-offerings, why would one bring a provisional guilt-offering for each act? He cites a general principle: wherever sin-offerings are divided, guilt-offerings are also divided.

items.text: Rava bar Chanan's objection and discussion on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Rava bar Chanan's objection and discussion on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: Rava bar Chanan objects to Abaye: if uncertain awareness divides liability, then eating fat before and after Yom Kippur would require two sin-offerings, but Yom Kippur atones for unknown sins. Abaye and Rava debate whether Yom Kippur atones only when one later becomes aware. A baraita is cited that Yom Kippur atones even at nightfall, exempting one from a provisional guilt-offering.

items.text: Rav Idi bar Avin's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin objects from a baraita: one who eats and drinks in one lapse is liable for only one sin-offering, despite a pause between them. If uncertain awareness divided liability, two sin-offerings would be required. The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, as the later clause about vinegar follows Rabbi's opinion.

items.text: Rava's objection from me'ilah and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection from me'ilah and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava objects from a baraita on me'ilah: eating consecrated food over multiple days, even years, combines for liability, despite Yom Kippur intervening. The Gemara answers that Yom Kippur atones for prohibitions but not for monetary liability, or it atones only for a full measure, not a partial one.

items.text: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute and a contradiction
items.text_en: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute and a contradiction
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan repeat the dispute of Rabbi Zeira and Rava. The Gemara notes a difficulty: for Rabbi Yochanan, the baraita correctly links guilt-offerings to sin-offerings, but for Resh Lakish, it should link sin-offerings to guilt-offerings. A contradiction is raised from a baraita on impurity and entering the Temple, which seems to support Resh Lakish's view that uncertain awareness divides liability.

items.text: Dispute about partial knowledge
items.text_en: Dispute about partial knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Shimon regarding a case where one walked in the first path and forgot while walking in the second. The first Tanna holds that partial knowledge is considered knowledge, while Rabbi Shimon holds it is not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Shimon exempts in this case, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda exempts in all cases in the name of Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda exempts even in the first path.

Rava explains the case: one walked in the first path and while walking in the second forgot the first; the first Tanna holds that partial knowledge (מקצת ידיעה) is considered knowledge, while Rabbi Shimon holds it is not.

items.text: Question on liability without knowledge
items.text_en: Question on liability without knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one is liable in the case where he walked in the first path and then in the second, since he had no knowledge. Resh Lakish answers that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael who does not require initial knowledge, while Rabbi Yochanan says that even according to the Rabbis, uncertain knowledge is treated as knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah's case of walking in the first path and then the second imposes liability, since the person had no knowledge of the first transgression.
Resh Lakish answers that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who does not require initial knowledge.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that even according to the Rabbis, uncertain knowledge is treated as knowledge in this case.

items.text: Contradiction raised against both opinions
items.text_en: Contradiction raised against both opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if uncertain knowledge is treated as knowledge here, it should apply to the entire Torah, but this contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's own view elsewhere. Similarly, a contradiction is raised against Resh Lakish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if uncertain knowledge is treated as knowledge here, it should apply to the entire Torah, but this contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's own view elsewhere; similarly, a contradiction is raised against Resh Lakish.

items.text: Resolution for Rabbi Yochanan's contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution for Rabbi Yochanan's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction for Rabbi Yochanan: here, regarding impurity, the verse 'and it was hidden from him and he is impure' includes uncertain knowledge, but elsewhere the verse 'or his sin is made known to him' requires definite knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction for Rabbi Yochanan by distinguishing between the case of impurity, where uncertain knowledge is treated as knowledge, and the rest of the Torah, where definite knowledge is required.

items.text: Resolution for Resh Lakish's contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution for Resh Lakish's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction for Resh Lakish: he establishes the mishnah as Rabbi Yishmael, teaching that Rabbi Yishmael does not require initial knowledge. This is necessary because one might think Rabbi Yishmael derives this from a verse but not from tradition, so the Gemara teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction for Reish Lakish: why establish the baraita as Rabbi Yishmael rather than as Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi?
The Gemara answers that Reish Lakish teaches that Rabbi Yishmael also does not require initial knowledge.
The Gemara objects that this is already taught in a mishna where Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse 'ונעלם ממנו' (and it was concealed from him) two obligations.
The Gemara resolves that it was necessary, because one might think Rabbi Yishmael has no verse but has a tradition, so Reish Lakish teaches us otherwise.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents cases of uncertain sin (e.g., eating either forbidden fat or leftover sacrifice, having relations with either one's wife or sister, working on either Shabbat or Yom Kippur). Rabbi Eliezer holds one is liable for a chatat, while Rabbi Yehoshua exempts. Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon qualify the dispute, and Rabbi Yehuda adds that even in cases of unintended action, Rabbi Yehoshua exempts, citing the verse 'which he sinned therein' to exclude one engaged in a permitted act.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah presents cases of uncertain sin and states that Rabbi Eliezer (Rabbi Eliezer) holds one is חייב (liable) for a chatat, while Rabbi Yehoshua (Rabbi Yehoshua) exempts.
Rabbi Yose (Rabbi Yose) qualifies the dispute, stating that both agree one who works during twilight is פטור (exempt) because part of the labor was done on each day.

Rabbi Yose (Rabbi Yose) specifies that the dispute is about one who works during the day and does not know whether it was Shabbat or Yom Kippur, or does not know which labor he performed, with Rabbi Eliezer (Rabbi Eliezer) holding him liable and Rabbi Yehoshua (Rabbi Yehoshua) exempting him.
Rabbi Yehuda (Rabbi Yehuda) adds that Rabbi Yehoshua (Rabbi Yehoshua) would exempt the person even from bringing an אשם תלוי (provisional guilt offering).

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon (Rabbi Shimon) and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri (Rabbi Shimon Shezuri) state that both agree one is liable when the uncertainty is within one category, but they disagree when it involves two categories, with Rabbi Eliezer (Rabbi Eliezer) holding liable and Rabbi Yehoshua (Rabbi Yehoshua) exempting.

Rabbi Yehuda (Rabbi Yehuda) reports that even in cases of unintended action (e.g., intending to pick figs but picking grapes), Rabbi Eliezer (Rabbi Eliezer) holds liable and Rabbi Yehoshua (Rabbi Yehoshua) exempts.
The mishnah expresses doubt whether Rabbi Yehoshua (Rabbi Yehoshua) actually exempts in such a case.
The mishnah answers that the verse 'אשר חטא בה' (which he sinned therein) serves to exclude one who acts unawares (מתעסק), not to exempt in cases of unintended action.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that in each case, whichever sin was committed, one is liable. Rabbi Yehoshua responds with the verse 'which he sinned therein' requiring knowledge of the specific sin. Rabbi Eliezer uses that verse to exclude one engaged in a permitted act.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that in each case, whichever sin was committed, one is liable.
Rabbi Yehoshua responds with the verse 'which he sinned therein' requiring knowledge of the specific sin.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer uses the verse to exclude one engaged in a permitted act.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on mit'asek
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on mit'asek
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of mit'asek (unintentional act) is being discussed. It distinguishes between cases where one benefits (e.g., forbidden fats or illicit relations) where one is liable, and Shabbat where one is exempt because the Torah requires intentionality for a forbidden labor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which type of mit'asek (unintentional act) is under discussion, distinguishing between forbidden fats/illicit relations where one is liable due to benefit, and Shabbat where one is exempt because the Torah requires intentionality for a forbidden labor.

items.text: Rava and Abaye's examples of mit'asek on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rava and Abaye's examples of mit'asek on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides specific examples of mit'asek on Shabbat according to Rava and Abaye. Rava's case is intending to cut detached produce but cutting attached; Abaye's is intending to lift detached but cutting attached. The dispute between Abaye and Rava is then cited regarding liability when one intends to cut detached but cuts attached.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rava, the case is one who intended to cut detached produce but cut attached produce, while according to Abaye, it is one who intended to lift detached produce but cut attached produce, and it cites the dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding liability.
The Gemara provides Abaye's example of mit'asek on Shabbat: intending to lift detached produce but cutting attached.
The Gemara cites the dispute: one who intends to lift detached but cuts attached is exempt because he intended no cutting at all.
Abaye rules that one who intends to cut detached but cuts attached is liable because he intended a cutting action.
Rava rules that one who intends to cut detached but cuts attached is exempt because he did not intend a forbidden cutting.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's statement and the question about twilight
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's statement and the question about twilight
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says the Sages did not disagree with him. The Gemara explains that the Sages asked him about lifting an object during twilight (bein hashmashot), and he responded that they scrutinized him but found nothing. The Gemara questions why he didn't answer that part of the lifting was today and part tomorrow, and explains that he meant they found no flaw.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that the Sages did not disagree with him, and a baraita reports that he told them they scrutinized him.
The Gemara asks what the Sages said to Rabbi Yosei that prompted his response, and explains that they asked him about lifting an object during twilight (בין השמשות).
Rabbi Yosei responds that they scrutinized him but found nothing.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei could have answered that part of the lifting was today and part tomorrow.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei indeed meant that they scrutinized him and found no flaw, implying that the question was unanswerable.

items.text: Contradiction regarding Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: according to Rabbi Yosei, one is exempt for a partial act, but Rabbi Eliezer elsewhere holds one liable for weaving three threads initially. Rav Yosef resolves that Rabbi Yosei taught the Mishnah according to Rabbi Eliezer's opinion, where Rabbi Eliezer requires two threads on the existing fabric.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei's ruling that a completed labor is exempt contradicts Rabbi Eliezer's position that one is liable, and Rav Yosef resolves that Rabbi Yosei taught Rabbi Eliezer's opinion differently, requiring two threads on the loom for liability.
Rav Yosef resolves that Rabbi Yosei taught the Mishnah according to Rabbi Eliezer's opinion, where Rabbi Eliezer requires two threads on the existing fabric.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's statement on Rabbi Yehoshua exempting from asham talui
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's statement on Rabbi Yehoshua exempting from asham talui
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda reports that Rabbi Yehoshua would exempt one even from the suspensive guilt-offering (asham talui) in a case of uncertainty, based on the verse 'ki techeta ve'lo yada' – excluding one who knows he sinned. Rabbi Shimon argues that this is precisely the case for asham talui, as the verse says 've'asah ve'lo yada' and this person does not know what he did.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda says Rabbi Yehoshua would exempt one even from an asham talui (conditional guilt-offering), based on the verse 'when you sin and do not know,' excluding one who knows he sinned, and Rabbi Shimon argues that such a person does bring an asham talui because he does not know what he did.

Rabbi Shimon argues that this case is precisely the one for which the suspensive guilt-offering (אשם תלוי) is brought, as the verse says 'ועשה ולא ידע' (and he did and did not know) and this person does not know what he did.

items.text: Uncertainty about eating forbidden fat and asham talui
items.text_en: Uncertainty about eating forbidden fat and asham talui
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a case where one is uncertain whether he ate forbidden fat (chelev) or not, and whether he brings an asham talui. It cites a baraita: one who sinned and does not know what sin, or is uncertain whether he sinned, brings an asham talui. Since Rabbi Shimon holds that one who sinned without knowing brings an asham talui, and the baraita includes uncertain sin, it follows that Rabbi Shimon holds one brings an asham talui for uncertain sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a case of doubt whether one ate forbidden fat, and resolves from a baraita that Rabbi Shimon holds that one who is uncertain whether he sinned brings an asham talui.

The Gemara cites a baraita that includes uncertain sin, and since Rabbi Shimon holds that one who sinned without knowing brings an asham talui, it follows that Rabbi Shimon holds one brings an asham talui for uncertain sin.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon's statement on mit'asek
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon's statement on mit'asek
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon say that the Sages did not disagree, and the verse 'asher chata bah' excludes one who acts unintentionally (mit'asek).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon say that the verse 'which he sinned therein' excludes the mit'asek (one who acts unintentionally).

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's challenge from the case of infants
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's challenge from the case of infants
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel: one who unintentionally eats forbidden fats or has illicit relations is liable because he benefits; one who unintentionally performs a forbidden labor on Shabbat is exempt. Rava challenges this from the Mishnah about two infants for circumcision, where Rabbi Eliezer holds liable and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts. Rava argues that Rabbi Yehoshua only exempts because it's a case of error in a mitzvah, but for a non-mitzvah act, even Rabbi Yehoshua would hold liable. Rav Nachman responds that the case of infants is different because one who damages while healing is liable, and one who unintentionally wounds is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Shmuel's ruling that one who unintentionally engages with forbidden fats or illicit relations is liable because he benefits, but one who unintentionally performs a forbidden labor on Shabbat is exempt because the Torah prohibited only intentional labor.

Rava challenges Rav Nachman from the Mishnah about two infants for circumcision, arguing that Rabbi Yehoshua only exempts because it's a case of error in a mitzvah, but for a non-mitzvah act, even Rabbi Yehoshua would hold liable.

Rav Nachman responds that the case of infants is different because one who damages while healing is liable, and one who unintentionally wounds is liable, so the Mishnah's ruling does not apply to Shabbat labor.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's objection and Shmuel's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's objection and Shmuel's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda objects to Shmuel from a Mishnah where one intends to pick figs but picks grapes, etc., and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts only when switching species, but within the same species even Rabbi Yehoshua would hold liable. Shmuel responds that the case is where one forgot and thought he was picking figs when he intended grapes, and the dispute is whether his intention was fulfilled.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda objects to Shmuel from a Mishnah where one intends to pick figs but picks grapes, etc., and Rabbi Eliezer holds liable while Rabbi Yehoshua exempts.

The Gemara notes that here the person is acting as a מתעסק (unintentional actor), yet Rabbi Yehoshua only exempts when switching species, but within the same species even he would hold liable, contradicting Shmuel's position.
Shmuel responds that the Mishnah's case is where one forgot and thought he was picking figs when he intended grapes, and the dispute is whether his intention was fulfilled.

items.text: Rav Oshaya's challenge from the baraita of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's challenge from the baraita of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon state that there is no dispute regarding a single prohibited category (shem echad) – all agree one is liable – but they dispute when two categories are involved. He questions what Rabbi Yehuda adds, since his case of intending to pick grapes and picking figs, or black and white, seems to be the same as the baraita's two categories.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon state that there is no dispute regarding a single prohibited category (shem echad) – all agree one is liable – but they dispute when two categories are involved.
Rav Oshaya questions what Rabbi Yehuda adds, since his case of intending to pick grapes and picking figs, or black and white, seems to be the same as the baraita's two categories.

The Gemara suggests that the difference between Rabbi Yehuda and the baraita is the status of מתעסק (an unintentional act): Rabbi Yehuda holds one is liable, while Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds one is exempt.

The Gemara rejects that answer, stating that all agree מתעסק is exempt; rather, the dispute is about whether one forgot the act (שכח מלקט מלבו) in a single category (all agree liable) or in two categories (Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says dispute, Rabbi Yehuda says dispute in both).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is Rabbi Yehuda saying that they dispute? If his case of intending to pick grapes and picking figs, or black and white, is about two categories, that is exactly the dispute of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon. So what does Rabbi Yehuda come to teach?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda's statement adds, since his examples of intending to pick grapes and picking figs, or black and white, seem to duplicate the dispute between Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: First answer: the dispute is about mit'asek (one engaged in a permitted act)
items.text_en: First answer: the dispute is about mit'asek (one engaged in a permitted act)
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri is the case of mit'asek – one who performs a prohibited act unintentionally while engaged in a permitted act. Rabbi Yehuda holds mit'asek is liable, while Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri is about mit'asek (one engaged in a permitted act), where Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds him exempt.

items.text: Rejection and alternative explanation: the dispute is about forgetting the intent
items.text_en: Rejection and alternative explanation: the dispute is about forgetting the intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the mit'asek explanation, stating that all agree mit'asek is exempt. Instead, the dispute is about one who forgot his intent while gathering (shachach melaket milibo). In a single category, all agree he is liable; in two categories, they dispute. Rabbi Yehuda holds that there is no difference between one and two categories – they dispute in both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the mit'asek explanation, stating that all agree mit'asek is exempt, and instead frames the dispute as about one who forgot his intent while gathering (shachach melaket milibo), where in a single category all agree he is liable.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is only in two categories, while Rabbi Yehuda holds that there is no difference between one and two categories – they dispute in both.

items.text: Rava's alternative: the dispute is about precedence (likdom)
items.text_en: Rava's alternative: the dispute is about precedence (likdom)
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different explanation: the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri is about the order of actions – whether one is liable if he intended to perform one action first but performed the other first.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri is about precedence (לִיקְדֹּם) – whether one is liable if he intended to perform one action first but performed the other first.

items.text: Supporting baraita about two candles and a single breath
items.text_en: Supporting baraita about two candles and a single breath
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if one had two long-burning candles and intended to extinguish one but extinguished the other, or to light one and lit the other, he is exempt. But if he intended to light and extinguish, and did both in one breath, he is liable. The Gemara explains that this teaches that even though the order was reversed (he extinguished first and lit later), he is still liable because the action was simultaneous.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if one had two long-burning candles and intended to extinguish one but extinguished the other, or to light one and lit the other, he is exempt; but if he intended to light and extinguish and did both in one breath, he is liable.

The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that even though the order was reversed (he extinguished first and lit later), he is still liable because the action was simultaneous, countering the possible objection that his intent was not fulfilled.

items.text: Dispute about one who rakes coals on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute about one who rakes coals on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught: one who rakes coals on Shabbat is liable for one sin-offering. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok: he is liable for two, because he extinguishes the upper coals and ignites the lower ones. The Gemara asks: if he intended both, why would the first Tanna exempt? If he did not intend to ignite, why would Rabbi Eliezer obligate two? Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Chanina explain: the case is where he intended to extinguish the upper coals in order to ignite the lower ones. The first Tanna holds that one who damages (mekalkel) in ignition is exempt, while Rabbi Eliezer holds he is liable. Rabbi Yochanan adds that this was taught regarding a blacksmith, and that the reason for this law has not been revealed.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute: the first Tanna holds one who rakes coals on Shabbat liable for one sin-offering, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok holds him liable for two, because he extinguishes the upper coals and ignites the lower ones.
The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances? If he intended both extinguishing and igniting, why would the first Tanna exempt? If he did not intend to ignite, why would Rabbi Eliezer obligate two?

Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Chanina both explain: the case is where he intended to extinguish the upper coals in order to ignite the lower ones; the first Tanna holds that one who damages (מקלקל) in ignition is exempt, while Rabbi Eliezer holds he is liable.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that this was taught regarding a blacksmith, and that the reason for this law has not been revealed.

items.text: Introduction of Ami bar Avin and Rav Chananya bar Avin's statement
items.text_en: Introduction of Ami bar Avin and Rav Chananya bar Avin's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Ami bar Avin and Rav Chananya bar Avin both said something, but the text cuts off, indicating the beginning of a new statement that continues on the next amud.

sub.text: Introduction of Ami bar Avin and Rav Chananya bar Avin
sub.text_en: Introduction of Ami bar Avin and Rav Chananya bar Avin
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Ami bar Avin and Rav Chananya bar Avin both said something, but the text cuts off, indicating the beginning of a new statement that continues on the next amud.

items.text: First dispute about intent to extinguish and ignite
items.text_en: First dispute about intent to extinguish and ignite
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains a dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok regarding a case where one intended both to extinguish and to ignite. Tanna Kamma follows Rabbi Yosi, who holds that the prohibition of burning is only a negative commandment (not subject to a sin-offering), while Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok follows Rabbi Natan, who holds that burning is a distinct category for liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first dispute concerns a case where one intended both to extinguish and to ignite, and Tanna Kamma follows Rabbi Yosi, who holds that the prohibition of burning (הבערה) was stated only for a negative commandment (לאו), not for liability to a sin-offering.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok follows Rabbi Natan, who holds that the prohibition of burning (הבערה) was stated to divide liability (לחלק), making each prohibited act of burning a separate category for a sin-offering.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava suggests that the dispute is about precedence: whether the prohibition of burning is mentioned before other prohibitions in the Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok concerns precedence (הקדים): whether the prohibition of burning is mentioned before other prohibitions in the Torah.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains the dispute as being about a case where one intended to extinguish but the fire ignited on its own. Tanna Kamma follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that an unintended act is exempt, while Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that an unintended act is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains the dispute as a case where one intended to extinguish but the fire ignited on its own, attributing the Tanna Kamma's position to Rabbi Shimon (unintended act exempt) and Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok's to Rabbi Yehuda (unintended act liable).

items.text: Baraita on raking coals for warmth
items.text_en: Baraita on raking coals for warmth
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute about one who rakes coals on Shabbat to warm himself and they ignite on their own. One teaching holds him liable, considering it a 'labor not needed for its own sake' as liable; the other holds him exempt, considering such labor exempt.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by presenting the case of one who rakes coals on Shabbat to warm himself and they ignite on their own.
The first teaching holds the person liable, considering this a 'labor not needed for its own sake' (מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה) as liable.
The second teaching holds the person exempt, considering such a labor exempt.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter that began with 'Safek achal chelev'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter that began with 'Safek achal chelev'.

items.text: Mishnah: Blood that is prohibited and exempt
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blood that is prohibited and exempt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists blood from slaughter of domesticated animals, wild animals, and birds (both kosher and non-kosher) as prohibited, as well as blood from piercing, from the throat, and from cupping that causes death. Blood from the spleen, heart, eggs, grasshoppers, and fish brine is exempt, though Rabbi Yehuda obligates for fish brine.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing blood from slaughter of domesticated animals, wild animals, and birds (both kosher and non-kosher), as well as blood from piercing, from the throat, and from cupping that causes death, as prohibited and liable.
The Mishnah lists blood from the spleen, heart, eggs, grasshoppers, and fish brine as exempt from liability.
Rabbi Yehuda dissents and obligates liability for blood of fish brine (תמצית).

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of prohibited blood from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of prohibited blood from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'All blood you shall not eat' that one might include blood of creeping things, eggs, grasshoppers, and fish. The verse 'for bird and beast' limits it to creatures with both light and severe impurity, and that are a type of meat, excluding creeping things which have only severe impurity.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'All blood you shall not eat' and raises the possibility that it includes blood of creeping things, eggs, grasshoppers, and fish.
The baraita answers by citing the limiting verse 'for bird and beast' and derives that only creatures with both light and severe impurity, and that are a type of meat, are included.
The baraita concludes by excluding blood of creeping things, which have only severe impurity and no light impurity.

items.text: Exclusion of certain bloods and reciprocal derivation of bird and animal
items.text_en: Exclusion of certain bloods and reciprocal derivation of bird and animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara first excludes blood of swarming things, fish, and eggs from the prohibition, then uses a reciprocal derivation to show that both bird and animal are included despite their differences regarding kilayim and the commandment of sending away the mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara excludes blood of swarming things, fish, eggs, and locusts from the prohibition because they lack severe impurity or are entirely permitted.
The Gemara questions why the verse specifies both bird and animal, since one might exclude bird due to its lack of kilayim (forbidden mixtures).
The Gemara uses a reciprocal derivation: the extra word 'ולבהמה' includes animal despite its lack of kilayim, and 'לעוף' includes bird despite its exemption from sending away the mother.

items.text: Application of klal u'frat u'chlal to include all blood with certain characteristics
items.text_en: Application of klal u'frat u'chlal to include all blood with certain characteristics
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the hermeneutic principle of klal u'frat u'chlal to the verse, showing that the general inclusion after the specification includes only items similar to the specification: those with both light and severe tumah, both prohibition and permission, and a type of flesh. It notes that this tannaitic school of Rabbi Yishmael uses this method even when the final klal does not resemble the first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if we apply the principle of כלל ופרט (general and specific), the verse 'כל דם' (all blood) is a general term, and 'עוף ובהמה' (fowl and beast) is a specific term, so only fowl and beast would be included, excluding all other blood.

The Gemara answers that the verse 'נפש אשר תאכל כל דם' (any person who eats any blood) repeats a general term, forming a כלל ופרט וכלל (general, specific, and general), so you only include items similar to the specific term.
The Gemara objects that the final general term ('כל דם' implying karet) does not resemble the first general term ('כל דם' without karet), so the principle of כלל ופרט וכלל should not apply.

The Gemara resolves that this Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael interprets using ריבויי ומיעוטי (amplifications and restrictions) and כלל ופרט (general and specific) in this manner, even when the final general term does not resemble the first.

items.text: Specification of the characteristics derived from the precedent
items.text_en: Specification of the characteristics derived from the precedent
items.desc_en: Mar explains that the precedent (bird and animal) is specified as having light and severe tumah, prohibition and permission, and a type of flesh, and thus all similar items are included.

sub.desc_en: Mar specifies the characteristics derived from the precedent (bird and animal) for the כלל ופרט וכלל (general-specific-general) hermeneutic: items must have light and severe tumah, prohibition and permission, and a type of flesh.

items.text: Inclusion of the koy and derivation of its other laws
items.text_en: Inclusion of the koy and derivation of its other laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the additional 'all' includes, and Rav Adda bar Avin answers: the blood of a koy. It then derives the prohibition of its fat, its neveilah, its gid hanasheh, and its tumah and shechitah from various verses or logic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the additional word 'all' in the Mishnah comes to include.
Rav Adda bar Avin answers that it includes the blood of a koy, and explains that the koy is considered a distinct species, not a doubtful case.
The Gemara derives the prohibition of the koy's fat from 'all fat' and its neveilah from 'all carrion'.
The Gemara derives the prohibition of the gid hanasheh (sciatic nerve) for the koy because it has a hip socket, which the Torah links to the prohibition.

The Gemara concludes by logical reasoning that since the Torah treats the koy like a domestic animal in all respects, its tum'ah (ritual impurity) and shechitah (ritual slaughter) also follow the laws of a domestic animal.

items.text: Challenge regarding blood of two-legged creatures and the need for intent
items.text_en: Challenge regarding blood of two-legged creatures and the need for intent
items.desc_en: Mar's statement that blood of two-legged creatures (humans) is excluded because it has severe tumah but not light tumah is challenged by a mishnah requiring intent for a piece of human flesh to be susceptible to tumah. The Gemara resolves that the need for intent applies only to light tumah from a living person, but after death it has severe tumah.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that the blood of two-legged creatures (humans) is excluded from the prohibition because it has severe tumah but no light tumah.
The Gemara challenges Mar by citing a mishnah that a piece of human flesh requires intent (מחשבה) to become susceptible to tumah, implying it has light tumah.
The Gemara objects that intent should be unnecessary for human flesh, and Reish Lakish answers that the case is where one cuts the flesh for a dog, for which intent is not considered intent.

The Gemara objects with a baraita that food designated for human consumption remains tamei until unfit for a dog, and the Gemara distinguishes between removing tumah (where dog-fitness matters) and introducing tumah (where human-fitness is primary).
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah's requirement for intent applies only to light tumah from a living person, but after death human blood has severe tumah, so Mar's exclusion stands.

items.text: Discussion of tumah of blood and neveilah, and the need for intent and hechsher
items.text_en: Discussion of tumah of blood and neveilah, and the need for intent and hechsher
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether blood of a neveilah imparts severe tumah, citing a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. It then examines the need for intent and hechsher for various types of neveilot, and concludes that for a mixture containing less than a kezayit of neveilah, intent is needed but not hechsher, unlike other foods.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asserting that after death, both the meat and blood of a kosher animal impart severe טומאה (ritual impurity).
The Gemara cites a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether blood of a neveilah imparts severe טומאה (ritual impurity), with Beit Hillel ruling that it does.

The Gemara cites another baraita detailing the rules of intent and hechsher for different types of neveilot, distinguishing between impure animals, pure birds in villages, and pure animals in markets.
Rav asks Rabbi Chiyya why intent is needed for a neveilah that already imparts severe טומאה (ritual impurity), since the item itself is already impure.
Rabbi Chiyya answers that the case involves less than a kezayit of neveilah combined with less than a k'beitza of other foods, forming a k'beitza mixture that requires intent to be considered food.

The Gemara objects that if intent is needed, then hechsher should also be required, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael's principle that anything which does not impart severe טומאה (ritual impurity) requires hechsher.

Rabbi Chiyya resolves that the principle requiring hechsher applies only to ordinary foods without neveilah, but here, since the neveilah component could combine to a kezayit and then impart severe טומאה (ritual impurity) without hechsher, the mixture also does not require hechsher.

items.text: Exclusion of a corpse from impurity of foods
items.text_en: Exclusion of a corpse from impurity of foods
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a corpse, even if it fills a vessel, does not impart food impurity because people disregard it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a corpse is excluded from imparting food impurity because people disregard it, even if it fills a vessel.

items.text: Rabbi Chananya's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Chananya's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chananya suggests that even if the corpse is an olive-sized piece, it is covered with dough, so it does not impart impurity by contact but does by carrying. The Gemara refines this, noting that a corpse imparts severe impurity even when covered.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chananya proposes that even if the corpse is an olive-sized piece, the case involves it being covered with dough.

The Gemara objects that if the corpse is covered, it should still require prior wetting (הכשר) to receive impurity, but then refines that while it does not impart impurity by contact due to the covering, it should still impart impurity by carrying since one carries it.

The Gemara resolves that a corpse, even when covered with dough, imparts severe impurity (טומאה חמורה) because its impurity 'bursts upward and bursts downward' (בוקעת ועולה בוקעת ויורדת), overriding the covering.

items.text: Exclusion of creeping things from impurity
items.text_en: Exclusion of creeping things from impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that creeping things are excluded from certain impurity because they do not impart impurity by carrying, only by contact.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that creeping things are excluded from the impurity category.
The Gemara questions how creeping things can be excluded, since they do impart impurity by contact.
The Gemara answers that creeping things do not impart impurity by carrying, only by contact, so they are excluded from the impurity category that includes carrying.

items.text: Exclusion of fish and locust blood
items.text_en: Exclusion of fish and locust blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the blood of fish and locusts, which is entirely permitted. It rejects explanations based on permitted fat or absence of the sciatic nerve, concluding that the permission is because they do not require slaughter.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that the blood of fish and locusts is entirely permitted.
The Gemara asks what 'entirely permitted' means.
The Gemara objects that if the permission were due to permitted fat, a wild animal's fat is permitted yet its blood is forbidden.
The Gemara objects that if the permission were due to the absence of the sciatic nerve, a bird lacks that nerve yet its blood is forbidden.
The Gemara resolves that the permission is because fish and locusts do not require slaughter (שחיטה).

items.text: Exclusion of kilayim for birds
items.text_en: Exclusion of kilayim for birds
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'behemah' teaches that only domesticated animals are subject to kilayim, not birds. Abaye clarifies that this refers to wool, which is not subject to kilayim for birds.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that just as birds are not subject to kilayim, the verse 'behemah' teaches that only domesticated animals are subject to kilayim.
The Gemara asks which type of kilayim is meant, noting that for kilayim of breeding and plowing, a baraita already includes wild animals and birds.
Abaye explains that the exclusion refers to wool (צמר) of birds, which is not subject to the prohibition of kilayim (shatnez).

items.text: Liability for blood of creeping things
items.text_en: Liability for blood of creeping things
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says one is liable for an olive-sized amount of blood from creeping things. A baraita is cited that says such blood is forbidden but not punishable by karet, and the Gemara reconciles this by noting the baraita excludes it from a positive commandment as well.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that one receives lashes for an olive-sized amount of blood of creeping things.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists blood of creeping things as forbidden but not punishable by karet, contradicting Rav's claim of liability.
The Gemara initially suggests that 'not punishable' refers only to karet, implying lashes still apply.
The Gemara rejects the initial answer, noting that the baraita also excludes the blood from the negative commandment, as it says 'excluded is blood of creeping things, which have no severe impurity'.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira rules that if one is warned for the creeping thing itself, he is lashed, but if warned for the blood, he is not lashed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira rules that if one is warned for the creeping thing itself, he is lashed, but if warned for the blood, he is not lashed.

items.text: Blood of fish and locusts
items.text_en: Blood of fish and locusts
items.desc_en: Rav says that collected fish blood is forbidden. A baraita permits it even initially, but the Gemara distinguishes between collected and uncollected blood. For fish without scales, Rav's ruling applies.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that collected fish blood is forbidden.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that permits fish and locust blood even לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between uncollected blood (permitted) and collected blood (forbidden).
The Gemara objects: if the distinction is based on collection, then for creeping creatures (מהלכי שתים) uncollected blood should be permitted, but a baraita shows it is forbidden.
The Gemara cites a baraita that permits uncollected blood of creeping creatures, showing that the distinction by collection applies to them as well.
The Gemara resolves the objection: the baraita permitting fish blood refers to fish with scales, while Rav's prohibition applies to fish without scales.

items.text: Blood of eight-legged creatures
items.text_en: Blood of eight-legged creatures
items.desc_en: Rav Shashet says that even the obligation to separate from the blood of eight-legged creatures does not apply. A baraita says it is forbidden, but the Gemara notes that the baraita refers to a different context.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shashet states that the blood of eight-legged creatures carries no obligation even to separate from it.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists the blood of eight-legged creatures as forbidden, contradicting Rav Shashet's leniency.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita's prohibition refers to a different context, not to the case Rav Shashet addresses.

items.text: Blood of creeping things and the status of their milk and blood
items.text_en: Blood of creeping things and the status of their milk and blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies Rav's statement about blood on bread, distinguishing between blood that separated and blood that did not. It then cites a baraita that uses a verse to exclude the milk and blood of creeping things from prohibition, and Rav Sheshet concludes that even the obligation to distance oneself from them does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rav's statement about blood on bread applies only when the blood did not separate, citing a baraita that one may scrape and eat blood on bread and suck blood from between teeth without concern.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Sheshet's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Sheshet's statement
sub.desc_en: Some teach Rav Sheshet's statement in context of a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְזֶה לָכֶם הַטָּמֵא' that the milk of creeping things is not טָמֵא (impure) but rather טָהוֹר (pure), rejecting a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) that would have prohibited it.
