The baraita raises and rejects the argument that blood of creeping things might be prohibited as it is shared across all, and yet the verse excludes it as well, concluding that blood of creeping things too is only טָהוֹר (pure).
Rav Sheshet concludes that the milk and blood of creeping things are so entirely permitted that even the obligation to distance oneself from them (מצות פרוש) does not apply.

items.text: דם הלב – דין לב עוף ולב בהמה
items.text_en: Blood of the heart and the dispute about liability for karet
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one tears the heart and removes its blood; otherwise, one does not transgress. Rav Zeira quotes Rav distinguishing between a bird's heart (no olive's bulk) and an animal's heart (has an olive's bulk, thus liable for karet). An objection is raised from a baraita listing bloods that are only prohibited but not liable for karet. The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to the blood inherent in the organ, while Rav speaks of blood that comes from elsewhere, i.e., the blood that spurts when the soul departs.
items.desc: רבי זירא בשם רב מבחין בין לב עוף שאין בו כזית דם לבין לב בהמה שיש בו כזית, שחייבים עליו כרת. מותבינן מברייתא האוסרת דם הלב בלא תעשה בלבד, ומתרצים שהברייתא עוסקת בדם שבתוך הלב עצמו, ואילו רב בדם שבא מבחוץ בשעת יציאת הנשמה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one tears the heart and removes its blood; otherwise, one does not transgress.
sub.desc: רבי זירא בשם רב מבחין בין לב עוף שאין בו כזית דם לבין לב בהמה שיש בו כזית, שחייבים עליו כרת.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zeira quotes Rav distinguishing between a bird's heart (no olive's bulk, thus no liability) and an animal's heart (has an olive's bulk, thus forbidden and liable for karet).
sub.desc: רבי זירא מסביר שהדם החיצוני מגיע ללב בשעת יציאת הנשמה, כשהלב שואב דם.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita listing bloods (including heart blood) that are only prohibited but not liable for karet.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא האוסרת דם הלב בלא תעשה בלבד, בניגוד לדברי רב המחייב כרת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to the blood inherent in the organ, while Rav speaks of blood that comes from elsewhere.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהברייתא עוסקת בדם שבתוך הלב עצמו, ואילו רב בדם שבא מבחוץ.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the blood inherent in the organ is already included in 'blood of limbs', and resolves that the baraita merely repeats categories.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שדם הלב העצמי הוא בכלל דם איברים, ומתרצת שהברייתא כפולה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that the blood from elsewhere is the blood that spurts when the soul departs.
sub.desc: רבי זירא מסביר שהדם החיצוני מגיע ללב בשעת יציאת הנשמה, כשהלב שואב דם.

items.text: דם הנפש – דם קילוח לעומת דם שותת
items.text_en: Definition of blood of the soul in bloodletting
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines the blood for which one is liable: blood that flows when the soul departs. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish dispute the criterion: Rabbi Yochanan says as long as it spurts, Resh Lakish says from the blackening drop onward. An objection is raised from a baraita that defines blood of bloodletting as long as it spurts, excluding the trickling blood, which seems to refute Resh Lakish. The Gemara deflects by distinguishing between first and last blood, and then cites another baraita where Tannaim dispute the same point, with Rabbi Elazar agreeing with Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shimon with Resh Lakish. A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael adds that spurting blood does not render seeds susceptible to impurity.
items.desc: מחלוקת רבי יוחנן וריש לקיש מהו דם שהנשמה תלויה בו: רבי יוחנן אומר כל זמן שמקלח, ריש לקיש אומר מטיפה המשחירה ואילך. מותבינן תיובתא לריש לקיש מברייתות, ומתרצים שפלוגתא היא בין תנאים (רבי אלעזר ורבי שמעון).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the general rule: blood from which the soul departs incurs liability.
sub.desc: פותח במחלוקת רבי יוחנן וריש לקיש על הגדרת דם שהנשמה תלויה בו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the precise definition of the blood of bloodletting that carries the soul.
sub.desc: פותח במחלוקת רבי יוחנן וריש לקיש על הגדרת דם שהנשמה תלויה בו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan defines the blood as long as it spurts.
sub.desc: פותח במחלוקת רבי יוחנן וריש לקיש על הגדרת דם שהנשמה תלויה בו.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish defines the blood from the blackening drop onward.
sub.desc: מקשה מברייתא נוספת המגדירה דם ראשון רק בזמן מקלח, ומוציאה ראשון ואחרון השותתים – קושיה חוזרת על ריש לקיש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that defines the blood as long as it spurts, excluding trickling blood.
sub.desc: מקשה מברייתא הסוברת שרק דם מקלח הוא דם הנפש, ומשמע שאף ראשון ואחרון השותתים אינם בכלל – קושיה על ריש לקיש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that even first and last blood, which trickles, is excluded, presenting a refutation of Resh Lakish.
sub.desc: מקשה מברייתא הסוברת שרק דם מקלח הוא דם הנפש, ומשמע שאף ראשון ואחרון השותתים אינם בכלל – קושיה על ריש לקיש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects by distinguishing: the baraita excludes only the blackening blood, but first and last blood, though trickling, is still blood of the soul.
sub.desc: דוחה את הקושיה: הברייתא ממעטת רק דם משחיר, אבל דם ראשון ואחרון אף על פי ששותת – הרי הוא דם הנפש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection from a baraita that defines first blood as long as it spurts, excluding first and last blood, again refuting Resh Lakish.
sub.desc: מקשה מברייתא נוספת המגדירה דם ראשון רק בזמן מקלח, ומוציאה ראשון ואחרון השותתים – קושיה חוזרת על ריש לקיש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects by asserting that the dispute is among Tannaim, not a single authoritative baraita.
sub.desc: מקשה מברייתא נוספת המגדירה דם ראשון רק בזמן מקלח, ומוציאה ראשון ואחרון השותתים – קושיה חוזרת על ריש לקיש.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Tannaim dispute the same point: Rabbi Elazar agrees with Rabbi Yochanan (spurting), Rabbi Shimon agrees with Resh Lakish (from the blackening drop).
sub.desc: מקשה מברייתא נוספת המגדירה דם ראשון רק בזמן מקלח, ומוציאה ראשון ואחרון השותתים – קושיה חוזרת על ריש לקיש.

sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael adds that spurting blood does not render seeds susceptible to impurity.
sub.desc: מביא ברייתא מבית רבי ישמעאל המלמדת שדם קילוח אינו מכשיר את הזרעים, להבדיל מדם היוצא לאחר מיתה.

items.text: Bloodletting an animal into two cups and the dispute about liability
items.text_en: Bloodletting an animal into two cups and the dispute about liability
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about bloodletting an animal into two cups: is one liable for the last cup? Rabbi Zeira says it is a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, where Resh Lakish holds one liable for two sin-offerings and Rabbi Yochanan for one. The Gemara adds that Rabbi Yehuda holds one liable for trickling blood, but Rabbi Elazar notes that for atonement, only blood of the soul atones. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita that includes all blood for atonement, and identifies it as following Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about bloodletting an animal into two cups: whether one is liable for the last cup.
Rabbi Zeira answers that this is a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish: Resh Lakish holds one liable for two sin-offerings, Rabbi Yochanan for one.
Rabbi Yehuda holds one liable for trickling blood, but Rabbi Elazar notes that for atonement, only blood of the soul atones.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's baraita citation
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's baraita citation
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita that includes all blood for atonement, and identifies it as following Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: משנה – ספק מעילה ואשם תלוי
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva and the conditional guilt offering for uncertain misuse
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Akiva requires a conditional guilt offering for uncertain misuse of consecrated property, while the Sages exempt. Rabbi Akiva agrees that one does not bring the actual payment until it becomes known, at which point he brings a definite guilt offering. Rabbi Tarfon proposes a procedure: bring the value plus a fifth, a guilt offering worth two selas, and stipulate. Rabbi Akiva concedes that Rabbi Tarfon's method is preferable for a small amount of misuse, but for a large amount, it is better to bring only a guilt offering.
items.desc: משנה: רבי עקיבא מחייב אשם תלוי על ספק מעילה, וחכמים פוטרים. רבי טרפון מציע דרך להביא מעילה ואשם בתנאי, ורבי עקיבא מודה לו במעילה מועטת.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Akiva requires a conditional guilt offering (אשם תלוי) for uncertain misuse of consecrated property, while the Sages exempt; Rabbi Akiva agrees that one does not bring the actual payment until it becomes known, at which point he brings a definite guilt offering (אשם ודאי).
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת במחלוקת: רבי עקיבא מחייב אשם תלוי על ספק מעילה, וחכמים פוטרים; ומודה רבי עקיבא שאינו מביא את מעילתו עד שיתוודע לו ויביא אשם ודאי.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon objects to bringing two guilt offerings and proposes a procedure: bring the value plus a fifth, a guilt offering worth two selas, and stipulate conditionally.
sub.desc: רבי טרפון מציע דרך חלופית: יביא מעילה וחומשה ואשם בשני סלעים ויתנה – אם ודאי מעל הרי אלו מעילתו ואשמו, ואם ספק – המעות נדבה והאשם תלוי.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva concedes that Rabbi Tarfon's method is preferable for a small amount of misuse, but for a large amount, it is better to bring only a guilt offering.
sub.desc: רבי עקיבא משיב: דברי רבי טרפון נראים במעילה מועטת, אך בספק מעילה במאה מנה לא יפה לו להביא ספק מעילה במאה מנה; ובסוף מודה רבי עקיבא לרבי טרפון במעילה מועטת.

items.text: Opening baraita: dispute on me'ilah and asham talui
items.text_en: Opening baraita: dispute on me'ilah and asham talui
items.desc_en: The baraita states that Rabbi Akiva holds one liable for a suspensive guilt-offering (asham talui) for uncertain me'ilah, while the Sages exempt. This sets up the Gemara's analysis of their disagreement.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Akiva holds one liable for a suspensive guilt-offering (אשם תלוי) for uncertain me'ilah, while the Sages exempt.

items.text: Gemara's initial suggestion: dispute over learning upper from lower
items.text_en: Gemara's initial suggestion: dispute over learning upper from lower
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute hinges on whether one can derive laws of the upper (me'ilah) from the lower (standard sacrifices) using a verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute is about whether we derive the upper case (me'ilah) from the lower case (chatat) through a verbal analogy.

items.text: Rav Pappa's rejection: Sages' exemption via gezeirah shavah
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's rejection: Sages' exemption via gezeirah shavah
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that all agree one can learn upper from lower; the Sages exempt me'ilah because a gezeirah shavah from chatat teaches that asham talui applies only to sins with karet for intentional violation, which me'ilah lacks. Rabbi Akiva limits the gezeirah to fixed offerings, excluding the sliding-scale offering.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asserts that all agree one can learn the upper case from the lower case; the Sages exempt me'ilah because a gezeirah shavah from chatat teaches that asham talui applies only to sins with karet for intentional violation, which me'ilah lacks.
A baraita is cited to show that me'ilah lacks karet, supporting the Sages' exemption.
Rabbi Akiva limits the gezeirah shavah to fixed offerings, excluding the sliding-scale offering, thus including me'ilah.

items.text: Alternative explanation: dispute over hekesh and gezeirah shavah
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: dispute over hekesh and gezeirah shavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that Rabbi Akiva holds a partial gezeirah shavah. Instead, it explains that Rabbi Akiva uses a hekesh from the word 'vav' to learn upper from lower, while the Sages use the gezeirah shavah to override the hekesh. Rabbi Akiva derives the requirement of silver shekels for asham from 'zot torat ha'asham'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that the Sages hold a partial גזירה שוה (verbal analogy), asserting that everyone agrees a גזירה שוה cannot be applied partially.

sub.text: Gemara's alternative explanation for Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Gemara's alternative explanation for Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva derives the upper case from the lower case via a היקש (analogy) from the word 'וְאִם' (and if), which adds to the previous subject.
The Sages hold that the lower case (asham of a nazirite or metzora) learns from the upper case (asham me'ilah) regarding the requirement of silver shekels.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Akiva would then hold a partial היקש (analogy), which is also not accepted.
The Gemara resolves that everyone agrees a היקש cannot be partial; the Sages use the גזירה שוה of 'מִצְוֹת' to override the היקש.

sub.text: Gemara's supporting derivation for Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Gemara's supporting derivation for Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva derives the requirement of silver shekels for all asham offerings from the verse 'זֹּאת תּוֹרַת הָאָשָׁם' (this is the law of the guilt-offering), establishing a single law for all guilt-offerings.

items.text: Sages' response: necessity of 'vav' for hekesh from lower to upper
items.text_en: Sages' response: necessity of 'vav' for hekesh from lower to upper
items.desc_en: The Sages argue that despite 'zot torat ha'asham', the Torah needed the 'vav' in 've'im nefesh' to teach that the lower (asham talui) learns from the upper (asham me'ilah) regarding silver shekels, otherwise one might think asham talui should be a ram worth a shekel like a chatat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: And the Rabbis — even though it is written 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הָאָשָׁם (This is the law of the guilt offering)', it was necessary to write 'וְאִם נֶפֶשׁ (And if anyone sin)' with a vav to teach that the lower (asham talui) learns from the upper (asham me'ilah).

The Gemara explains: If derived only from 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הָאָשָׁם (This is the law of the guilt offering)', one might say that the principle of one law for all guilt offerings applies only to other definite guilt offerings.

The Gemara concludes: But regarding the provisional guilt offering (אשם תלוי), since it comes for uncertain forbidden fat, one might think its uncertain case should not be stricter than its definite case — just as the definite case requires a sin offering worth a דנקא (danka), so its uncertain case should require a guilt offering worth a דנקא (danka); therefore the Merciful One wrote 'וְאִם נֶפֶשׁ (And if anyone sin)' with a vav to add to the previous matter.

items.text: Alternative derivation for those who do not expound 'zot torat ha'asham'
items.text_en: Alternative derivation for those who do not expound 'zot torat ha'asham'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for those who do not derive from 'zot torat ha'asham', the requirement of silver shekels for asham talui is learned via a gezeirah shavah from 'be'erkekha' in asham me'ilah, and for the betrothed maidservant, via 'ayil'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: This works out well for the one who expounds the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הָאָשָׁם' (This is the law of the guilt offering), but for the one who does not expound it, what can be said?
The Gemara answers: He derives it via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the term 'בְּעֶרְכְּךָ' (your valuation) in the guilt offering for misuse of consecrated property.
The Gemara objects: Regarding the guilt offering for a betrothed maidservant, the term 'בְּעֶרְכְּךָ' (your valuation) is not written in it!
The Gemara answers: We derive it via a verbal analogy from the word 'אַיִל' (ram) in the guilt offering for misuse of consecrated property.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Akiva's statement on asham talui
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Akiva's statement on asham talui
items.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Akiva's statement: if one remains in doubt forever, they bring an asham talui, because it is from the same type as the definite offering. The Gemara questions this, and Rava concludes that both agree a definite asham does not require prior knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Akiva's statement that if one remains in doubt, they bring an asham talui.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva means by this statement.
Rava explains that if one remains in doubt forever, they bring an asham talui, because it is from the same type as the definite offering.
The Gemara objects that eventually, when the doubt is resolved, one must bring a definite asham.
Rava concludes that from both opinions we learn that a definite asham does not require prior knowledge לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Mishnah: cases of uncertain offerings and asham talui
items.text_en: Mishnah: cases of uncertain offerings and asham talui
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents cases: a woman who brought a bird chatat and then learns she definitely gave birth; a piece of unconsecrated and consecrated meat; and two people eating the pieces. Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Shimon dispute the liability for asham talui.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of a woman who brought a bird chatat and then learned she definitely gave birth, ruling that she makes it a definite offering.

The mishnah presents the case of a piece of unconsecrated and consecrated meat, where one who ate one is exempt, but Rabbi Akiva obligates an asham talui, and eating the second brings a definite asham.

The mishnah records the dispute between Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Yosei regarding two people each eating one piece, with Rabbi Akiva obligating each to bring an asham talui, Rabbi Shimon obligating one asham for both, and Rabbi Yosei's position left incomplete.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of uncertain consumption and joint offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of uncertain consumption and joint offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases involving a piece of forbidden fat (חֵלֶב) and other meats, detailing the offerings brought when one or two people eat the pieces. It records disputes between Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Yosei regarding whether two people can bring a single hatat or asham together.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule that two people cannot bring a single asham (guilt-offering) together, then presents the first case of a piece of forbidden fat (חֵלֶב) and a piece of non-sacred meat.

The Mishnah details the first case: if one person eats both pieces, he brings a hatat (sin-offering); if two people each eat one piece, Rabbi Akiva says each brings an asham taluy (suspended guilt-offering), Rabbi Shimon says both bring one hatat together, and Rabbi Yosei says two cannot bring a single hatat.

The Mishnah presents the second case: a piece of forbidden fat and a piece of sacred meat; if one person eats both, he brings a hatat and a definite asham; if two people each eat one, Rabbi Shimon says both bring a hatat and an asham, and Rabbi Yosei says two cannot bring a single hatat and asham together.

The Mishnah presents the third case: a piece of forbidden fat and a piece of sacred forbidden fat; if one person eats both, he brings two hatats and a definite asham; if two people each eat one, Rabbi Akiva says both bring an asham taluy, Rabbi Shimon says each brings a hatat and both bring one asham, and Rabbi Yosei says two cannot bring one asham.

The Mishnah presents the fourth case: a piece of forbidden fat and a piece of leftover sacred meat (נותר); if one person eats both, he brings three hatats; if two people each eat one, Rabbi Shimon says each brings a hatat and both bring one hatat together, and Rabbi Yosei says any hatat that comes for a sin cannot be brought by two people.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Yosei agree with the first Tanna regarding asham taluy?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Yosei agree with the first Tanna regarding asham taluy?
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether Rabbi Yosei's statement implies that he agrees with the first Tanna that two people can bring an asham taluy together. Rav Nachman explains that the first Tanna is actually Rabbi Yosei himself, so the Mishnah teaches that Rabbi Yosei is the anonymous first view.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: according to Rabbi Yosei, who forbids two people from bringing a hatat together, does he permit them to bring an asham taluy together, which would make him identical to the first Tanna (Rabbi Akiva)?

Rav Nachman responds that the difference between Rabbi Yosei and the first Tanna is a single piece from two pieces, and he clarifies that the first Tanna in the Mishnah is actually Rabbi Yosei himself.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why no asham vadai for notar?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why no asham vadai for notar?
items.desc_en: Rava asks why the Mishnah does not require an asham vadai for the case of notar (leftover sacrificial meat), since notar is sacred. Rav Nachman answers that the piece of notar is worth less than a perutah. Rava objects that the Mishnah elsewhere requires four hatat offerings and one asham for a similar case, and Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a large and small animal, and between rainy and dry seasons.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman why the Mishnah does not require an asham vadai (guilt offering) for the case of notar (leftover sacrificial meat), since notar is sacred.
Rav Nachman answers that the piece of notar is worth less than a perutah (a small coin), so no asham vadai is required.
Rava objects that the Mishnah deals with a piece that originally had value of a perutah, as it mentions an asham vadai.
Rav Nachman clarifies that the piece that is not notar is worth a perutah, but the notar piece itself is not.
Rava objects citing a Mishnah elsewhere that requires four hatat offerings and one asham for a case involving notar in a single eating.
Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a large animal (גסה) and a small animal (דקה), and between rainy season (ימות הגשמים) and dry season (ימות החמה).

items.text: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Shimon hold that a severe prohibition can override a lighter one?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Shimon hold that a severe prohibition can override a lighter one?
items.desc_en: Rava questions whether Rabbi Shimon's ruling in the Mishnah (that two people bring one hatat for notar) is consistent with his view that a prohibition does not take effect where another already applies. The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon exempts one who eats nevelah on Yom Kippur, showing he holds that a severe prohibition (Yom Kippur) does not override a lighter one (nevelah). The Gemara resolves that in the case of notar, the Torah explicitly allows a severe prohibition to take effect on a lighter one.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether Rabbi Shimon holds that a prohibition can take effect where another prohibition already applies, given his ruling in the Mishnah.

The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon exempts one who eats nevelah on Yom Kippur, showing he holds that a severe prohibition (Yom Kippur) does not override a lighter one (nevelah).

sub.text: Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi answers that the case involves eating a kidney with its fat, where the prohibition of notar applies to the kidney itself.
The Gemara objects that even the kidney itself is already subject to the prohibition of עוֹלִין (sacrificial offerings), so how can the prohibition of notar take effect on it?

The Gemara objects further: if one claims Rabbi Shimon holds that a severe prohibition (notar) overrides a light one (עוֹלִין), then why in the baraita does Yom Kippur (severe) not override nevelah (light)?
The Gemara resolves that in the case of קָדָשִׁים (sacred offerings), the Torah explicitly allows a severe prohibition to take effect on a lighter one, unlike the general rule.

items.text: Gemara's proof that a prohibition can take effect upon another prohibition in sacred matters
items.text_en: Gemara's proof that a prohibition can take effect upon another prohibition in sacred matters
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the verse 'אשר לה׳' includes the sacrificial portions (אימורין). It argues that the prohibition of piggul (disqualification) applies to the אימורין, which are already subject to the prohibition of chelev (fat) with karet, and the prohibition of impurity (טומאה) takes effect upon them. This demonstrates that in sacred matters, a lighter prohibition (like impurity) can take effect upon a stricter one (like karet). The Gemara supports this with Rabbi's teaching that the verse 'כל חלב לה׳' includes the אימורין of lesser holy offerings for the prohibition of me'ilah (misuse), which carries the death penalty, showing that a lighter prohibition (me'ilah) takes effect upon a stricter one (karet).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the verse 'אשר לה׳' includes the sacrificial portions (אימורין), and argues that the prohibition of impurity (טומאה) takes effect upon them despite the existing prohibition of chelev (fat) with karet.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi holds that a prohibition can take effect upon another prohibition, and in sacred matters, even a lighter prohibition takes effect upon a stricter one.
The Gemara explains that the prohibition of me'ilah (misuse), which carries the death penalty, is lighter than the prohibition of karet, yet it takes effect upon the אימורין.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi teaches that the verse 'כל חלב לה׳' includes the אימורין of lesser holy offerings for the prohibition of me'ilah, proving that in sacred matters, a lighter prohibition takes effect upon a stricter one.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Shimon and resolution as a dispute among Tannaim
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Shimon and resolution as a dispute among Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says there is no piggul or notar in burnt-offerings (עולות), implying that a prohibition does not take effect upon another. The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute among Tannaim regarding Rabbi Shimon's opinion: some say that in sacred matters a prohibition can take effect upon another, while others say it cannot.

sub.text: Objection from baraita of Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Objection from baraita of Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon holds that piggul and notar do not apply to burnt-offerings (עולין), indicating a dispute among Tannaim about whether a prohibition can take effect upon another in sacred matters.
The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute among Tannaim regarding Rabbi Shimon's opinion: some say that in sacred matters a prohibition can take effect upon another, while others say it cannot.

items.text: Alternative interpretation of the verse for those who deny the principle
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of the verse for those who deny the principle
items.desc_en: For the opinion that even in sacred matters a prohibition does not take effect upon another, the Gemara asks what the verse 'כל חלב לה׳' teaches. It answers that it applies to the offspring of sacred animals (וַלְדֵי קָדָשִׁים), which become sacred simultaneously with their mother, so both prohibitions come at once.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the opinion that even in sacred matters a prohibition does not take effect upon another, what does the verse 'כל חלב לה׳' teach? It answers that it applies to the offspring of sacred animals (ולדות קדשים), which become sacred simultaneously.
The Gemara answers that the verse applies to the offspring of sacred animals (וַלְדֵי קָדָשִׁים), which become sacred simultaneously with their mother, so both prohibitions come at once.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of a suspended guilt-offering when no sin was committed
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of a suspended guilt-offering when no sin was committed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of one who brings a suspended guilt-offering (אשם תלוי) and later learns he did not sin. If before slaughter, Rabbi Meir says it goes out to pasture; the Sages say it grazes until blemished and sold, with proceeds for a freewill offering; Rabbi Eliezer says it is offered, as it atones for another sin. If after slaughter, the blood is poured out and the meat burned; if the blood was sprinkled, the meat is eaten. Rabbi Yosei says even if the blood is in the cup, it is sprinkled and the meat eaten. The Mishnah contrasts this with a definite guilt-offering, a stoned ox, and a heifer whose neck is broken.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of one who brings a suspended guilt-offering (אשם תלוי) and learns he did not sin; if before slaughter, Rabbi Meir says it goes out to pasture.
The Sages say it grazes until blemished and sold, with proceeds for a freewill offering; Rabbi Eliezer says it is offered, as it atones for another sin.
If after slaughter the blood is poured out and the meat burned; if the blood was sprinkled, the meat is eaten; Rabbi Yosei says even if the blood is in the cup, it is sprinkled and the meat eaten.
The Mishnah contrasts with a definite guilt-offering (אשם ודאי): before slaughter it goes to pasture, after slaughter it is buried, after blood sprinkling the meat is burned.
The Mishnah contrasts with a stoned ox (שור הנסקל): before stoning it goes to pasture, after stoning it is permitted for benefit.

The Mishnah contrasts with a heifer whose neck is broken (עגלה ערופה): before breaking it goes to pasture, after breaking it is buried in its place, since it came for a doubt and atoned for its doubt and is gone.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that since he does not need the animal, he does not consecrate it; the Sages hold that since his conscience troubles him, he completes the consecration. A baraita teaches that the dispute applies both when he learns he sinned and when he learns he did not sin, to show the strength of Rabbi Meir's view (even if he sinned, since at the time of separation he did not know) and the strength of the Sages' view (even if he did not sin, his conscience troubled him).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what principle do Rabbi Meir and the Sages disagree?
The Gemara explains: Rabbi Meir holds that since he does not need the animal, he does not consecrate it; the Sages hold that since his conscience troubles him, he completes the consecration.

A baraita teaches that the dispute applies both when he learns he sinned and when he learns he did not sin, to show the strength of Rabbi Meir's view (even if he sinned, since at the time of separation he did not know) and the strength of the Sages' view (even if he did not sin, his conscience troubled him).

items.text: Rav Sheshet's statement about Rabbi Meir's concession
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's statement about Rabbi Meir's concession
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet says that Rabbi Meir concedes to the Sages in a certain case, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet states that Rabbi Meir concedes to the Sages in a certain case.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's case of one who sets aside two ashamot for contingency and is atoned through one: the second must graze until blemished, be sold, and its proceeds fall to nedavah. The reason given is that since he set aside two, he revealed his intention that his heart was smiting him, so he completed the dedication.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the Mishnah's case of one who sets aside two ashamot for contingency and is atoned through one, stating that the second must graze until blemished, be sold, and its proceeds fall to nedavah.
The Gemara explains the reason: since he set aside two animals, he revealed that his heart was smiting him, so he completed the dedication of the second animal.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement: Sages agree with Rabbi Meir on asham talui with disqualified witnesses
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement: Sages agree with Rabbi Meir on asham talui with disqualified witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that the Sages agree with Rabbi Meir in the case of an asham talui whose witnesses were disqualified: it goes out and grazes in the herd. The reason is that the Sages only disagreed when he set it aside on his own, but when based on witnesses, he did not rely on them, thinking others might disqualify them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that the Sages agree with Rabbi Meir in the case of an asham talui whose witnesses were disqualified as conspiring witnesses, that it may go out and graze among the flock.
The Gemara explains the reason: the Sages only disagreed when he set it aside on his own, but when based on witnesses, he did not rely on them, thinking others might come and disqualify them.

items.text: Rava's objection from the gored ox
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the gored ox
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from the case of a gored ox: if before stoning witnesses come saying it gored and others say it did not, the ox goes out and grazes. He argues that this must be about disqualified witnesses, and the parallel case of asham talui would also involve disqualified witnesses, yet the Sages disagree (contradicting Rav Yehuda's claim).

sub.desc_en: Rava objects by citing the case of a condemned ox that is not so, questioning why we would follow the later witnesses over the earlier ones.
Rava argues that the case must be about conspiring witnesses, and the parallel case of asham talui with conspiring witnesses should also be disputed, contradicting Rav's statement.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: distinguishing the cases
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: distinguishing the cases
items.desc_en: Abaye answers that the gored ox case is where the victim came alive, and the parallel asham talui case is where the forbidden piece was identified. But where the asham talui was set aside based on witnesses, the Sages do not agree with Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rejects Rava's objection, suggesting the ox case is where the victim appeared alive, and the parallel asham talui case is where the forbidden piece was identified.
Abaye concludes that in the case where the asham talui was set aside based on witnesses, the Sages do not agree with Rabbi Meir, preserving Rav's statement.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on asham talui with disqualified witnesses
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on asham talui with disqualified witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rabbi Elazar compares it to the meal-offering of jealousy, which goes out to non-sacred use if witnesses are disqualified. Rabbi Yochanan says it grazes until blemished and is sold, with proceeds to nedavah, because unlike the meal-offering, the asham talui comes for atonement, and his smiting heart leads him to complete the dedication.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar compares the asham talui whose witnesses were disqualified to the minchat kena'ot, which goes out to non-sacred use.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the animal must graze until blemished, be sold, and its proceeds fall to nedavah.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan should compare it to the minchat kena'ot, but then rejects the comparison.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the minchat kena'ot comes only to clarify sin, not for atonement, whereas the asham talui comes for atonement, so due to his smiting heart he completes the dedication.

Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes: the meal-offering of jealousy comes only to clarify sin, not for atonement, whereas the asham talui comes for atonement, and because his heart smites him (ליבו נוקפו), he completes the dedication.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a gored ox with disqualified witnesses
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a gored ox with disqualified witnesses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yeruspadai says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a gored ox whose witnesses were disqualified – whoever takes possession of it acquires it. Rava explains the reasoning: if they said 'your ox was mounted,' he might not know and abandon it; but if they said 'your ox mounted,' he knows it didn't and would not abandon it, but would trouble to bring witnesses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yeruspadai reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a gored ox whose witnesses were disqualified is acquired by whoever takes possession of it.

Rava explains that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies only when the witnesses said 'your ox was mounted' (נִרְבַּע), leading the owner to abandon it; but if they said 'your ox mounted' (רָבַע), the owner knows it did not happen and would not abandon it but would trouble to bring witnesses.

items.text: Comparison to an apostate city with disqualified witnesses
items.text_en: Comparison to an apostate city with disqualified witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this differs from the case of an apostate city whose witnesses were disqualified, where Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabbah bar Itai in the name of Resh Lakish) ruled that whoever takes possession acquires it. The answer: in an apostate city, it involves many, each thinking 'I didn't sin, others did,' so they abandon their property; but here, it depends on him alone, so he knows it didn't happen and does not abandon it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes this from the case of an apostate city whose witnesses were disqualified, where Reish Lakish says whoever takes possession acquires it.

The Gemara answers that in the apostate city, many are involved, so each thinks 'I didn't sin, others did' and abandons property, but here it depends on him alone, so he knows he didn't sin and will not abandon it.

items.text: Resh Lakish's ruling on a gift refused
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's ruling on a gift refused
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says: one who gives a gift to another, and the recipient says 'I do not want it' – whoever takes possession of it acquires it. The Gemara contrasts this with a case where the recipient says 'this gift should be void' or 'I do not want it,' with different legal consequences.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish rules that if a donor gives a gift and the recipient says 'I do not want it,' anyone who takes possession acquires it.
The Gemara asks what distinguishes Resh Lakish's case from the ruling of Rabbah bar Avuha / Rav Sheshet, where a recipient who says 'I do not want it' after receiving the gift has his words stand.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Avuha / Rav Sheshet / Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Avuha / Rav Sheshet / Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: The cited ruling distinguishes between a recipient who says 'this gift should be void' (it is void), 'I do not want it' (his words stand), and 'it is void' or 'it is not a gift' (he says nothing).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of "דבריו קיימין"
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of "דבריו קיימין"
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase "דבריו קיימין" in the Mishnah means the animal returns to its owner. It answers that it means the owner's words stand, but he does not acquire it; whoever seizes it acquires it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's phrase 'דבריו קיימין' means the animal returns to its owner.
The Gemara answers that the phrase means the owner's words stand, but he does not acquire it; whoever seizes it acquires it.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about renouncing a field
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about renouncing a field
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where one says "אין לי עסק בה" or "ידי מסולקת הימנה" — which is like "אי אפשי" — and yet the statement is ineffective. The Gemara distinguishes: there, the speaker only removes himself from legal claims, not from the field itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: one who says 'I have no claim on this field' or 'my hand is removed from it' has said nothing, even though 'my hand is removed' resembles 'אי אפשר'.
The Gemara distinguishes: there, the speaker only removes himself from claims, not from the field itself.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about slaves and a second priest
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about slaves and a second priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where a donor gives slaves to others, and the recipient says "אי אפשי בהן". Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds the gift reverts to the donor, while the first Tanna holds the slaves become ownerless. The Gemara explains the Tanna Kamma's view: he holds that one who declares his slave ownerless frees him, but the slave requires a bill of manumission and eats terumah in the interim.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from a baraita about slaves
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from a baraita about slaves
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: one who writes his property to others, including slaves, and the recipient says 'אי אפשר בהם' — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the heirs have already acquired them.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that a gift is given on condition of acceptance; if not accepted, it returns to the giver.

sub.text: Gemara's question to the first Tanna
sub.text_en: Gemara's question to the first Tanna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the first Tanna: if saying 'אי אפשר' makes the property ownerless, then the slaves would become free and eat תרומה (priestly portion) as non-priests, which is problematic.

sub.text: Gemara's answer for the first Tanna
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for the first Tanna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the first Tanna holds that an abandoned slave goes free but requires a גט שחרור (bill of manumission), and while awaiting it, he still eats תרומה (priestly portion).

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's view on the suspensive guilt-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's view on the suspensive guilt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Eliezer requires a sin-offering for the suspensive guilt-offering, given that he holds one can donate a suspensive guilt-offering daily. Rav Ashi answers that Rabbi Eliezer's statement is in response to the Sages who tell him to wait until he enters a state of doubt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Eliezer requires a sin-offering for the suspensive guilt-offering, given that he holds one can donate a suspensive guilt-offering daily.
Rav Ashi answers that Rabbi Eliezer's statement is in response to the Sages who tell him to wait until he enters a state of doubt.

items.text: Contradiction between the Mishnah and a baraita about disposal of the meat
items.text_en: Contradiction between the Mishnah and a baraita about disposal of the meat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says the meat of a suspensive guilt-offering goes to the burning place, implying that non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard are burned. A baraita says a definite guilt-offering whose owner is absolved is buried. Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction by attributing the rulings to different Tannaim. Rabba distinguishes between a definite guilt-offering (not consecrated) and a suspensive one (consecrated due to anxiety). The Gemara then notes a contradiction within the baraita itself, again resolved by different Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if it became known after slaughter, the meat goes to the burning place, implying non-sacred animals slaughtered in the courtyard are burned.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says a definite guilt-offering whose owner is absolved is buried, not burned.
רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) resolves the contradiction by saying the mishna is disjointed — one tanna taught the first ruling and another taught the second.
The Gemara concludes that this is certainly a disjointed mishna — one tanna taught one ruling and another taught the other.
רבא (Rabba) rejects the contradiction by distinguishing between a definite guilt-offering (not consecrated when unnecessary) and a suspensive guilt-offering (consecrated due to anxiety).
The Gemara notes a contradiction within the definite guilt-offering itself: the baraita says it is buried, but the mishna says it is burned.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the first clause of the baraita about the suspensive guilt-offering (meat to burning) is not problematic because it appears like a disqualified sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the first clause about the suspensive guilt-offering (meat to burning) is not problematic because it appears like a disqualified sacrifice.

items.text: Question about the blood being sprinkled after knowledge
items.text_en: Question about the blood being sprinkled after knowledge
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the blood was sprinkled, the meat may be eaten. The Gemara asks why, since the owner now knows of his sin. Rava answers that the verse requires forgiveness at the time of atonement, and here there was no knowledge at that time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the meat is eaten after the blood is sprinkled, since the owner now has knowledge of the sin.
Rava answers that the verse 'והוא לא ידע ונסלח לו' indicates that atonement requires no knowledge at the time of forgiveness.

items.text: Rabbi Yose's ruling and its basis
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's ruling and its basis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose says even if the blood is in the cup, it should be sprinkled. The Gemara asks why, since there is knowledge at the time of atonement. Rava says Rabbi Yose follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that anything standing to be sprinkled is considered as already sprinkled. The Gemara objects that this case is not standing to be sprinkled, and the Westerners answer that Rabbi Yose holds that service vessels sanctify even a blemished animal initially fit for sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yose's ruling that even if the blood is in the cup, it should be sprinkled.
The Gemara asks why the blood should be sprinkled according to Rabbi Yose, since there is knowledge at the time of atonement.
Rava answers that Rabbi Yose follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that anything standing to be sprinkled is considered as already sprinkled.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon's principle applies only to something standing to be sprinkled, but this blood is not standing to be sprinkled.
The Westerners answer that Rabbi Yose holds that service vessels sanctify even a blemished animal initially fit for sacrifice.

items.text: Dispute about when the heifer whose neck is broken becomes forbidden
items.text_en: Dispute about when the heifer whose neck is broken becomes forbidden
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rav Hamnuna and Rava: Rav Hamnuna says from the moment it is designated, Rava says only after the neck is broken. The Gemara questions Rav Hamnuna's view, asking from when exactly it becomes forbidden.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the עגלה ערופה (broken-necked heifer)
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the עגלה ערופה (broken-necked heifer)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rav Hamnuna says the עגלה ערופה (broken-necked heifer) becomes forbidden from its lifetime, while Rava says after the breaking of the neck.
The Gemara asks: according to Rava, the prohibition begins at the act of breaking the neck; but according to Rav Hamnuna, from when does it become forbidden?
Rava states that the heifer becomes forbidden only after the act of breaking its neck.
The Gemara questions Rav Hamnuna's view: from what exact moment does the heifer become forbidden if it is from its lifetime?

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's forgotten tradition
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's forgotten tradition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai states he heard a tradition about the boundary of the עגלה ערופה but forgot it; the colleagues suggest that its descent to the river valley prohibits it from life.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Shimon exempts and the Sages obligate for slaughtering a פרה אדומה, a stoned ox, or an עגלה ערופה. He argues that if the prohibition is from life, the dispute fits: Rabbi Shimon holds that an unfit slaughter is not considered slaughter, while the Sages hold it is. But if the prohibition is after decapitation, why would Rabbi Shimon exempt? The Gemara rejects the possibility that Rabbi Shimon considers the עגלה ערופה valid by slaughter, citing a baraita that contrasts the laws of the פרה and the עגלה.

items.text: תשובת רבא: רבי שמעון סובר עגלה בשחיטה כשרה
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's regret and response
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna is silent initially, then after leaving he regrets not answering that Rabbi Shimon holds the עגלה is valid by slaughter. The Gemara notes that Rav Hamnuna would respond that there is no Tanna who explicitly states that the עגלה is valid by slaughter, so one could not attribute that view to Rabbi Shimon.
items.desc: לאחר שרב המנונא יצא, רבא אומר שהיה יכול להשיב שרבי שמעון חולק על המשנה וסובר שעגלה ערופה כשרה בשחיטה. הגמרא דוחה שאין מקור לתנא האומר שעגלה כשרה בשחיטה.

items.text: ראיית רבא ממשנת עגלה ערופה: איסור לאחר עריפה
items.text_en: Rava's proof from the Mishnah of עגלה ערופה
items.desc_en: Rava cites a Mishnah: before the עגלה is decapitated, it may go out and graze; after decapitation, it is buried. If the prohibition is from life, why would it go out and graze? The Gemara suggests emending the text to 'before it is seen for decapitation' and 'after it is seen for decapitation'. But then the continuation says that if it came on a doubt, it has atoned and goes away; if the prohibition is from life, it has not yet atoned. This shows the debate is between Tanna'im.
items.desc: רבא מביא ראיה ממשנת סוטה (מו:) שאם נודע הרוצח לפני עריפה – העגלה יוצאת ורועה, מה שמוכיח שהאיסור חל רק לאחר עריפה. הגמרא דוחה את הראיה ומציעה לגרוס 'עד שלא נראתה לעריפה'. רבא מקשה מסיפא שאם נענעה – תיקבר, ומסיים שהסיפא מוכיחה שהאיסור חל לאחר עריפה, שכן אז כיפרה ספיקה.

items.text: ברייתא: מחלוקת תנאים במועד האיסור
items.text_en: The Tannaic dispute explained
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that there is a Tannaic dispute based on a gezerah shavah: just as inside the Temple, the 'מכשיר' (preparatory act) is treated like the 'מכפר' (atonement), so too outside, the preparatory act is treated like the atonement. This resolves the contradiction in the Mishnah.
items.desc: הגמרא מסבירה שהמחלוקת היא בין תנאים, כפי שמובא בברייתא המשווה בין מכשיר ומכפר בפנים ובחוץ, ומסיקה שעגלה ערופה אסורה מחיים, כדעת רב המנונא.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute about אשם תלוי
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute about אשם תלוי
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Eliezer's view that one may voluntarily bring an אשם תלוי any time, called אשם חסידים, and relates that Bava ben Buta would bring one daily except after Yom Kippur. The Sages say an אשם תלוי is only brought for a sin whose intentional violation is כרת and unintentional is חטאת. The Mishnah then discusses the effect of Yom Kippur on various obligations: definite חטאות and אשמות must be brought after Yom Kippur, but אשמות תלויים are exempt; a woman with a doubtful חטאת העוף must bring it after Yom Kippur because it permits her to eat sacrifices.

items.text: גמרא: טעמי המחלוקת באשם תלוי
items.text_en: Gemara: Reasoning of Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning? If the אשם תלוי were an obligation, why would one bring a חטאת when the sin becomes known? Rather, it is a voluntary gift. The Sages respond that only עולה and שלמים come as vows or gifts, but חטאת and אשם are obligations; the אשם תלוי is brought before the sin is known to protect the person, as the Torah is merciful. Rav Acha bar Rava suggests to Rav Ashi that perhaps the אשם תלוי is like עולה and שלמים, which come both as obligation and gift. Rav Ashi rejects this, noting that עולה and שלמים are primarily written as gifts, while the אשם תלוי is primarily written as an obligation.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת את טעמו של רבי אליעזר: אם אשם תלוי חובה, מדוע כשיודע שחטא מביא חטאת? אלא נדבה היא. חכמים משיבים שעולה ושלמים באים בנדר ונדבה, אבל חטאת ואשם חובה, ואשם תלוי בא להגן על הגוף. רב אחא בריה דרבא מקשה: אולי אשם תלוי כעולה ושלמים שבאים גם חובה וגם נדבה? רב אשי דוחה: עיקר עולה ושלמים בנדבה כתיבי, אבל אשם תלוי עיקרו בחובה.

items.text: תחילת ברייתא: רבי חייא תני קמיה דרבא
items.text_en: Introduction to Rabbi Chiyya's teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches a baraita before Rava, introducing further discussion on the topic.
items.desc: הקטע מתחיל בברייתא שרבי חייא שונה לפני רבא, אך הקטע נקטע ואינו ממשיך.

items.text: Challenge to the Mishnah's ruling on asham talui
items.text_en: Challenge to the Mishnah's ruling on asham talui
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised: the Mishnah states that the asham talui is brought only for a sin whose intentional violation is karet and unintentional violation is a chatat, but Rabbi Eliezer holds that it can be brought voluntarily even for other cases, such as eating neveilah. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer's view as stated in a baraita.

items.text: Rava explains the reasoning of the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rava explains the reasoning of the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rava explains the scriptural basis for the Sages' position that the asham talui is only for sins with karet and chatat, deriving it via a gezeirah shavah from the chatat of chelev. He also explains the reasoning of those who said to wait until entering a state of doubt.

items.text: The five ashamot and the status of asham talui
items.text_en: The five ashamot and the status of asham talui
items.desc_en: A baraita states that five ashamot provide complete atonement, but the asham talui does not. Rav Yosef explains that the baraita means the five ashamot provide complete atonement, while the asham talui does not, and this is not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer who holds that asham talui can be brought for neveilah.

items.text: Ravina's alternative explanation and the rule for Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative explanation and the rule for Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: Ravina explains the baraita differently: the five ashamot require bringing a sacrifice after Yom Kippur if the sin becomes known, but the asham talui does not, as per the Mishnah that those liable for suspensive guilt-offerings are exempt after Yom Kippur. The Gemara then asks for the source of this rule.

items.text: Source for Yom Kippur's atonement for sins without a sacrifice
items.text_en: Source for Yom Kippur's atonement for sins without a sacrifice
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi quotes Rabbi Ami quoting Rabbi Chanina that a verse teaches Yom Kippur atones for sins that are not eligible for a sacrifice, but not for sins that are. Abaye challenges this, arguing the verse refers to the inner goat, not the scapegoat. Abaye then cites a different verse from the scapegoat to prove the same point.

items.text: Challenge to the proof from pesha'im
items.text_en: Challenge to the proof from pesha'im
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi challenges Abaye's proof, questioning whether the 'pesha'im' in the verse refer to sins that are not eligible for a sacrifice, as there is a Mishnah that four people bring a sacrifice for intentional sins as if unintentional. Ravin then cites Resh Lakish supporting Abaye's view, but Abaye notes the challenge remains. Ravin responds that most pesha'im are not eligible for a sacrifice, but Abaye objects that the verse does not say 'most'.

items.text: Abaye's final proof from the verse's structure
items.text_en: Abaye's final proof from the verse's structure
items.desc_en: Abaye provides a definitive proof from the beginning of the verse: 'avonot' refers to intentional sins, and the word 'all' in 'all their sins' serves to equate sins to pesha'im, meaning only sins not eligible for a sacrifice are atoned for by Yom Kippur, not those that are.

items.text: Source for the exemption of asham talui after Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Source for the exemption of asham talui after Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar cites a verse to show that Yom Kippur atones for a sin known only to God, which is the case for an asham talui. Rav Tachlifa then adds a comment about the earlier discussion.

items.text: Refining the principle of atonement for unknown sins
items.text_en: Refining the principle of atonement for unknown sins
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier derivations from Rav Dimi and Abaye and instead derives from a baraita that Yom Kippur atones only for a sin known to none but God, but not for a sin known to the sinner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier derivations from Rav Dimi and Abaye.
The Gemara derives from a baraita that Yom Kippur atones only for a sin known to none but God, but not for a sin known to the sinner.

items.text: Lashes and Yom Kippur atonement
items.text_en: Lashes and Yom Kippur atonement
items.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Rav Huna in the name of Rava states that one liable for lashes who has Yom Kippur pass over him remains liable. The Gemara questions why this is obvious, and explains that one might think lashes are different because they involve the body, but the teaching shows they are not exempted by Yom Kippur.

sub.text: Rav Tachlifa bar Rav Huna in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Rav Huna in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Rav Huna in the name of Rava states that those liable for lashes who have Yom Kippur pass over them remain liable.
The Gemara questions why this ruling is not obvious, asking how lashes differ from definite sin-offerings and guilt-offerings which are not exempted by Yom Kippur.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought lashes, being a bodily punishment, are different from monetary obligations, so the teaching informs us that Yom Kippur does not exempt them either.

items.text: Reconciling with the Mishnah
items.text_en: Reconciling with the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction with a Mishnah that lists cases where Yom Kippur does not atone, and resolves it by distinguishing between cases where the sinner was warned (lashes apply) and where not (Yom Kippur atones).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a Mishnah that lists cases where Yom Kippur does not atone, including sins of which one was aware.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the sinner was warned (lashes apply, Yom Kippur does not atone) and where not warned (Yom Kippur atones).

items.text: Case of a doubtful woman after childbirth
items.text_en: Case of a doubtful woman after childbirth
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that a woman after childbirth who is uncertain whether she sinned should not bring a sacrifice after Yom Kippur, since her sin is unknown. Rav Hoshaya answers that the verse 'for all their sins' excludes impurities. Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's view is addressed: the woman brings the sacrifice not for atonement but to permit eating sacrificial food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from the case of a woman doubtful about childbirth: since Yom Kippur atones for unknown sins, she should no longer bring a sacrifice after the day.

Rav Hoshaya answers that the verse 'for all their sins' (לכל חטאתם) excludes impurities (טומאות), so Yom Kippur does not atone for impurity-related obligations; therefore the woman still brings her sacrifice.

sub.text: Gemara's objection regarding Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection regarding Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, who holds a woman after childbirth is a sinner, her sacrifice should be for atonement and thus Yom Kippur should exempt her.
The Gemara resolves that the woman brings her korban (sacrifice) not for atonement (כפרה) but to permit her to eat sacrificial food (קדשים), so Yom Kippur does not affect the obligation.

items.text: Support from a Mishnah
items.text_en: Support from a Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a Mishnah that a woman with a doubtful bird sin-offering who has Yom Kippur pass over her must still bring it afterward, because it permits her to eat sacrificial food.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a Mishnah that a woman with a doubtful bird sin-offering who has Yom Kippur pass over her must still bring it afterward, because it permits her to eat sacrificial food.

items.text: Case of a doubtful leper
items.text_en: Case of a doubtful leper
items.desc_en: The Gemara similarly questions a doubtful leper, and Rabbi Oshaya answers with the same exclusion. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that leprosy comes for seven sins, but the leper brings a sacrifice to permit eating sacrificial food, not for atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a doubtful leper whose Yom Kippur passed should not bring a sacrifice, since Yom Kippur atones for a sin known only to God.
Rabbi Oshaya answers by citing the verse 'לְכׇל חַטֹּאתָם' (for all their sins) to exclude ritual impurities from Yom Kippur atonement.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan states that leprosy comes for seven sins, but the leper brings a sacrifice only to permit eating sacrificial food, not for atonement.

items.text: Case of a doubtful nazirite
items.text_en: Case of a doubtful nazirite
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a doubtful nazirite, and Rabbi Oshaya answers with the same exclusion. Rabbi Elazar ben Hakkappar's view is addressed: the nazirite brings a sacrifice to permit eating sacrificial food, not for atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a doubtful nazirite should bring a sacrifice after Yom Kippur, since Yom Kippur atones for unknown sins.
Rabbi Oshaya answers that the verse 'לְכׇל חַטֹּאתָם' excludes cases of ritual impurity (טוּמְאָה), so Yom Kippur does not atone for the nazirite's impurity.

sub.text: Gemara's objection regarding Rabbi Elazar ben Hakkappar
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection regarding Rabbi Elazar ben Hakkappar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Elazar ben Hakkappar, who says a nazirite is a sinner, the nazirite's sacrifice should be for atonement, not just for permitting sacrificial food.
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Elazar ben Hakkappar, the nazirite brings the sacrifice only to permit eating sacrificial food, not for atonement.

items.text: Case of a doubtful sotah
items.text_en: Case of a doubtful sotah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a doubtful sotah, and Rabbi Hoshaya answers with the same exclusion. Abaye says the husband knows of the sin, and Rava says the sotah brings the offering to clarify the sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge: if Yom Kippur atones for unknown sins, then a doubtful sotah (סוֹטָה) whose Yom Kippur has passed should not need to bring her offering.
Rabbi Hoshaya answers by citing the verse 'לְכׇל חַטֹּאתָם' (for all their sins) — excluding cases of ritual impurity (טוּמְאָה), so the sotah's offering is still required.
Abaye argues that the husband (בּוֹעֵל) knows of the suspected sin, so it is not an unknown sin and Yom Kippur does not atone for it.
Rava explains that the sotah brings her offering not for atonement (כַּפָּרָה) but to clarify the sin (לְבָרֵר עָוֹן), so Yom Kippur does not exempt her.

items.text: Case of the eglah arufah
items.text_en: Case of the eglah arufah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the eglah arufah, and Abaye says the murderer knows. Rava cites a verse that the land cannot be atoned for the spilled blood. Rav Papa cites another verse that this atonement is fitting for the generation of the Exodus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the eglah arufah (עגלה ערופה) should be exempt after Yom Kippur, since the sin is unknown to anyone but God.
Abaye answers that the murderer knows the sin, so it is not a sin known only to God.
Rava cites a verse that the land cannot be atoned for the spilled blood, implying Yom Kippur does not atone for this sin.
Rav Papa cites a verse that this atonement is fitting for the generation of the Exodus, not for the eglah arufah.

items.text: Deriving that a sin-offering is brought after Yom Kippur when the sin becomes known
items.text_en: Deriving that a sin-offering is brought after Yom Kippur when the sin becomes known
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if Yom Kippur atones for unknown sins, why bring a sin-offering when the sin becomes known after Yom Kippur? Rabbi Zeira answers that the Torah requires 'knowledge' (ידיעה) for a sin-offering, written regarding an individual, a prince, and the community. The Gemara then engages in a lengthy derivation (בנין אב) to show that the verse about the prince is superfluous and teaches that one brings a sin-offering even after Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if Yom Kippur atones for unknown sins, why bring a sin-offering when the sin becomes known after Yom Kippur?
Rabbi Zeira answers that the Torah requires 'knowledge' (ידיעה) for a sin-offering, written regarding an individual, a prince, and the community.
The Gemara engages in a lengthy derivation (בנין אב) to show that the verse about the prince is superfluous and teaches that one brings a sin-offering even after Yom Kippur.

items.text: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye offers a different reasoning: without the verse about the prince, one could not derive it from the individual and community because they are not subject to change, unlike the prince.

sub.desc_en: Abaye offers an alternative reasoning: without the verse about the prince, one could not derive it from the individual and community because they are not subject to change, unlike the prince.

items.text: Opening question about the nasi
items.text_en: Opening question about the nasi
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a nasi who is subject to change, but the text is fragmentary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a fragmentary question about a nasi who is subject to change.

items.text: Abaye's derivation and the challenge regarding asham taluy
items.text_en: Abaye's derivation and the challenge regarding asham taluy
items.desc_en: Abaye derives from the three mentions of 'yedi'ot' that a hatat is brought only when the sin becomes known after Yom Kippur. The Gemara objects that asham taluy, which atones for the same sin, might exempt one from bringing a hatat later.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by deriving from the shared word 'מצות' (commandments) that the three mentions of 'yedi'ot' (awareness) in the Torah are superfluous for their own context.
Abaye resolves that the superfluous mentions teach that a חטאת (sin-offering) is brought only when the sin becomes known after Yom Kippur.
The Gemara objects that an אשם תלוי (conditional guilt-offering), which atones for the same sin, might exempt one from bringing a חטאת (sin-offering) later.

items.text: Rava's resolution and the purpose of asham taluy
items.text_en: Rava's resolution and the purpose of asham taluy
items.desc_en: Rava cites the verse 'or it became known to him' to show that whenever knowledge comes, a hatat is brought. Rabbi Zeira and Rava debate the purpose of asham taluy: to protect from punishment if one dies, or to shield from suffering.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves by citing the verse 'או הודע אליו' (or it becomes known to him) to show that whenever knowledge comes, a sin-offering is brought; the guilt-offering of doubt (אשם תלוי) serves to protect from suffering, not to atone.
The Gemara asks: given that a חטאת is always brought upon knowledge, what is the purpose of the אשם תלוי (suspended guilt-offering)?
Rabbi Zeira answers that the אשם תלוי protects one from dying with sin if death occurs before knowledge.
Rava objects that death itself atones (מיתה ממרקת), so the אשם תלוי is unnecessary for that purpose.
Rava resolves that the אשם תלוי serves to shield one from suffering (יסורים) in this world.

items.text: The case of hatat ha'of on safek and the ruling of Rav
items.text_en: The case of hatat ha'of on safek and the ruling of Rav
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a hatat ha'of brought on safek is buried. Rav says it atones, so why bury it? The Gemara explains that it is not guarded, and resolves that the Mishnah refers to a case where it became known she did not give birth, and the burial is rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a hatat ha'of brought on safek is buried.
The Gemara notes that Rav says the bird atones, so why is it buried?
The Gemara answers that it is because the bird is not guarded, but then questions when it is not guarded.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to a case where it became known she did not give birth, and the burial requirement is rabbinic.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on hatat ha'of after melikah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on hatat ha'of after melikah
items.desc_en: Rav rules that if after melikah it becomes known she gave birth, the bird's blood is sprinkled and it is permitted to eat. Rabbi Yochanan forbids it as a decree. Levi's baraita supports Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rav's statement was about a woman who brought a bird sin offering due to uncertainty: if before melikah it became known she definitely gave birth, she makes it a definite offering.
Rav rules that if after melikah it became known she gave birth, the priest sprinkles and squeezes the blood, she achieves atonement, and the bird is permitted for consumption.
Rabbi Yochanan objects: the bird is prohibited for consumption, as a decree lest people say that a bird sin offering brought due to uncertainty is eaten.

Levi teaches a baraita supporting Rav: if after melikah it became known she definitely gave birth, the blood is sprinkled and squeezed, she achieves atonement, and the bird is permitted for consumption.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan: if after melikah it becomes known she gave birth, the bird is forbidden even in benefit, since it atoned for its doubt.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if before melikah it becomes known she did not give birth, the bird goes to non-sacred use or is sold; if it becomes known she certainly gave birth, she renders it a definite sin offering.
The baraita concludes that if after melikah it becomes known she gave birth, the bird is forbidden even in benefit, since it atoned for its doubt.

items.text: Mishnah: Separating two selaim for asham
items.text_en: Mishnah: Separating two selaim for asham
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details cases where one separates two selaim for an asham and buys rams, specifying which ram is offered and what happens to the other.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: one who separates two selaim for an asham and buys two rams, where one is worth two selaim—that one is offered, and the other grazes until blemished, sold, and its proceeds go to the Temple fund.
The Mishnah states the second case: one buys two non-sacred rams with the two selaim—the one worth two selaim is offered as his asham, and the other goes for his me'ilah (misuse payment).

The Mishnah states the third case: one ram is for asham and one for non-sacred use—if the asham ram is worth two selaim, it is offered, the other goes for me'ilah, and he brings an additional selah and its fifth.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'me'ilato' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'me'ilato' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'me'ilato' in the first clause, initially thinking it refers to an asham ram, but rejects this based on verses and the latter clause. It concludes that 'me'ilato' means the benefit he derived from hekdesh, i.e., the principal (gezelo).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'me'ilato' means in the first clause of the Mishnah.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that 'me'ilato' means the asham ram, citing the verse that the fifth (חומש) is brought with the principal (גזילו), not with the ram.
The Gemara further supports its rejection by citing the latter clause of the Mishnah, which explicitly states that the fifth is brought with the principal.
The Gemara concludes that 'me'ilato' in the first clause refers to the benefit he derived from hekdesh, i.e., the principal (גזילו).
The Gemara objects that the latter clause of the Mishnah uses 'me'ilato' to mean the asham ram, creating an inconsistency.
The Gemara resolves the inconsistency by stating that in the first clause 'me'ilato' refers to the principal (גזילו), while in the latter clause it refers to the asham ram.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's distinction between the first and last clauses
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's distinction between the first and last clauses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah calls the animal 'his me'ilah' in the first clause but 'a guilt-offering ram' in the last clause: in the first case he had a ram and its value plus a fifth, so the animal is called 'his me'ilah'; in the last case he did not have a ram, so the animal is called 'a guilt-offering ram' and he brings a selah and its fifth with it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah calls the animal 'his me'ilah' in the first clause but 'a guilt-offering ram' in the last clause.

The Gemara explains: in the first case he had a ram and its value plus a fifth, so the animal is called 'his me'ilah'; in the last case he did not have a ram, so the animal is called 'a guilt-offering ram' and he brings a selah and its fifth with it.

items.text: Rav Menashya bar Gadda's question about gathering fifths
items.text_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda's question about gathering fifths
items.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda asks whether one achieves atonement by gathering multiple fifths (without a principal). The Gemara frames the dilemma: perhaps one is atoned through the appreciation of consecrated property because he exerted himself, but here he did not exert; or perhaps one is not atoned through appreciation because he did not separate the principal, but here he did separate the fifths. This is linked to the unresolved question of whether a person is atoned through the appreciation of consecrated property.

sub.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda asks whether gathering multiple fifths (without a principal) achieves atonement.
The Gemara frames one side of the dilemma: perhaps one is atoned through appreciation of consecrated property only because he exerted himself, but here he did not exert, so he is not atoned.
The Gemara frames the other side: perhaps one is not atoned through appreciation because he did not separate the principal, but here he did separate the fifths, so he may be atoned.
The Gemara notes that this dilemma is linked to the unresolved question of whether a person is atoned through the appreciation of consecrated property.

items.text: First attempted proof: two rams from two selahs
items.text_en: First attempted proof: two rams from two selahs
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: one who sets aside two selahs for a guilt-offering and buys two rams, one worth two selahs – that one is sacrificed, the other grazes until blemished and is sold, with proceeds falling to a donation. The Gemara initially assumes he bought with four selahs and the ram appreciated to eight, proving atonement through appreciation. It rejects this: the shepherd discounted the price.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about one who sets aside two selahs for a guilt-offering and buys two rams, where one ram appreciates to two selahs and is sacrificed, while the other grazes until blemished and is sold for donation.
The Gemara infers that the person bought with four selahs and the ram appreciated to eight, proving that atonement is achieved through appreciation of consecrated property.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the shepherd discounted the price, so the ram was actually worth only two selahs from the start.

items.text: Second and third attempted proofs: fattening the ram
items.text_en: Second and third attempted proofs: fattening the ram
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita: one who bought a ram for one selah and fattened it to two selahs – it is valid. The Gemara initially thinks this proves atonement through appreciation, but rejects it because the owner spent money (the ram cost him two selahs). A third baraita says the same, but the Gemara distinguishes: the first case is buying for four and appreciating by four (cost eight), the second is buying for four and appreciating by three (worth eight).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about buying a ram for one selah and fattening it to two selahs, which it initially interprets as proof that one can achieve atonement through appreciation (שבח הקדש).
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing the case because the owner spent money on fattening (the ram cost him two selahs overall).
The Gemara brings a third baraita about buying a ram for one selah that is now worth two selahs, and the Gemara immediately dismisses it by saying the same case of fattening applies.

The Gemara resolves the apparent redundancy between the two baraitot by distinguishing: the first case is buying for four selahs and appreciating by four (total cost eight), the second is buying for four selahs and appreciating by three (total worth eight).

items.text: Analyzing the baraita's conclusion: paying a selah
items.text_en: Analyzing the baraita's conclusion: paying a selah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's statement that he pays a selah: if he lacks seven selahs, what does 'pay a selah' mean? It explains it means payment of a selah. If one holds that there is no atonement through appreciation, paying a selah is insufficient because we need a ram worth two selahs. The Gemara concludes that the baraita holds that atonement through appreciation is valid, but the payment is a decree lest people say a ram worth less than two selahs atones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the baraita's case is as explained, its conclusion that he pays a selah is problematic because he lacks seven selahs, not one.
The Gemara explains: 'pay a selah' means he pays the value of a selah as compensation for the shortfall, not an additional selah.
The Gemara objects: if the baraita holds that there is no atonement through appreciation (שבח הקדש), paying a selah is insufficient because a ram worth two selahs is required.
