The Gemara resolves: the baraita actually holds that atonement through appreciation (שבח הקדש) is valid, so the ram's value reaches two selahs.
The Gemara objects: if atonement through appreciation is valid, why require payment of a selah at all?
The Gemara resolves: the payment of a selah is a decree (גזירה) lest people mistakenly think that a ram worth less than two selahs atones.

items.text: A baraita ruling against atonement through appreciation
items.text_en: A baraita ruling against atonement through appreciation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: if at the time of designation the ram was worth one selah but at the time of atonement it was worth two selahs, he has not fulfilled his obligation. This contradicts the previous conclusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita ruling that if the ram was worth one selah at designation but two selahs at atonement, he has not fulfilled his obligation, contradicting the previous conclusion.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's question and Rabbi Yochanan's answer from the Todah
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question and Rabbi Yochanan's answer from the Todah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether a person is atoned through the appreciation of consecrated property. Rabbi Yochanan says he grew up with him for years and never heard this law from him. The Gemara infers that Rabbi Yochanan did state it, citing a Mishnah about the offspring of a Todah: after atonement the offspring does not require bread, but before atonement it does, implying atonement through appreciation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether a person achieves atonement (כפרה) through the appreciation in value of consecrated property.
Rabbi Yochanan expresses surprise, saying he never taught this law to Rabbi Elazar despite years of study together.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yochanan's denial that he actually did state the law, and identifies the context.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that the offspring of a Todah (תודה) does not require bread after atonement.

sub.text: Rav Chananyah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Chananyah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Chananyah reports in Rabbi Yochanan's name that the Mishnah's rule applies only after atonement, implying that before atonement the offspring does require bread.
The Gemara concludes that before atonement the offspring requires bread, proving that Rabbi Yochanan holds that one is atoned through the appreciation of consecrated property.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's question about disqualification of living animals
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question about disqualification of living animals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether living animals are subject to disqualification (dichui). Rabbi Yochanan again says he never heard this law from him. The Gemara infers he did, citing a case of a partnership animal: one partner consecrated his half, then bought the other half and consecrated it – it is consecrated but not sacrificed, and it effects temurah. This proves three things: living animals are subject to disqualification, sanctity of value can cause disqualification, and there is disqualification regarding monetary value.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether living animals are subject to disqualification (דיחוי).
Rabbi Yochanan exclaims that Rabbi Elazar never heard this law from him, implying he did teach it.
The Gemara infers that Rabbi Yochanan did teach this, citing his ruling about a partnership animal that is consecrated but not sacrificed, proving living animals can be disqualified.
The Gemara derives three principles from this case: living animals are subject to disqualification, sanctity of value can cause disqualification, and disqualification applies to monetary value.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's question about price fluctuation and Rabbi Yochanan's tradition
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question about price fluctuation and Rabbi Yochanan's tradition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks: if lambs become cheap, what is the law? Do we require 'the choice of your vows' (which exists) or 'silver of shekels' (which is lacking)? Rabbi Yochanan says they never heard this law. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan himself cited Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that the Torah did not fix a price for those lacking atonement lest lambs become cheap and they have no remedy to eat sacrifices. The Gemara resolves that they had not learned this law, or it was not asked of him in the study hall. Abaye and Rava then challenge the reasoning: why not fix a price for a fat-offering sin-offering (which is for atonement, not for eating) or a Nazirite's guilt-offering (which comes to nullify)? The Gemara concludes it is difficult.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether, if lambs become cheap, the requirement is 'the choice of your vows' (which exists) or 'silver of shekels' (which is lacking).
Rabbi Yochanan says they never heard this law in the study hall.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan himself cited Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that the Torah did not fix a price for those lacking atonement lest lambs become cheap and they have no remedy to eat sacrifices.
The Gemara resolves that they had not learned this law, or it was not asked of him in the study hall.

The Gemara cites the tradition of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that the Torah did not fix a price for those lacking atonement lest lambs become cheap and they have no remedy to eat sacrifices.
Abaye challenges: if the reason is to enable eating sacrifices, then why not fix a price for a fat-offering sin-offering (חטאת חלב), which comes for atonement and not for eating?
Rava challenges: why not fix a price for a Nazirite's guilt-offering (אשם נזיר), which comes to nullify (לבטלה) and not for eating?
The Gemara concludes that the difficulty remains unresolved.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: A son may not bring his father's sin-offering
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: A son may not bring his father's sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one designates a sin-offering and dies, his son may not bring it in his stead. One may not transfer a sin-offering from one sin to another, even if the sin is of the same type, as the verse says "his offering for his sin" – the offering must be for that specific sin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a son may not bring his father's designated sin-offering, and one may not transfer a sin-offering from one sin to another, even of the same type.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation from the verse and discussion of possible exceptions
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation from the verse and discussion of possible exceptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of this law and cites a baraita that derives from "his offering" that one only fulfills his obligation with his own offering, not his father's. It then considers various possible exceptions: whether one could use his father's animal for a similar sin, or his father's money for any sin, or his own animal for a different sin, or his own money for a different sin. Each possibility is rejected by the verse "his offering for his sin," requiring the offering to be specifically for that sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's law that a son cannot bring his father's sin-offering.
A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'קרבנו' (his offering) that one fulfills his obligation only with his own offering, not his father's.
The Gemara raises a possible exception: perhaps the son could use his father's animal for a similar sin (e.g., light for light or severe for severe), but the verse 'קרבנו' rejects this.
The Gemara raises another possible exception: perhaps the son could use his father's money for any sin, since a nazirite shaves on his father's unspecified money, but the verse 'קרבנו' rejects this.
The Gemara raises a further exception: perhaps the son could use his own animal for a different sin, but the verse 'קרבנו על חטאתו' requires the offering to be specifically for that sin.

The Gemara raises a final exception: perhaps the son could use his own money for a different sin, since money can be redeemed and atone, but the verse 'קרבנו על חטאתו' requires the offering to be specifically for that sin.

items.text: Clarification of the distinction between animal and money
items.text_en: Clarification of the distinction between animal and money
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Shimi explains before Rav Pappa the reasoning behind the distinction between an animal and money: with an animal, since one cannot misuse it (by changing its designation), it cannot atone for a different sin. But with money, since one can misuse it and bring a guilt-offering for misuse, one might think he could bring it for a different sin from the outset, so the verse teaches that he cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by the phrase 'he did not misuse and did not atone' in the baraita.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Shimi's explanation before Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Shimi's explanation before Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Shimi explains before Rav Pappa that the baraita means: since one cannot misuse an animal designated for a sin-offering by changing its purpose, it cannot atone for a different sin; but with money, since one could misuse it and bring a guilt-offering for misuse, one might think he could bring it for a different sin from the outset, so the verse teaches that he cannot.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Upgrading and downgrading sin-offerings based on wealth
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Upgrading and downgrading sin-offerings based on wealth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one may bring a sin-offering of lesser value from the consecration of a more valuable one, and vice versa: from a lamb to a goat, from a goat to a lamb, from a lamb or goat to birds, and from birds to a tenth of an ephah. If one designated a lamb or goat and became poor, he brings a bird; if he became poorer, he brings a tenth of an ephah. If he designated a tenth of an ephah and became wealthy, he brings a bird; if wealthier, he brings a lamb or goat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: one may upgrade or downgrade a sin-offering from a lamb to a goat, from a goat to a lamb, from a lamb or goat to birds, and from birds to a tenth of an ephah.

The Mishnah illustrates the rule with examples: if one designated a lamb or goat and became poor, he brings a bird; if poorer still, a tenth of an ephah; if he designated a tenth of an ephah and became wealthy, he brings a bird; if wealthier, a lamb or goat.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the laws of upgrading and downgrading
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the laws of upgrading and downgrading
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source and cites a baraita that derives from the repeated phrases "from his sin-offering" and "for his sin-offering" that one may bring a lesser offering from the consecration of a greater one, and vice versa. It explains that both phrases are necessary: "from his sin-offering" is written regarding a lamb or goat to teach that one may downgrade to a bird, and regarding a bird to teach that one may downgrade to a tenth of an ephah. "For his sin-offering" is written regarding the tenth of an ephah to teach that one may upgrade to a bird or a lamb or goat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's rule about upgrading and downgrading sin-offerings.

A baraita is cited that derives from the repeated phrases 'מֵחַטָּאתוֹ' and 'עַל חַטָּאתוֹ' the rule that one may bring a lesser offering from the consecration of a greater one, and vice versa, with examples of upgrading and downgrading.
The baraita adds a case where the animal became disqualified, teaching that one may bring a bird with its redemption money, but a bird cannot be redeemed for a tenth of an ephah.
The baraita concludes that therefore the phrases 'מֵחַטָּאתוֹ' and 'עַל חַטָּאתוֹ' are written to teach these laws.

The Gemara explains that both instances of 'מֵחַטָּאתוֹ' are necessary: one for downgrading from a lamb/goat to a bird (both animal offerings), and one for downgrading from a bird to a tenth of an ephah (a grain offering), to prevent the mistaken assumption that only similar types can be exchanged.

The Gemara explains the reverse direction: one who consecrated money for a tenth of an ephah and became wealthy may add to the money and bring a bird, and if wealthier, add further and bring a lamb or goat.

The Gemara explains why 'עַל חַטָּאתוֹ' is written specifically regarding the tenth of an ephah: to teach that even from a poor person's offering one may upgrade to a bird or animal, and the original money falls to the Temple treasury as a donation.

items.text: Beginning of a new statement by Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Beginning of a new statement by Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: A wealthy person who defiled the Temple and designated a bird-offering... (the statement is cut off, continuing on the next amud).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states in the name of Rabbi Oshaya a halacha about a wealthy person who defiled the Temple and designated a bird-offering (the statement is cut off).

items.text: Rav Huna's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Huna's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua derives three principles from the Mishnah's case of a poor person who designated a lamb for his sin-offering and then became wealthy: that living animals can be 'pushed off' (nidchim), that sanctity of money can also be pushed off, and that something pushed off from the start is considered permanently pushed off.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a poor person designated a lamb for his sin-offering and then became wealthy, since it was pushed off, it remains pushed off.

Rav Huna bar Yehoshua derives three principles from the Mishnah: that living animals can be pushed off (נִדְחִים), that sanctity of money can also be pushed off, and that something pushed off from the start is considered permanently pushed off.

items.text: Rav Ukva bar Chama's objection from the Mishnah of a female designated for a Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Rav Ukva bar Chama's objection from the Mishnah of a female designated for a Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: Rav Ukva bar Chama cites a Mishnah where a female animal designated for a Paschal lamb before Passover must graze until blemished and be sold, but Rabbi Shimon says the male offspring itself may be offered as a Paschal lamb. This implies that living animals are not pushed off, contradicting Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ukva bar Chama cites the first part of the Mishnah about a female designated for a Paschal lamb, which requires the offspring to graze until blemished and be sold, implying living animals are pushed off.
Rabbi Shimon states that the male offspring itself may be offered as a Paschal lamb, contradicting the notion that living animals are pushed off.
The Gemara concludes from Rabbi Shimon's statement that living animals are not pushed off, challenging Rav Huna's inference.

items.text: Resolution from the school of Rabbi Oshaya: Rabbi Shimon's view on living animals and the lot
items.text_en: Resolution from the school of Rabbi Oshaya: Rabbi Shimon's view on living animals and the lot
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Oshaya explains that Rabbi Shimon holds that living animals are not pushed off and that the lot is not indispensable. This is supported by a baraita where if one of the two goats for Yom Kippur dies, the other is brought without a lot, according to Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Oshaya states that Rabbi Shimon holds that living animals are not permanently disqualified.

sub.text: School of Rabbi Oshaya (citing a baraita)
sub.text_en: School of Rabbi Oshaya (citing a baraita)
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Oshaya adds that Rabbi Shimon also holds the lot is not indispensable, citing a baraita where if one of the two Yom Kippur goats dies, the other is brought without a lot.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon indeed holds that living animals are not permanently disqualified and that the lot is not indispensable.

items.text: Rav Chisda's principle: Bird offerings are distinguished only by purchase or priestly action
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's principle: Bird offerings are distinguished only by purchase or priestly action
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that bird offerings (kinim) are not distinguished as to which is for a sin-offering and which for a burnt-offering except either at the time of purchase by the owner or at the time of the priest's action. Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains the scriptural basis: verses mention 'taking' and 'doing'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that bird offerings (קינין) are designated as sin-offering or burnt-offering only either at the time of purchase by the owner or at the time of the priest's action.

Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains the scriptural basis for Rav Chisda's principle: verses mention 'taking' (לקיחה) and 'doing' (עשייה), indicating that designation occurs at purchase or at the priest's action.

items.text: Objection from a baraita on the lot and resolution by Rav
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita on the lot and resolution by Rav
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that the lot designates the goat as a sin-offering, not the name or the priest. This seems to contradict Rav Chisda, as the lot operates without purchase or priestly action. Rav explains that the baraita's argument is that just as the lot does not require purchase or priestly action, so too the name should not; but the verse teaches that the lot alone designates, not the name.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states the lot designates the goat as a sin-offering, not the name or the priest.
The baraita presents a possible a fortiori inference that the name should designate, just as the lot does.
The baraita concludes that the verse teaches the lot alone designates, not the name.
The Gemara objects that the baraita compares name to lot, implying name also does not require purchase or priestly action, contradicting Rav Chisda.

Rav explains that the baraita's argument is that just as the lot does not require purchase or priestly action, so too the name should not; but the verse teaches that the lot alone designates, not the name.
The verse is cited again to support Rav's interpretation that the lot alone designates, not the name.

items.text: Objection from the case of a poor person who defiled the Temple and designated money for his bird offering
items.text_en: Objection from the case of a poor person who defiled the Temple and designated money for his bird offering
items.desc_en: Another objection is raised: a poor person who designated money for his bird offering and then became wealthy can bring his obligation from the money designated for the sin-offering but not from the burnt-offering money. This seems to show that designation alone (without purchase or priestly action) distinguishes the offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: a poor person who designated money for his bird offering and then became wealthy can bring his obligation from the money designated for the sin-offering but not from the burnt-offering money, showing that designation alone (without purchase or priestly action) distinguishes the offerings, contradicting Rav Ḥisda.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's resolution: The Mishnah is problematic, and the designation was made at the time of poverty
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's resolution: The Mishnah is problematic, and the designation was made at the time of poverty
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges the Mishnah itself, citing Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya that a rich person who brings a poor person's offering does not fulfill his obligation. He resolves that the case is where the person designated the money while still poor, so the designation is effective. For Rabbi Chaggai's view that he does fulfill the obligation, the Mishnah must be read as 'afterwards he purchased and said'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges the Mishnah by citing Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya that a rich person who brings a poor person's offering does not fulfill his obligation.
Rav Sheshet resolves that the Mishnah's case is where the person designated the money while still poor, so the designation is effective.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet's alternative resolution for Rabbi Chaggai
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet's alternative resolution for Rabbi Chaggai
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet offers an alternative resolution for Rabbi Chaggai's view that he does fulfill the obligation, requiring the Mishnah to be read as 'afterwards he purchased and said'.

items.text: Objection from the metzora's offering and resolution distinguishing metzora from one who defiled the Temple
items.text_en: Objection from the metzora's offering and resolution distinguishing metzora from one who defiled the Temple
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a poor metzora who brings a rich person's offering fulfills his obligation, but a rich metzora who brings a poor person's offering does not. This contradicts Rabbi Chaggai's view. The Gemara resolves that the metzora is different because the Torah uses 'zot' to exclude the rich metzora, but 'Torat' includes the poor metzora. This does not apply to one who defiled the Temple, where a rich person who brings a poor person's offering does fulfill his obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a metzora: a poor metzora who brings a rich person's offering fulfills his obligation, but a rich metzora who brings a poor person's offering does not, contradicting Rabbi Chaggai's view.

Rabbi Chaggai distinguishes the metzora case: the Torah uses 'זאת' (this) to exclude a rich metzora who brings a poor person's offering, while 'תורת' (the law of) includes a poor metzora who brings a rich person's offering.
The Gemara objects: if 'זאת' excludes the rich metzora, then the poor metzora should also be excluded; the Gemara answers that 'תורת' includes the poor metzora.

The Gemara resolves that the metzora's law is unique to him, based on the verse 'וְאִם דַּל הוּא' (if he is poor), so a rich metzora who brings a poor person's offering does not fulfill his obligation, but one who defiled the Temple — a rich person who brings a poor person's offering does fulfill his obligation.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon on precedence of lambs, doves, father, and teacher
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon on precedence of lambs, doves, father, and teacher
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that lambs precede goats, doves precede pigeons, and father precedes mother in honor, but in each case a verse shows they are equal. However, the Sages said father precedes mother because both are obligated in the father's honor, and similarly a teacher precedes a father because both are obligated in the teacher's honor.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that lambs precede goats everywhere, but a verse shows they are equal.
The Mishnah teaches that doves precede pigeons, but a verse shows they are equal.
The Mishnah teaches that father precedes mother in honor, but a verse shows they are equal; however, the Sages said father precedes mother because both are obligated in the father's honor.
The Mishnah teaches that a teacher precedes a father because both are obligated in the teacher's honor.

items.text: Gemara: The four cries of the Temple courtyard
items.text_en: Gemara: The four cries of the Temple courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic: the four cries that the Temple courtyard cried out, the first being to remove the sons of Eli who defiled the Sanctuary, and the second to open the gates for Yochanan ben Nidbai to fill his belly from the sacred offerings.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the Temple courtyard cried out four cries, the first being to remove the sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, who defiled the Sanctuary.
The baraita continues with the second cry: to open the gates for Yochanan ben Nidbai, who would fill his belly from the sacred offerings, and it describes his gluttony.

items.text: Opening description of the High Priest's practice
items.text_en: Opening description of the High Priest's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes that the High Priest would wipe his hands after the meal, and it was said that no leftover meat ever remained in the Temple courtyard during his tenure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes the High Priest's practice of wiping his hands after the meal, noting that no leftover meat ever remained in the Temple courtyard during his tenure.

items.text: Third proclamation: Elishama ben Pichai enters
items.text_en: Third proclamation: Elishama ben Pichai enters
items.desc_en: The third proclamation calls for the gates to open for Elishama ben Pichai, a disciple of Pinchas, to serve as High Priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the third proclamation calling for the gates to open for Elishama ben Pichai, a disciple of Pinchas, to serve as High Priest.

items.text: Fourth proclamation and the story of Yissachar of Kfar Barkai
items.text_en: Fourth proclamation and the story of Yissachar of Kfar Barkai
items.desc_en: The fourth proclamation calls to expel Yissachar of Kfar Barkai, who disgraced sacred matters. The Gemara recounts how he was asked by King Yannai and his wife whether a goat or lamb is better, and he gestured incorrectly, leading to his hand being cut off. Rav Yosef blesses God for removing him from the High Priesthood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the fourth proclamation, which calls to expel Yissachar of Kfar Barkai for disgracing sacred matters, and describes his practice of wrapping silk around his hands while performing the Temple service.

The Gemara asks what happened to Yissachar, and recounts how King Yannai and his queen, disagreeing whether a goat or lamb is better, decided to ask Yissachar as High Priest who would know the matter.

Yissachar answers that if a goat is better it should be offered as the daily sacrifice, but he gestures with his hand, leading the king to order his right hand cut off; Yissachar bribes them to cut off his left hand instead.
The king hears of the bribe and orders Yissachar's right hand cut off as well.
Rav Yosef blesses God for removing Yissachar of Kfar Barkai from the High Priesthood.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation: Yissachar did not know the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation: Yissachar did not know the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Yissachar was not learned in the Mishnah, which teaches that lambs precede goats everywhere, but both are equal, implying he should have known not to gesture.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the story by explaining that Yissachar was not learned in the Mishnah, which teaches that lambs precede goats everywhere but both are equal, implying he should have known not to gesture.

items.text: Ravina's objection: He did not even read the verse
items.text_en: Ravina's objection: He did not even read the verse
items.desc_en: Ravina argues that Yissachar did not even read the verse, which says 'if a lamb' and 'if a goat', implying no precedence.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects that Yissachar did not even read the verse, which uses 'if a lamb' and 'if a goat' to show both are equal, so he should not have given precedence to the goat.

items.text: Concluding statement on Torah scholars increasing peace
items.text_en: Concluding statement on Torah scholars increasing peace
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Chanina states that Torah scholars increase peace in the world, as derived from the verse 'And all your children shall be taught of the Lord, and great shall be the peace of your children.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina declares that Torah scholars increase peace in the world, citing the verse 'And all your children shall be taught of the Lord, and great shall be the peace of your children.'
The gemara adds a homiletic reading: do not read 'your children' (בָּנֶיךָ) but 'your builders' (בּוֹנָיִךְ), identifying Torah scholars as the builders of peace.
